summary: The respondent was charged under section 7 read with section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for an offence under section 16 read with Section 16 of that Act. The Food Inspector found that the respondent had adulterated pieces of Kajus and the sample was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kabus. He accordingly convicted the respondent under section 8 read with sections 16(1)(f) and 16(2) of the Act. On appeal, the High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the respondent. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insect fraested or to bring the case within its purview. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was clearly wrong in its inter pretation of section 2(i)(f). [473F] 1.2 The High court was clearly right in its view that the appellant had not established by any cogent evidence that the Lal mirchi powder was adulterated. [473G] 1:3. The High Courts were, therefore, right in their interpretation of Section 2(1) (f). The High courts were wrong in their respective judgments. [474H; 475A] 1 Whether the article of food was unfit for human consumption or not is a question to be decided on its own facts and circumstances. [476B] 1 In the instant case, the appellant has not established that the quantity of Kaju was adulterated because it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid or disguntur animal or Vegetable substance or that on account of presence of the meal worms the sample had been unfit for life. [477C] 2.1 In the present case, there is no evidence to show that the food article was adulterated within the contemplation of section 7 of the . [476D] 2:2 The appellant has failed to establish by any acceptable evidence that he was guilty of an offence punishable under section 3 read with sec. 16 of Act. [478E] 2 2.3 The HighCourt was wrong in holding that the prosecution had not proved by any satisfactory evidence the requirement of section 6(1), proof of 'unfitness of the articles for human food ' is a must for bringing the case under its purview and it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfit or for human life. The appellant had failed to discharge this burden by leading evidence. [479B] 2 3.1 There is no doubt that the High Courts have been wrong in coming to the conclusion of the trial court that the offence under sec. 7 readwith section 16, proof of "unfigus" was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution has failed in establishing by cogent evidence the requirements of section 4(2)(a) of Act and it is not necessary in this case to establish further that it was unfit to human consumption. [481C D] 2 4.2 In the absence of any satisfactory or reliable evidence the appellant cannot be convicted under secs. 16(i) (b). The prosecution had failed in proving by cogent and reliable evidence that Lal mirchy powder was either worm. infested or insect rued or that it consisted of insect florities to the extent of 21% of the quantity not being "filthy, putric, dis gusting", rotten.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3(2) of the order. The High Court dismissed his revision petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1) the appellant was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case cannot be drawn; (2) the presumption under para 3(3) could not be drawn against him; and (3) the High Court erred in holding that the presumption was not drawn. HELD : The High court was right in holding the appellant guilty of the offence under section 4 of the Act. [901 D] The High Courts have to see whether they are genuine or not and whether they have been able to prove that the appellant is an agriculturist. If they are satisfied that the evidence which was led before the Magistrate was sufficient, then the case against him stands unproved because of exemption from cl.3(2). [902 D] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , referred to. The presumption under paragraph 3(1) could be drawn only if there is something intrinsically wrong with that evidence. In the present matter, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, the presumption is not drawn against the appellant.

The appellant was a monthly tenant in respect of certain premises. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the tenancy was determined by a notice to quit, and the defendant continued to be a tenant from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. The trial judge held that the defendant had no permanent right in the land and therefore he could not be evicted. On appeal the High Court confirmed the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the rent was determined under a notice, and (ii) the suit was one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease. HELD : The tenancy of the defendant was one from month and not month under Section 106 Transfer of property Act. [277 D] The word 'lease ' is defined in section 106 of the TP Act, which means a transfer of any interest in land by way of lease or otherwise. It does not include a lease for a period exceeding six months. The word "lease" has been used in the Transfer and it includes a lease from month. [278 D] In the instant case, the rent fixed was Rs. 10,000 per annum and the appellant became a tenant on the expiry of the second annual lease. The suit was therefore one for eviction of a tenant under section 106. [279 E F] The respondent had not acquired any permanent right to the land by prescription or otherwise and that by reason of the payment of rent he became a monthly tenancy under section 107 Transfer of the Property Act, terminable by fifteen days notice.

The appellant assessee, a third party, filed an application under Section 137 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of privilege under Section 138(1)(b) on the ground that the documents, records etc. were not produced by the assessee during the assessment proceedings before him and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privileges under Section 139(1) (b) had no relation to the power of the court to summon the production of documents from the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964 in respect of assessment years 1965 65 onwards and that he was not entitled to make any application to the Commissioner to obtain information thereafter as to the amount of tax determined, as payable by an assessee in respect thereof. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the omission of Section 137 did not make any difference and that it could not be called in question in any court of law. In further appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that after the repeal of Section 138 of the 1961 Act by Act V of 1964 there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summoning the production before an Income tax officer after April I, 1964 relating to assessment years1964 65 onwards, and that since the finality attaching to an earlier order of assessment under section 137 of 1961 Act had not been challenged in any Court of law, the civil court could summon the material on which the order was made. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The finality attached by the Commissioner under Section 136(1), is limited to the cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the section is called for by any person, other than a court of Law by a judicial order. [565C D] 2. The jurisdiction of the courts to summon a material witness in a case pending before them is restricted to the transactions which are entered into by the Income tax authorities prior to April 1. 1964 in regard to assessment proceedings for the said years taking place under the Indian Income Tax Acts, 1961 and 1961. [567D E] 3. The power of a court to call a material witnesses from the IncomeTax Authorities after April l, 1964 is restricted only to cases where information etc., as contemplated in the section was called for on being summoned by it without the approval of the Commis sioner of Income Tax. [568F G] 4. In the instant case, the order of reference made by the Appellate Assistant Commis tions Officer under Section 143(1 ) (b), 1961 is not a final and cannot be called into question in a court.

The appellant was the father of a minor. He made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinaba and he accepted the gift on behalf of Seinabai. The gift was by a registered deed. Seinavi died in 1947 without leaving an issue. Seinsaba died in 1948. On the death of Seinsai, the appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the gift was invalid and not binding on Seinbai. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the gift by the husband to his minor daughter was valid; (ii) the appellant had no legal guardian of her property in existence, and (iii) the gifts were made by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammotty to his mother. HELD : (1) The gift is complete under Muhammadan Law and it seems impossible to hold that by handing over the deed to Seinsi, the donee had been sent from her father 's house to his wife. [550 E] (2) The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's mother when the gift is from the husband or his executor or by the grand father or his attorney or by a guardian or not is irrelevant for the purpose of determining the question whether the donee has been handed over to the minor. [552 F G] (3) The fact that the appellant was given a gift to Seineaba and as the gift in the present case was by the registered deed no question in this behalf can arise. Possession was not delivered to Seinesi but to her mother, the first appellant.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for better administration of Hindu religious institutions and endowments in the State. Section 76(1) provides that every religious institution shall from the income derived by it, pay to the Commissioner annually such contribution not exceeding five per centum of its income as may be prescribed. The Commissioner has to determine the fee for audit of accounts of each religious institution separately and prescribing the method for determining contribution. The appellant was a religious institution. It had applied for restraining the State from enforcing any of the provisions of the Act. The High Court held that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and therefore the demand for payment of contribution was not justified. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Commissioner had not determined the fee in accordance with section 76(2), and (ii) that no rule had been made under section 101(1). HELD: The High court was right in holding that the Commissioner has not determined any audit fee. [920 B] The Commissioner may not under section 76 (2) impose a flat rate of audit fee on the religious institutions governed by the provisions Of the Act, and he has to decide whether the audit fee is payable or not. [ 921 C D] H. The Act does not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution is to be levied.

The appellant, a contemner in the High Court, filed an application under section 19(1) of the for setting aside the order dated 2nd April 1975 passed by the High court directing the issue of notice to show cause against him. The High Court directed the issue to the appellant and directed the issuance of notice. In appeal to this Court it was contended that no appeal lies to this court under section19(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide any question. This Court cannot be asked in such an appeal to decide whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt of the High Courts or not. [512C] 2. The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Curt affecting the right of the party aggrieved. Such an order is not appealable under section 20. In a given case special leave may be granted under article 136 of the Constitution from an order initiating the proceedings. But there are no observations by this Court or on the facts of that case there can be any, to show that an appeal would lie to this Hon 'ble Court under section 18. [511D E] 3. The proceeding is initiated under section 17 by issuance of a notice. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal against the order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner asking the High Tribunal to drop the proceeding. It is neither possible nor advisable to make an exhaustive list of the typo of orders which may be appealable under Section 19. [506E F] 4. The matter has to be decided either finally or, may be, even at an earlier stage an order rejecting prayer for bearing the case piecemeal. What has been decided in this case is that on a reference made by the Advocate General if the Court declines to take cognisance and to initiate proceeding for contempt, the order is no order initiating contempt proceedings. [504E F; 506F] 5. The appeal filed under section 16 of the Act does not lie and is incompetent. It may be an appeal under section 38. But it is not an appealable under s 19. But if the alleged contemnor in response to the notice appears before the Court and asked it to drop, the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section20 of the .

The appellant was prosecuted for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment, and the appellant was convicted under section 6(1 A) of the Act for possessing the wireless transmitters in contravention thereof. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) section 6 (1 A), as amended by the 1952 Act, was repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1952, and (ii) if section 6A was not on the statute book at the time of the alleged commission of the offence, not only the sentence but also the conviction thereunder would be bad. HELD : (i)(a) The amendment made in the 1952 Acts was retrospective in operation and did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the Act. [455 B] (b) Section 6( 1 A) is designed to provide for a different situation, namely, the repeal of an earlier Act which has been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later Act. The section does not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. It only prohibits the possession thereof. The intention of the legislature in passing the said Act was to expurgate section 6 of the 1952 act and it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. [557 B C] (c) Section 4 of the Amending Act of 1949, which is designed for providing a different situations, namely the repeal or modification of an already existing law, does not affect continuance of any such amendment made under the earlier Act. It does not prevent the possession and use of the wireless apparatus in contravention with the provisions contained in section 3. [506 C D] (d) The intention to expugn the said provision is to expel a person from his own property and not to bring it within the mischief of section 6. [504 E F] (ii)(a). The words "in any other case" in section 6, are comprehensive enough to take in a wireless transmittedter. The language of an enactment does not restrict its operation to cases where an earlier amending Act is repealed by a later statute. [ 506 B C]. (b). The intention was that the intention of legislature in passed the said act was to repeal the earlier law and not the previous law.

The appellant was the owner of certain properties in the State of West Bengal. The properties were sold and they were put to auction for the purpose of sale. The appellant 's bid was accepted by the court and the sale was confirmed on the same day. On the passing of the decree, the appellant filed a suit against the judgment debtors for restoration of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that the appellant had no right to claim restoration of those properties. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) in a proceeding under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decreeholders on record were in fact benamidars for another person; (ii) even if Aghore was proved to have advanced the money upon which the Chakrabortys obtained the decrees, in reopening the decrees and in working out the rights of the parties in accordance with the provisions of the Act, namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Indian Contract Act, the court could treat the decree holder as the purchaser of these properties within the meaning of that section; (iii) even assuming that Aghor was proved not to have any right which could be protected under clause (c), the court cannot go behind a decree and start an enquiry into the question as to who were in actual possession of the property when the decree was reopened. Held, further, that the High Courts had erred in holding that in a proceedings under section 37 of the Bihar Money Lender Act it is open to them to go beyond the decree. The court cannot enter into the questions as to what would be the effect of the order passed by the courts below on the basis of the evidence adduced before them and decide whether the judgment debtor was in fact a benamidar for another persons in respect of the execution of the decrees.

The appellant was the owner of a property in which he had an interest. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract against the appellant on the ground that the appellant had not executed the decree and that the respondent had no right to execute it as a transferee. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the transfer was not made by the respondent in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "decree holder" must be construed as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that is, where there was no decree in existence at the time of the assignment, such an agreement could not be enforced by a suit. [705 D] (ii) The word "decree" in Order XXI Rule 16 means a decree or order passed after the date of the document. It does not mean a decree which is transferred before the transfer takes place. The words 'decree holder ' must be interpreted as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including any party who, in equity, may subsequently become entitled by assignment in writing or by operation of law. [805 D E] (iii) The expression "decreeholder" in section 146(1)(2) means a person who has an interest in the decree after it is passed. It is not necessary that the words "judgment holder" should be interpreted in such a way as to include a party whose interest is affected by the provisions of Order 21, rule 17(1). [806 D E; 807 F] (iv) The language of Order XX Rule 16(old section 232) cannot be construed so as to apply to a case where there is no decree or an agreement to transfer a decree. [820 G H] (v) The provisions of the Order XXI rule 16(new section 232 of the Civil Procedure Code are intended to give effect to the intention of the legislature and not to affect the effect of the provisions contained in Order XX, Rule 16. [821 D E].

The respondent was a manufacturer of steel doors, windows and other goods. The respondent submitted an invitation by the Executive Engineer to fit out the windows and the door leaves in a specified building. The Executive Engineer found that the windows were not properly constructed and that the doors and windows were in a condition attached to the windows. The appellant issued a notice to the respondent calling upon him to show cause why he should not be prosecuted under section 7 of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954 for failure to comply with the provisions of the Act. The notice was replied by the respondent. The Deputy Commissioner Excise & Taxation in appeal held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted: one for providing doors and window and the other for "fixing" those doors and doors in a certain building and that it was not a contract for sale of windows and for rendering service in connection with the fixing of those windows. He therefore held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had no right to claim the amount agreed to be paid to him. The High Court, however, held that there was no evidence on record to show that the respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling window and door leaves and sashes etc. and entered into a contract with the Executive Engineers for "sale of windows" and to promote sale of its manufactured goods undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that service, and therefore the contract did not attract section 7(1)(a) of the Sales Tax. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The contract was a works contract and not a sale of glass or for rendering services in connection therewith. [505 H] (ii) The contracts were for work, labour and service and were not rendered under a separate contract. The contract may be for work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials used in the execution of the works for a price; it may be a contract of work in which the use of materials is 'accessory or incidental to the execution thereof. [506 B C] (iii) The question whether the contract is one of service in the executing of which property in the goods passes under the terms of the contract, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case, the specifications of the windows are set out in the contract. There was no agreement to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows as a chattel to the buyer. The service is not rendered by the manufacturer the contract must be deemed one for sale and not of service. [504 C D] (iv) The test in each case is whether the object of the party sought to be taxed is that the chattel as chattel passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection With the installation are under a different contract or are incidental to it. If the windows have become a part of the building construction that the property in them passes to another party and, therefore, the services render customarily or generally as incidental to its execution. [405 D E] (v) The tests in each cases are whether the objects of the parties sought to taxed are that the goods passed to the person who supplies window leaves. If they were not so, the property was to pass to the War Office under the head contract. [500 C D].

The appellant was charged with the offence of cheating under section 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. The prosecution case was that on November 8, 1967 Shankerlal had entered into a contract with the appellant for sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The appellant agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates at the rate of Rs. 38/ per piece. Formal order, it was then agreed that the goods would be supplied on the following day. Ram Avtar was also told that this transaction would fetch him a profit of Rs 3200/ . On November 16, 1967 Shankar Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to the shop of Ram Avtar with the said goods. The complainant agreed to the proposal and wanted to see the seller of the foreign goods in question. On November 15, 1967, Shankerlal handed over the formal order to Ram Avtar who was also informed that this deal would fetch Rs. 3200 per piece and that the price of the goods washer plate. The accused were thereafter discharged from the charge under section 120 B I. P.C., read with Section 120B Indian Penal code. The trial court acquitted the appellant on the ground that he had not been convicted by the Magistrate. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of acquittal and convicted him. In this appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant State that there is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High court as the prosecution has failed to prove the case against him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwalla respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report. [280E] 2. The evidence led by the prosecution is not sufficient to establish that Raj Kr. Agawalla was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. It is clear from the evidence that the part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought him and asked him to see him. That circumstance, as pointed out by the High Courts, would hardly warrant an inference that Rajta respondent too was a member of conspiracy to cheat or cheating Ram Avtar, [280G H] 3. The fact that the appellant was not a party in any conspiracy is not enough to establish his case. [281A B] 4. The finding of the trial court as regards the charge framed against him is set aside and he acquitted.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of Kerala, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of motor vehicles. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country were owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional obligation by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The respondents contended that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and had pointed out that the accident of June 6, 1981 on a river bridge in Bihar State was attributable to this factor only. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. It is true that the petitioner has maintained that he has been carrying on his business as a carrier of motor vehicle. But it does not fall for consideration here if a monopoly based public utility should ever be a commercial venture geared to support the general revenue of the state but there is not an iota of hesitation in this regard in our view. [329B] 2. The quality of the service should improve. It may be under the obligation of the Union of India and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this Country. It was necessary that this is worked out also in the Railways and as quickly as possible classification conforming to this is introduced. [330C D] 3. It has been pointed out by the respondents that they have denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to improve this great public utility. The fact that the respondents have denied certain allegations of the petitioners, yet nothing has been stated in the counter affidavit and it does appear that there is no iota of doubt that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. [ 330C D; 331D] 4. It would be wrong to say that the public utility has, as a result of the decision taken by the Government and its agencies would fall within the scope of Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The petitioners have maintained that they are problems of law and order and have pointed out this to the stand taken in the writ petitions. [332D] 5. It will be wrong for the Court to consider whether a monopoly is based on any monopoly based or declared by law which is not to be needlessly or vexatiously exacted but which, in my humble judgment, is necessary at once for the interests of the public and for the protection of the Public. [333E] 6. It cannot be said that the private undertakings are owned by Central Government or on account thereof, no dispute had been generally taken to the stands taken in this case. The State Government has limitations, both of resources and capacity, yet we hope that the Government, the Administration would rise to the necessity of the occasion and take it as a challenge to improve these great public utilities in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. giving directions in a matter like this where availability of resources have a material bearing, policy regarding priorities is involved, expertise is very much in issue, is not prudent and we do not, therefore, propose to issue directions. [328H; 331A] 7. It appears that Government have limitations both of resource and capacity. But the quality of service should develop in this area. The nature of the services should improve and the conditions of service which would be equal to operational expenses, interest on investment, depreciation and payment of public obligations if any. [33D] 8. It must also be borne in mind that it is not a commercial enterprise geared by the Union Government or its instrumentalities. It does not come within the purview of Article 14 of the constitution. The Court has to consider the question whether a State has a monopoly or not.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in Bombay. The lands were acquired by the State Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for the purpose of development of the land. The appellants filed applications before the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal under section 14(1) of the Act for restoration of their lands to the respondent. The Tribunal dismissed them on the ground that they had not been served with a notice of the date of hearing of the appeals and hence the applications were barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the applications holding that the applications for restoration were barred under section 15(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in dismissing the applications of the appellants on merits. [143 G] (ii) The order of the Gujarat revenue Tribunal dismissing appeals was passed by the High Court as final and conclusive and not to be questioned in any suit or proceeding in any court. [144 C] (iii) The expression "decide it on merits" is used in section 17(1)(a) of Act 21 of 1894, which states that "no order shall be made under section 13 unless the State Govt. has given notice to the parties concerned and an opportunity of being heard before such decision is taken". [144 D] (iv) The word 'decide ' in section 15 of the Jagirs Abolition Act makes a decision of the Tribunal in appeal as final, and not merely a decision on merits but also a decision by the appellate authority.

The appellant 's father was the Mahant of a temple in which he had been worshipped for more than three years. The respondent, who was the manager of the temple, filed a suit against the appellant and his brother for a declaration that the temple belonged to him as early as 1857 by virtue of the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the dedication of the village Telibandha had not been proved; but the High Court agreed with the Trial Court on the question whether the dedication was proper or not. Held, that the High court was right in holding that it was not open to the appellant to take the indication of the words "from the profits and income" as out weighing or neutralising the numerous other provisions which point to an intention that Ramsaran Lal would not have the absolute ownership of the Village. The fact that Ram Saran Lal used to credit the income from Telirice to the Gharu Khata which was maintained for the general expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication. The High Court had no jurisdiction to take this view. The mere fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity. The document (the Panch Faisala Award of 1896) clearly and unambiguously shows an intention to prove the words 'from the profit and income ' as out weigh or neutralizing the several other provisions of section 4(1)(c) of the Act.

The appellants were the President of the Uttar Pradesh Bar Association and Chairman, Action Committee of the Avadh Bar Association. The High Court discharged them notices. The appellants filed a writ petition in the Allahabad High Court challenging the validity of the resolution dated April 22, 1973 passed by the Uttar Prades tive Bar Association, which was passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 2. The contention of the appellants was that they were not guilty of contempt of court and that the resolution was not in accordance with the provisions of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. The writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court on the ground that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as MP No. 1 was actively associated with passing of the Resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of contumacious conduct and the High court had discharged them. The Division Bench held that the appellants were guilty of criminal contempt. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High Courts order discharging the notices was not a proper and valid one. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts orders are set aside. [606B] 1.2 The High court was right in discharging the noticees. [707C] 1:3. The language used by them was unfortunate. The words "indiscreet" were not proper and it should have been passed in that manner. It should not have been passing in that way. It must have been done in a very partisan manner under the influence of Allahabad Bar Association which is a matter of regret. [613D] 1 4. The contempt proceedings are not maintainable against the appellants. They cannot be said to have committed contempt of Court. [507E] 2.1 In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the foregoing observations. [625H] 2:2. The question whether the Chairman or the Chairman was actively associate ated with passing the resolution which contained admonition about the chief Justice and if he also issuing that resolution to the appellants, is a question of fact. It is true that the Court referred to the contumacious acts of the appellant but the High Cour t did not wish to proceed against the respondents. The judgment of the Single Judge was therefore set aside and the appeals were disposed of in terms of the directions given by the Division Bench. [600H] 3.1.

The appellants filed an application before the Sub Registrar for return of the award to the arbitrators on the ground that they had not been served with the notice of the arbitration proceedings. The Sub Registrar refused to give them a copy of the order of the Court and did not direct the arbitrators to keep the award in the custody of the court. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order and directed return of award to them. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order made by the Sub Judge directing the arbitrators not to keep a particular award in their custody was wrong and without jurisdiction as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order made on 28th of January 1978 is set aside. [691C] 2.1 The Sub Judge has no power to compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform and an act of the High Courts shall prejudice no man would apply with full vigour in the facts of this case and if that is the position then the award as we have noted before was presented before the sub Registrar, from 28th January 1978 to 24th November, 1983. [613D] 2(a) The Sub Court has power to order return of an award for presentation to the court on the date specified in the order. It is not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A the decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M.V. V.S.Sundaram vs M/s. P.K. Velayudhan & Ors., [1985] Supp. 2 SCR 823, referred to. (b) The order passed by the sub Judge directing maintenance of status quo and 20th December, 1982 was not a valid order. [591C D] 3(a).

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent gave notice to the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for eviction of the appellant on the ground of nonpayment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent on the grounds (i) that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises; (ii) that the tenant had not sub let, and (iii) that he had waived his right to sublet the premises. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the tenancy by the letter of June 7, 1948, was a new tenancy and not a continuation of the old and that the sub tenants were tenants of the landlord and not licensees of the respondents and in this view the respondent could not evict them under section 14(1) (e) Of the Act. The High Court also held that the appellant had waived the right of statutory rights conferred by the Act and that there was no violation of the provisions of the Act which prevented it from doing so. Held, that the High court was in error in holding that section 13 (1)(a) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates Regulation Act, 1949, was not a new enactment and could not be said to have been enacted merely for the protection of private rights of the landlords. The right of the sub tenant to sue for ejectment on the basis of the notice given by him under section 12(1), (e), (f) and (g) of section 13, was an additional remedy which could be availed of by a landlord in case of non payment of rent. The suit for eviction was not brought within the provisions Of section 14 (1) of Act.

The respondent Board was constituted under the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Act, 1956. The Board was entrusted with the task of conducting examinations and dealing with the use of unfair means at final examination conducted by the Board. The respondent Board had to conduct the examinations in accordance with the directions given in its order dated January 30, 1991. The procedure for conducting the examinations was laid down in the Regulations framed under the Act. The Regulations were made in exercise of powers conferred on the Board under section 3(1) of the Act and the Regulations were framed by the State Government under section 4 of the said Act. In exercise of its power under section 5A of the Regulation, the Board issued a notification dated January 31, 1991 appointing the respondent as an Assistant Engineer for conducting examinations in the subject of final examination including fabrication of documents issued by the respondent Board. On December 12, 1990, the respondent was appointed as an Executive Engineer with effect from February 1, 1992. The appointment order was published on March 29, 1993 and the respondent had been appointed as a temporary Executive Engineer on May 27, 1993. The appellant Board challenged the validity of the aforesaid notification before the High Court by way of writ petitions under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Regulations and the Resolutions were not binding on the State Board as they were framed in exercise or purported exercise of the powers conferred upon it under Article 226 of Constitution, by the High Courts. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Regulations and Resolutions are made in furtherance of the constitutional scheme of the State Legislature. They are not binding upon the Board as a statutory authority. [799C] 1.2 The Regulations have been framed under section 6 of the Maharashtra Electricity Distribution Co operative Act, 1949. The regulations and the resolutions are made by the Executive Committee, etc., to be in conformity with the provisions of the law or in violation of the principles of natural justice. [899D E] 1:3 The Regulations are not inconsistent with the statutory provisions of law or the rules framed thereunder. They have been made in pursuance of the directions issued by this Court in its judgment dated January 29, 1991 in Maharashtra State Board vs Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation, ; , and the regulations are not consistent with the principles laid down by this court in its decision dated January 20, 1991, in Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation Ltd. vs The Workmen & Ors., [1986] 2 SCR 899. [999F G] 1 Whether the Regulations or the Resolutions are binding on both the parties is a question of fact and not an issue which can be decided by this Tribunal. [789G H; 792A] 1(a) The regulations have been enacted in exercise thereof, and the Board has also framed regulations for the purpose of carrying out its functions under the provisions. [779C D] (b) The Regulations or Resolutions are not statutory rules and they are not enforceable by any court. They do not create any statutory authority or statutory body. They cannot be said to have been passed in exercise o the executive power conferred on them under Article 162 of the constitution, by virtue of the provisions contained in the Act or in contravention of the statutory provision. [780D E; 793A] (c) The Board has not made any law authorising the State Electricity Board to carry out its duties and functions under section 12A of that Act. It is only a statutory body which can exercise its powers under the statute. [781E F] (d) The Regulation and the Resolution are made without prejudice to their contention and directed the Board to allow all the candidates referred to in the Notification of August 31, 1990 to appear at the S.S.C. examination to be conducted in March, 1991 by the board.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that the appellants had demanded and accepted illegal gratification from Madan Lal and that they had been falsely implicated in the case. The trial court acquitted them but convicted them under section 6(1)(d) read with section 7(1) (d) of Prevention of corruption Act, and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by the appellants the High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the intention of the Legislature was to create by means of clause (d), an offence different from a single act of bribery and that the object of the Act was to bring about a complete and comprehensive investigation into the case, that the offence as defined in clause (c) did not come within the meaning of bribery. HELD : The intention of Parliament was to confer on the accused persons the benefit of the presumption under section 20(1). But to go further and contend that the act as defined by clause (e) does not come with in the meaning Of bribery is to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. Under the Act as it stood before it was amended by Act XVII of 1955, every railway servant was deemed to be a public servant only for the purposes of Chapter IX of the Penal Code and it was provided by sub section (2) that notwithstanding anything in section 21 of the I.P.C., a railway servant shall not be deemed to have been a public Servant for any of the purposes mentioned in section 161 of the Code unless he habitually accepts or obtains or agrees to accept or attempts to obtain from any person for himself or for any other person any valuable thing without consideration or for a consideration which he knows to be inadequate. The definition of "public servant" is wide enough to include a public officer as defined under section 21 and under sub section 2(c) it is made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. [188 D E] In the present case, the offence was not committed by the appellant in his capacity as a public servants but was only a munim of a firm and not a partner or proprietor as the other appellants and that therefore the offence under section 4(2)(d), read with s.7(1), (d). [188 E F] The definition given to the expression "public Servant" in section 5 of the , is wide and includes a person who is alleged to have committed an offence under the Act. Therefore, the appellant was not only a member of a partnership firm but also a partner of a company. [189 G H] In re: The King Emperor, (1934) L.R. 58 I.A. 65, referred to.

The appellant, a Bank, was the guarantor of a loan advanced by the respondent Bank to the respondent bank. The respondent bank issued a letter dated September 16, 1957, stating that the security offered by the appellant was one of the pledge of goods given by the principal debtor in favour of the Bank and endorsed in favour the Bank. The Bank refused to accept the said offer on the ground that the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledged goods given to the Bank, and the Bank had not exercised such care as a prudent man would in the circumstances of the case, which resulted in loss of security. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368 04 P. from the legal representative of the respondent. The trial court found that there was negligence on the part of the surety and decreed the suit. On appeal by the Bank the High Court held that the two promissory notes were offered by one creditor in favour and the surety was discharged to the extent of the value of security and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the surety could not be discharged from his liability under the guarantee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of clause 5 of letter of guarantee Ext. 31 dated September 17, 1957 the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal creditor pledging oil tins as and by way of security for the advance and, therefore, two securities were offered, namely, pledge of good faith and the guarantor was discharged from the liability undertaken under the letter of Guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on the clear understanding that the principal debt was offered by way Of security for advance and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of them with the security. [83G] 2.1 In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the sureties gave personal guarantee in respect of the security given by him, if the creditor lost or without the consent of the sureties parts with the surety, the sureties is discharged to a extent of his security lost as provided by section 141. [84E] 2(a) The surety has agreed to give personal guarantee for the loan and therefore, he is discharged from liability undertaken by the creditor Bank. In any event if the debt was not found proved that security of pledged goods was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor bank, yet the surety would not be able to discharge the obligation undertaken under this letter of undertaking. [85F] 2 (b) The guarantee given by a surety is one of a pledge of property and is not a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee. [86G] 3(a).

The appellant was the owner of certain lands in the possession of respondent No. 1, and the respondent No 1 had no right to resume them. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to hold the "patelki inam" lands as his remuneration for services rendered by him from the Rokade family. The Government held that the appellant was not entitled to any share in the emoluments of office. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 applied. [768 B] (ii) The appellant could not claim as of right that he had a share in them. He could not therefore be allowed to retain his hereditary rights in the lands. [868 C D] (iii) The respondent No 2 was entitled as of rights to a share of the emoluments. The grant is not a service grant, and no question of title by adverse possession arises against Government, even though the land was shown as excluded from the jagir. [668 G H] (iv) The grants were made by way of remuneration or emoluments for the services rendered to be rendered by the respondent. There was nothing in them on the basis of which the appellant could claim as a matter of right any share therein. [688 B C] (v) The High Courts have consistently held that there is no distinction between a grant and a service grants. In the present case, the grant was not a Service grant but a service Grant. [689 E F] (vi) The Government had no power to resume the lands in accordance with the provisions contained in the Peshatels Act, 1900.

The appellant was a Cutchi Memons. The respondent, who was the Cutchi memon, was the cutchi Memon, and his father was the Match Memons, and the Cutche Memons were settled in Madras. On the death of his father, the appellant filed a suit for partition of his properties and for possession of the same. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had no right to the property as he had settled down first in Madras and then in Bangalore. In appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any share in the property and dismissed the suit. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a Hindu Law of inheritance would apply to Cutchi Memorandum of Settlement governed matters of succession and inheritance is a matter of law which cannot be said with certainty. [233 B] (ii) The Act came into force as from November 1, provided that all Cutchi Merits, including the Khojas and the Memons would in matters of property, inheritance and succession, include rules as to joint family property, the right of a son therein by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship. [234 C] (iii) The definition of "family" in section 3(1)(d) of the Act is wide enough to cover all classes of persons governed by Hindu law including Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs, Christians, Christians and Christians. [235 D E] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that as there was only one solitary decision of the High court which limited the application of Hindu Law to matters of inheritance and inheritance, the Bombay view was the correct one. [236 F G] (v) The word "family", in section Haji Aboo Bucker Sait vs Ebrahim Hajee Aboo Ducker, A.I.R. , referred to.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics. They manufacture fabrics in different types. The process of weaving the fabrics is carried on by them at an intermediate stage. The appellants were manufacturing fabrics in their own factory and subjected to the integrated process of spinning, weaving and weaving of fabrics, and were paying excise duty on the same. The appellant No. 1, a manufacturer of fabrics in the State of Delhi, was manufacturing fabrics of different types, which were manufactured by them in the same premises. The goods manufactured at an intermediary stage were sold to the appellants at an inter state sale price. The factory was situated at a place where the appellants were engaged in the manufacture of fabrics and were also selling their products at an Inter State sales tax. The Central Excise authorities issued show cause notices to the appellant No 1, for recovery of excise duty, on the ground that the goods manufactured by the appellants had been sold at an independent stage in the factory of the appellants and subjected not only to the inter state sales tax but also to the composite process of manufacture of the fabrics. The notice was rejected by the Assistant Collector. The appeal filed by the appellant Nos. 1 and 2 before the Appellate Collector was dismissed. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "place of removal" in section 3(1) of the Act means a factory or any other place or premises of production or manufacture of goods which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf whether for consumption, export or manufacture or any premises appurtenant thereto. It was further submitted that the word "place" in the definition of "placeof removal" has been used in the context of section 3 (1) and therefore, the expression 'place of manufacture ' has to be construed as a place of removal. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The words "place or premises appurtenant to such place" have been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force. [710C] 2.1 The definition of 'placeof manufacture ' in section 2(f) of Central Excise Act is not exhaustive and that is why it has been given prospective effect by virtue of section S l of the Finance Act, 1982. [811D] 2(a) The expression " place of manufacture" has to mean a factory where the excisable goods are manufactured or cured or if such goods are used in any other manner than for consumption or use in the production of another commodity. It is not necessary that the words 'place or premise appurtenant thereto ' should be given retrospective operation so as to give effect to the provisions of section 11 of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. [911D E] 2 (b) The definition has been interpreted by this Court in the case of M/s. Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Collector of Central excise, ; and Commissioner of Sales Tax vs M/S. Hindustan Zinc Ltd., ; , referred to. 2(c) The word 'place ' has been defined in section 4(1)(b) of Finance Act 1982 as a factory within the meaning of Section 3(2) of that Act. It has been held by this court in the aforesaid case that if a commodity is taken outside the factory it will be removed and when the excisable article is removed from one plant to another it will not be a case of removal for the purpose of payment of excise duties. [1012D E; 1013E] 2.(d) The words ' place of manufacturing ' have been used with reference to the place where goods are produced, cured or manufactured and therefore they cannot be made of the place of manufacturer or production of the excisable articles. In other words, if a particular commodity is brought outside the premises it will fall within the definition.

The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for staying the hearing of the suit till disposal of a special leave petition. The Civil Judge rejected the application on the ground that it did not disclose any cause of action. The petitioner then moved the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the revision petition holding that the jurisdiction of the civil court in such matters was impliedly barred. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an injunction restraining the hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The procedure laid down for preparation of the scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D of the Act. Section 68 D provides that where any State Transport Undertaking is of opinion that for the purpose of providing an efficient, adequate, economical and properly co ordinated road transport service it is necessary in the public interest that road transport services in general or any particular class of such service in relation to any area or route or portion thereof should be run and operated by the State Transport undertaking whether to the exclusion, complete or partial of other persons or other vise, the State Road Transport Services may prepare a scheme giving particulars of the nature of the service proposed to be rendered, the area or routes proposed tobe covered and such other particulars respecting thereto as may be prescribed. [545B C] 2. The provisions of section 68 D are applicable only in cases where there is no dispute about the merits of a scheme or the desirability of bringing it within the purview of section68 D of Act. The jurisdiction of State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 68D) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil Court to issue an order of injunction restraining, the hearing authority from proceeding further with the trial of the case and exercising its statutory functions. [546C E] 3. Section68 D provides for the particulars relating to the manner in which objections or representations can be filed under section68D(i) and the procedure to be followed at the hearing. The rules also provide for the details to be incorporated in the scheme published under section 69 C of the . [546E F] 4. In view of the provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the , it is clear that on the publication of the Scheme under section 70 C of Act any person who is aggrieved by the proposed introduction of the schemes is entitled to file his representations and objections and to appear before the Hearing Authority, under section 63 D of . [547F G] 5.

The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that on August 29, 1963 at about 9.30 or 10 P.m., the appellant went to the house of his sister 's husband, Nathaniel and his wife to make arrangement for bringing up a child. At about 9 p.m. the appellant asked the girl to come to the place of her sister 'S ' and told him that she would pay him Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 161, Indian Penal code. The appellant was asked to make arrangements for bringing the child with him. On August 29th, 1963 the appellant made an application to the police station for permission to take the child. The police officer refused to permit the appellant to take her. The Police Inspector took the girl and sent a letter to the Magistrate stating that she had no child of his own and wanted to adopt a child and asked him to pay something to him. The Magistrate accepted the request and directed the appellant "to make arrangement" for bringing her to the hospital. On appeal by the appellant, the Sessions Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 420 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ or in case of default to pay the amount of fine. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment. On the question whether the appellant could be prosecuted under section 120B I. P.C., HELD : (i) The order of sanction in the present case satisfies the requirements of section 6 of the Act. [184 E] (ii) The High court was not right in holding that the appellant had grossly abused his position as a police officer and extorted money from Russel Nathanite and his marriage with the girl child. [185 G] (iii) The appellant, therefore, did not commit any offence under section 6(1)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act. He could not be prosecuted either Miss Eylene or RusselNathaniel or anybody else for any offence and obtain money by the accused for refraining from any such imaginary prosecution cannot be said to be an offence under the Indian Penal.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but on appeal by special leave, Held (per Sinha, C. J., Sarkar and Das Gupta JJ.) that the sanction accorded by the Magistrate was not a valid sanction. The sanction was not invalid because it did not give him the necessary material upon which he decided to proceed in a court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The order granting the certificate was not one passed by the High Court and therefore could not be challenged in this Court. The appellant had, in fact, applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice he should be prosecuted. The power conferred on him under section 6(c) of Act II of 1947, did not confer any right upon him to claim a certificate under section 4(2). The sanction given by the magistrate was not valid as it had been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation and therefore the order granting a certificate was invalid. The case of Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1924) L.R. 60 I.A. 206, relied on. The fact that the appellant did not call for any record in connection with the matter from his office does not make him a competent authority to grant the certificate. The procedure prescribed by section 6 of the Act was not followed and therefore it could not have been contended that the order sanctioning the certificate had been passed without jurisdiction. The provisions of section 6 were not applicable to the case as the sanction was given in respect of an offence under section 3 of the , and the sanction granted by the Chief Commercial Superintendent, Eastern Railway, Calcutta, had not been a valid one. The question whether or not there was a proper sanction for the prosecution of the appellant was a question serious enough to justify the grant of a certificate.

The appellant was the owner of a house in which his son and son were living. The landlord filed an eviction petition against the tenant on the ground that he had no right to evict the tenants under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The appellate authority allowed the appeal holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction of the respondents from the premises in question on the grounds of demolition and reconstruction. In revision, the High Court set aside the orders of the appellate authority and restored the order of eviction. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own motion or on behalf of another or on its behalf and who would so receive the rents or be entitled to get the rent, if the building were let to a tenant". The expression "landlord" in section 2 (6) means a person who has been receiving or was entitled to received the rent from the tenants. [275E F] 2.1 A landlord who holds a life interest in the premises and who admittedly has been on his behalf living at that time shall enjoy the property subject to identical charges as absolute owners, with right of sale, gift etc. from the tenant. The word "landlord ' is defined in section 3(6). It means a landlord who has received rents of the premises from the landlords. [276F] 2(a) A person who holds an estate in the property and who also holds an interest therein cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se, be not bona fide. [277B] 3.2 The expression 'landlord ' has been defined under Section 2(7) of Madras Buildings Lease and Rent control Act, 1959. It is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. Thus a controversy that may arise between a landlord and others who are not his tenants under the Act, is outside the ken of this Act. [278F G] 3(a). The expression tenant ' includes a person whose interest in any premises is affected by the eviction of tenants under this Act; but subject to the provisions of section 12 and 13, on an application made by a landlord the Controller shall, if he is satisfied (b) that the building is bona fide required by the landlord for the immediate purpose of demolishing it and such demolition is to be made for the purpose of erecting a new building on the site of the building sought to be demolished, pass an order directing the tenant to deliver possession of the property to the landlord before a specified date. [279F G; 280A] 3 (b).

The respondent decree holder filed a suit against the appellant decree holder for possession of the land in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the trees were not part of the grove and that they were not entitled to any right, but only a compensation for the trees. The first appellate court dismissed the appeal. In second appeal, the High Court held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the Act read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that after the vesting of the estate, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these remain with the intermediary and that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section6(h) of U. P. Zamindari abolition and Land Reform Act, 1951. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The position taken by the executing court, while passing the decree in execution proceedings in respect of any part of bhumidhari right, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by it that there is a distinction between trees and a grove and grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench). [804C D] 2. The principle laid down by this Court in the case of Ram Nath vs State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , applied.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction of all the accused under Section 326/149 IPC, but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) no offence under Section 304 Part I or 149 IPC could be made out against them; (ii) there was no evidence to show that they were guilty of an offence punishable under Section 324/149 and sentenced them to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of one year each, and (iii) there is no evidence on record to show the complicity of the first appellant with the other accused. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly convicted the appellants for an offence under section 326/ 149 IPC. [89B] 1.2 In the instant case, none of the injuries allegedly caused by the appellant were on any vital part of the body, though some of the injury caused by blunt weapons was grievous in nature. There is no material to show as to how the injuries inflicted by the first Appellant with the chopper were inflicted. The injuries attributed to him were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the deceased. [90E] 1:3 In the present case, all the six accused persons were charge sheeted for an offences under Section 325/149 I.P.C. and sentenced each of them to undergo rigorous imprisonment of one month each.

The assessee, a resident of India, was assessed to income tax on cash basis for the assessment year 1967 68 and 1968 69. The Income Tax Officer included the amount of Rs. 1,970,71,960/ in the books of the Indian Company as the receipt of royalty. The assessee 's appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner failed. The Tribunal held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash consideration for 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1969 70 and not on cash payment. In reference to the High Court under Section 256(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the High court answered the question in favour of the assessee. Hence this appeal by the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the amount was not liable to be assessed as it would be received in England and not in India. [105B] 2.1 In the instant case, the assessee did not say that the method of accounting regularly adopted by it for all its income was on cash receipt basis. His contention was that the mere entry in the account books of Indian Company does not amount to receipt of income by the assessee and is accordingly taxable. [106C] 2(a) The assessee could be said to have received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U.K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own Books at Coventry. [107D] (b) In the circumstances of the case, it must be held that in the circumstances, the method adopted by the appellant for all the income was really irrelevant. [108E F] 2.(a) It is not necessary to express any opinion on the question whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between section 5(2)(b) and section 145 of the Act nor is it necessary to give an opinion on that question. The question whether the royalty should be taxed at all as it was not actually received, but the assessee firm was a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a) cannot apply. [109F G] 2 (b). In the present case, there is no conflict or contradiction between section 6(2), 7(1)(a) and 7(2). The assessee did neither say that it maintained its accounts on cash income nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books of account. [110G H] 2 Case law referred to.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the evidence of the approver had been corroborated in material particulars and qua each accused; (ii) the statement of the co accused was not corroborated in materials particulars and as such could not be relied upon by the trial court without corroboration in material details. HELD : (1) The High Courts were right in holding that the conviction of the first accused on the testimony of the accomplice cannot be sustained, [834 B] (2) The evidence of an approver is admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act and it can be safely relied upon to connect the appellant with the murder. It cannot be doubted that under section a conviction based merely on uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice may not be illegal, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Martin B in Res. vs Boyes (1), as follows : "Their Lordships are unable to agree with the view of the High Court that a conviction founded merely on the uncor morroborated evidence of a co accused is admissible in law, because the courts have no power to convict upon his testimony alone." [835 C D] (3) The statement of an accused person is not substantive evidence and cannot be relied on for the purpose of corroboration. It can be used only in exceptional circumstances and in exceptional cases where it is necessary to do so. In the present case, there was no independent corroboration of the testimony qua the appellant. [836 C] (4) The conviction of an appellant on the basis of the uncoroborated deposition of an co accused cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will not lose sight Of the rule that the uncoverroborated witness is admissible only in cases where the evidence is untrue and there is no corroboration of his story. [820 G] (5) The appellant was rightly convicted on the evidence given by him.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by the respondent the High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to two years ' rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1 ) the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21, Indian Penal Code and section 21 of the Indian Penal code; (2) the appellant had been convicted under section 161 I.P.C., and section 161, I. P.C. and section 5 of the prevention of Corruption act, 1947; (3) the respondent was not an officer in the service or pay of a local authority within the terms of section 3(1) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act; (4) the High court erred in holding that the appellant could be said to be an officer within the definition of section 2 of the Act, and (5) the conviction was bad. HELD: (i) The appellant cannot be deemed to be a public Servant within the ambit of section 81 of the because he was not acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of that Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Stock Act, 1965 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ . The High Court modified the sentences passed on him by reducing the sentence from six months to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court having set aside the conviction and sentence in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964, it was illegal to maintain the order regarding forfeiture of the Juar seized from the house of the appellant because he says, the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale and Control of Movement) Order 1964, and the Buldana District Juar (Price Control) Order 1965, did not contain any provision authorising the Court to forfeit the juar. HELD: The order of the High court maintaining the forfeiture was perfectly valid. [273 D] The order passed by the High. Court maintaining the order of forfeiture is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. Rule 141(2) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1 ) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 and the High Courts have not been able to show any case in which a rule like r. 141(3) has been challenged, much less declared ultra vires. [274 D] In the instant case, the order was passed by a competent authority under the Defence Of India Act. The order was therefore illegal.

The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge for offences under sections 302 and 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted all the accused but convicted them under section 302 read with Section 34, I.P.C., and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Sia was not in any manner concerned with the deep seated enmity between the appellant Sia and the deceased. It was further contended that Siya Ram and his companions were carrying guns and hockey sticks and therefore they had all gathered to commit the murder of Kunwar Singh. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The circumstances that Shri Ram had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour. But the High Court was not impressed by the evidence on record. [512 B] 2. The circumstance that Sian Ram and Sia were carrying lathis and hocice sticks and, therefore, he could identify them is sufficient to establish that they had been guilty of murderous design. [506 C D] 3. The fact that Shri Sia had voluntarily admitted the risk and identity of Sian was not enough to prove that he was a party to the murderous designs. It is difficult to believe that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happened to facilitate the commission of the crime. There is nothing at all to show that she was aware of the nefarious design of SIA and his associates. [ 506 D E] 4. The evidence of Shri Ram shows that he knew Shri Ram and was therefore able to identify him. It appears that he had a standing of but 2 years in the District when he was supposed to have appeared for the complainant in the particular case. He was unable to say who had engaged him or who was examined as a witness in the case or who used to instruct him in the Case. The young Dubey had astanding of but two years in his District when the appellant was supposed loitering the risk, he knew no details of an important murder trial. [504 E F] 5. In view of the serious infirmities from which the evidence of Dubey suffers we are unable to agree with the High court that the High Courts ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court in favour of Shri Sema Ram and Shri Soney Lal 's evidence appears insufficient to sustain the conviction of Shri R.S. Mishra and ViOlet.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the accused on the ground that it was doubtful whether any one of them participated in the commission of the offence and convicted him under section 304, I.P.C., and sentenced him to imprisonment till death. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD : (1) The High court found that though accused 1, 3 and 4 were not identified but only named persons, it could not be said that they participated in any of the offences. [615 D] (2) The evidence was adduced to prove that the said persons along with others were guilty of murder under section302 read with Section 34, I P.C.
