The appellant company was a company incorporated in the year 1961 and it went into production in the years 1964 65, 66 and 67. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project could not be treated as separate establishment for purposes of section 16(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the Alloy Steel project was a separate establishment and therefore could not claim bonus under section 16 of the Payment Of Bonus Act; (ii) the workmen were not entitled to bonus at all because they had been paid consolidated balance sheets and profit and loss accounts. HELD : (1) The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because Alloy steel Project was owned, controlled and managed by Hindustan Steel Ltd., it has to be treated a part of the establishment for computation of bonus under the Act, but the proviso to section 3 will not apply in such a case. [637C D] (2) The proviso to sub section (2), however, does not stand in the way of this claim because there is no evidence at all that in any year after Alloy Steels Project was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. [643D] (3) The expression "any year" in section 3(1), does not mean a period of three years, and it is only when alloy steel project is set up that bonus is paid to employees of both the units. It is only where alloy workmen are working for more than one unit that they can claim bonus at any time during the period of their employment.

The appellant State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution Act, 1974 was constituted under the Act. The cess was payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I thereof as the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette specify. The appellant State Government issued a Notification under section 3(1) of the Act exempting from payment of cess, duty and cess, the cess payable on the ground that it was exempted from payment thereof. The respondent State Government passed an order dated 25th September, 1986 under Section 3(2) of Water (Prevention and Control) Act, 1977 directing that the cess be levied by every local Authority and every Local authority and was to be calculated on its basis of Water consumed by each person or a local authority. The appellants challenged the said order before the High Court which allowed the writ petition holding that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products industry". The High Court also held that the levy of cess under Section 5A was not justified. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the impugned notification dated 25.9.1986 was ultra vires the Constitution and was liable to be struck down as violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The levy of tax under the Central Act is a tax on goods produced by an industry specified in Schedule I. [528C] 2.1 The word "vegetable" has been used in Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act. It has to be borne in mind that the word 'veg etable ' has been defined in common parlance as a verb, which is generally understood to mean as bringing into existence a new substance and does not mean 'merely ' to produce some change in a sub stance, however minor in consequence, the change may be. [525D E] 2:2 The word 'megetable ' means product of or made of or out of vegetable. If the botanic meaning of vegetable as referring to any and every kind of plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule 1 like Paper industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry 25 of Schedule II. [ 525F G] 2(a) The word vegetable in the context does not attract the bhatanic interpretation. The sugar manufacturing industry do not, therefore, come within the Entry 15. [ 526B C] State of West Bengal vs Delhi Cloth and General Mills, AIR 1963 SC 79; State of Bihar vs Delhi cloth & General Mills AIR 1963SC 79; and State of Gujarat vs Gujarat Rayons Ltd., AIR 1963 Guj. 79; referred to. (b) The industry manufacturing sugar itself is not an industry within the meaning of Entry 15 and a fortio ri the manufacture of alcohol from molasses could not be considered to be an industry in Entry 25. [ 527F G]. (c) The sugar factories do not fall within Entry No. 15 of schedule I. They are covered under Entry 15 by Notification dated 25/9/86 issued under Section 4(1)(a) of U.P. Sugarcane Act, 1953. [ 528B] State Of West Bengal & Ors.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the said application and held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for the purpose of carrying on the profession as a 'business ' within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority under the Andhra Act which was dismissed. In revision, the High Court held that it did not fall within the definition of 'business " in section 2(1)(d) (ii) of that Act. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. It is true that the expression business occurring in Section 10 (3) (a)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice of profession of an Advocate or a Doctor which he is carrying on in the relevant year. [14 E] 2. The word 'business" has been used in the Andhra Nadu Buildings ( Lease, Rent & Eviction) control Act, 1961. The words "business" and "profession" are used in different senses. The expression "business", as defined in section 10(1) of Act, is used to include a practice of business which he was carrying on. [15 F G] 3. It would indeed be anamolous to hold that all the provisions of the Act including Section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and Section 10, which bars the eviction of tenants apply to nonresidential buildings owned by an Advocate but not section 10 (1) which bars a eviction of tenant from a non residential building. [16 G] 4. The term 'business' is used only in a broad sense so that it may be an activity of business. It does not mean any profession or trade or business within the ambit of Section 2(i)(d)(iii). [17 E] 5. The definition of business occurring under section 10 of the Madras Buildings (lease, Rentand Eviction) Act, 1959 is used for a wide meaning so as including the practice in connection with a profession which he has been carrying on and was not the carrying on of a trade or commerce within the scope of that phrase in the Landlord and Tenant Act. [17 G] 6.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 4,00,000 with interest and costs. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there were six principal reasons to indicate that it was a case where money was deposited under an agreement and that it had been paid on demand. HELD: (i) The words "deposit" are not defined in the Act. They are used in the context of the transaction between the appellant and the respondent. [577 F] (ii) The word deposit is used in connection with a contract of sale or purchase. It is not a case of an ordinary loan of Rs 4,000. The mere fact that the amount was deposited by the respondent with the appellant under an arrangement that the same would be paid on demands does not mean that the parties were different from each other. [578 F] In the instant case, the transaction was between the parties and the appellant was not bankers and therefore it was improbable that the respondents who were bankers would deposit with the traders the sum of Rs 1,00.000 in its account with the respondent thus reducing the indebtedness of the appellant. The High Court was wrong in holding that there was a demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 because the history of the transactions between the appel lant and the respondents shows that the appellant had to be put on a footing of financial stability by giving the appellant the use of the sum. [579 F H] (iii) The High court was wrong when it held that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can star in case of demand for return of the money deposited. It was not a question of default on the part of either party giving loan to the appellant or his agent. [580 F H; 580 A] (iv) The mere circumstance that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners, of India Supplies and of ale respondent, did not make any difference in the question whether it was an ordinary debt of Rs 2,00.,000 or not. [581 F H].

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under section 3(1) of the , on the ground that he had been in jail for a period of two years. The grounds of detention were served on him and he was also in custody. He was thereafter taken into custody. On his being released, he was again in jail. In the writ petition filed by him challenging the order of detention, it was contended that the order was passed without any summons and the detenu had been remanded to judicial custody on the 27th February, 1986 with the direction to be produced before the Metropolitan Magistrate on 28th February 1986. The petitioner contended that he was already in custody at the most one day. Allowing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The fact that the detenu is already in jail and yet he has been remanded does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive detention. [845C] 2.1 In the instant case, there was no summons and therefore, the detenu could not be detained under section 108 of the Customs Act. [820F] 2:2 The fact of the detenu being in jail is not taken into consideration by the detaining authori ty while passing an order for detention. It is only after the order is passed that the detaining autho rity was satisfied that his detention was necessary. [821C D] 3.1 There is no warrant for holding that summons under section 107 of the Act was in existence. The fact remains that the petitioner is now in jail, for at least one day, and he has not been detained thereafter. Therefore, it would not be proper to hold that summons could only be issued to a person in jail if the detaining authorities were satisfied that he is likely to get bail. [822D] 3:2 In the present case there was neither any summons nor the detenu 's statement recorded against him in the criminal case and therefore he had no opportunity of making an application for bail under section 111(1)(a) of Cr. P.C.

The petitioners are working as casual labourers in the Telecom Department of the Telecom. The Government of India, Ministry of Communications and Department of Telecommunications issued a notification dated 5th February, 1986 under Section 3(1) of the . The petitioners were appointed as casual labour on daily wages basis for a period of one year. They were paid regular pay scale of Rs.210 270 and Rs.260 350 in the scale of semi skilled/skilled labour. The petitioners challenged the said notification by filing writ petitions before this Court contending that since they had been working for the last ten years as casual labourer, the wages paid to them are very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to regular employees of the Posts and Telegraphs Department belonging to each of the categories referred to above and thirdly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits. The respondents contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour, the pay scales for the semi skilled labour employed in the telecom Department were as under: (i) Casual Labour who had not completed 720/1200 days of service over a period Of three years or more with the department; and (ii) no scheme had been prepared for absorption of casual labourers belonging to the various categories referred above, the petitioners have been discriminated against. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners belong only to the categories of casual Labour and are not being regularly employed. They are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. [609C] 1.2 The petitioners have not been able to show that they were being regularly appointed for the first ten years. They have been working as causal labourers for more than six months. They cannot be denied the same benefits which the regularly employed workers are enjoying by reason of their continuous service over long period of time. [709D] 1:3 The petitioners are therefore directed to pay wages to the workmen who are employed as casual Labour in the corresponding cadres and to direct the Union to regularise the service of the casual labourers who have been in continuous service for morethan six months, if they occur in the Postal and Telegraph's Department. [809E] 1 4. The benefits of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to the regular workers who have not completed 7 years of service prior to 5th of February,1986 on which date the first of the two petitions, namely, Writ Petition No.

The assessee, who was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 47, filed a return under section 22(3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on January 5, 1950, showing an income of Rs. 1,00,000/ as taxable income. The Income tax Officer rejected the return and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had failed to file a return within the assessment years in question. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that since he had submitted a return for the previous year, it was not open to him to make a return at all. In further appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notice under section 24(2) of that Act was served on the assessee and a return showing an amount of Rs 1,50,000 as taxable profits was filed before the Income tax officer. [120 B] (ii) The assessment proceedings commence either with a notice under s.24(2), or with the filing of a return disclosing taxable income, but not a return of income which shows a loss or is below the taxable limit. The assessee 's case that he had no assessable income was not accepted by the Income Tax Officer and the order of the Appellate Authority was set aside. [121 E] (iii) The word "assessed" in section 22 of the Act means "a return of taxable income". It does not mean a return which is assessed under section 23(1)(a). If the return filed on January 4, 1950 was a return in respect of which no notice under sub s. 24(3), as corresponding to section 34 (1) or even section 24, could be said to have been issued, it would be open to the Incometax Officer to serve a notice upon him requiring him to furnish within such period not being less than thirty days.

The Central Government issued a notification dated 23.8.1982 under section 9 of the , declaring that the Central Government would be the appropriate authority to make a scheme for the constitution of the Board of Directors so as to include representatives of employees and other speci fied categories. The Central Government, by its order dated 27.9.1985, directed that the said notification shall remain in force until further orders. In pursuance of this direction, the Central Govern ment issued a Notification dated 23rd August, 1985 under section 10(1) of the . The Central Governmen ties issued another Notification dated 3rd September, 1985 which was published on 30th October, 1985. The petitioners who were working as Assistant Directors in the Central Bank of India and were working in the same bank at different places in the State of Andhra Pradesh challenged the validity of the said Notification by filing writ petitions before this Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that the notification dated 3.9.'85 was ultra vires the Act and the Scheme framed thereunder, and directed the Central Govt. to make the scheme in consultation with the Reserve Bank ofIndia. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of the board of Directors and the choice between them is left to the Central government, but it is not an unrestrained or unrestricted discretion, but a discretion which must be reasonably exercised so as not to give effect to the true intent of the legislature as to the composition of the Boards of Directors. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act contemplates only election or nomination and if election were to be construed to be the proper mode of choosing the representatives of the employees, appointment by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by the representative Union would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle enshrined in Articles 19(1)(c) and 43(A). [561C D] 1.2 The Act does not contemplate either election or nominations to be made by nomination or nomination, but only contemplates election or nominating one person as an elector.

The appellant was assessed to sales tax for the year 1962 63. The respondent filed a return of his income showing that he had been assessed to tax under section 45 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on the ground that the amount of tax due from him was not paid within the time allowed by the assessing authority and that the appellant had failed to pay the tax in time. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim for stay of collection of the penalty imposed by the departmental authorities on an assessee during the pendency of an appeal before it. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Tribunal had the power under section 255(5) of the Act to stay the recovery proceedings and directed the appellant to make a deposit of the amount in the Government Treasury within one month from the date of receipt of the order. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) Section 255(6) provides for stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pending appeal. The section does empower the Appellate Tribunal to regulate its own procedure but it is very doubtful if the power of stay can be spelt out from that provision. [69F] (ii) Under section 255, the power conferred on the Appellate Assistant Commissioner under section 256(6), is not a matter for the legislature to consider whether to stay recovery proceedings or to stay proceedings as would prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. The power of staying the recovery of tax is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. [70G H] (iii) Section 256(5), which deals expressly with a situation when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Authority, does empower it to regulate the own procedure, but it does not say that where a certificate has been issued to the Tax Recovery Officer for the recovery thereof, he will grant time for the payment of the tax. [71G H; 72A] (iv) The power conferred by section 255 is not intended to enable an assessee who has preferred an appeal, to obtain from the appellate forum a stay of recovery of any tax, either in whole or in part, on furnishing suitable security, is a matter which the legislature has to consider. [72B C] (v) Section 254(5)(a) deals expresslywith a situation where an appeal was pending before a Appellate Tribunal and the Act provides for such a matter being dealt with by the Income tax officer. It does not require that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the Appeal if successful, from being made nugatory.

The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental trial. He was charged with committing cognizable offences and was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with remissness in the discharge of his duty and unfitness for the same. The District Magistrate sent an endorsement on the report to the Superintendent of Police stating that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against him and recommended the transfer of the respondent to the State Government. The State Government, however, did not agree with the recommendation. Thereupon the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal on the ground that the report was not in the first instance received by the Magistrate and forwarded to the police for inquiry. The High Court held that the enquiry was vitiated by a number of serious irregularities and therefore the Superintendent 's order should be set aside. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent was charged of committing cognizable offence and therefore sub paragraph (1) of para. 486 of the police Regulations was only directory in nature and inasmuch as no prejudice was caused to the respondent the non compliance with the said regulations would not affect the validity of the order. [655 D] (ii) The High Courts have held that there was no magisterial inquiry in respect of the matter which was the subject matter of the enquiry and the departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect thereof. In such cases, and in other cases until and unless a magisterial enquiry is ordered, inquiry will be made under the direction of the Superintendent or Police in accordance with the following rules: "A police officer may be departmentally tried under section7 of the Indian Police Act (1 of 1861) after he has been tried judicially. In the case of civil appeal No. 270 of 1955 decided on April 12, 1956, the High Courts held that a preliminary inquiry was necessary and that the Superintendent had no power to dismiss him, since an order in such circumstances could only be made by a police officer senior in rank to a Superintendent; but the fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries did not affect its validity. [676 G H] (iii) The departmental inquiry is only a continuation of the investigation and it does not affect any question whether substantially the subject matters of the magisterial inquiries are cognizable offences or not. It is not necessary to decide whether there was an magisterial investigation in respect Of these matters. If the order is held to have been made under section 6 of the Act, the enquiry would be a preliminary one and if it is held that it was not done in the course of the same transaction, the Superintendent would be competent to proceed with the departmental proceedings without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph. (1).

The appellant was appointed as a Director of Health Services in January, 1971. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971 and was posted as Additional Deputy Director of Medical Education, Manipur. On the basis of an order dated March 12, 1971, he was promoted as Additional Director of Medicine on February 1, 1971 with effect from April 1, 1972. The appellant challenged the promotion by a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the post of Director of medicine was not included in the cadre of Assistant Director of Surgery and that the appellant was entitled to be promoted as Professor from that date. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The post of Deputy Director is a selection post and he is only an officer who is eligible to be appointed to that speciality and not some one who is on top of the general seniority list in Specialists ' grade or general duty officers ' grade from which promotion is to be made. [53E] 2.1 The appellant was promoted by way of promotion as Additional Medical Director, Manipur, but he was not qualified for promotion to super time grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' Grade I. He could not therefore be considered eligible for promotion when some one was already in that grade. [54F] 2(a) The appellant is a senior and otherwise qualified person who has been promoted as an Additional Medical Officer, Manipur and is entitled to get his promotion from those who have put in the prescribed period of service. [55G] 3.1 In passing a contention of the appellant that all 28 posts which were deducted from the strength of permanent posts in Specialist 's grade and added to super Time grade II must on that account alone be filled in by promotion, it is difficult to entertain the contention that in refusing promotion to him when some posts were converted into a specified post, he could not be said to have been superseded in violation of article 16. [56A B] 3(b) The post which was deducted from his strength of temporary posts was unspecified Specialists' grade post and was sanctioned at Willingdon Hospital and the post vacated by him which was in super time scale II was offered to the appellant as and by way off promotion which in fact was done in this case there is no justification for giving a direction that the said post could only be filled up by promotion. The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) was enacted to provide for the acquisition of certain lands and for the payment of compensation. Section 19B provides that the excess land shall be at the disposal of the State Government for utilization as surplus. The appellants who were tenants in possession of the land acquired by the State, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of section 19B on the ground that the land inherited by them and later transferred to their sons and wife was not hit by section 10A and section 19 B of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the lands inherited by the appellants and subsequently transferred to his sons and widow were not hit under section 10 A and section 18B of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures Rules, 1953. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the State had no power to utilise the excess area for the resettlement of tenants ejected or to be ejected under section 9A; (2) that section 19 A was ultra vires the Constitution and was void as violative of article 14 of the Constitution. HELD : (i) The Act is a self contained code and does not contain any provision which would enable the State to utilise excess area in the manner prescribed by section 19A. [634 B] (ii) Section 19 B provides that if after the commencement of the Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1954 any person acquires any land by inheritance or bequest or gift from a person to whom he is an heir any land, or in after the date of such transfer, any person acquiring any right by inheritance shall effect the utilization thereof in clause (a). The scheme of the section was that no one held in excess of the permissible area and since by the gift to the son or wife the latter had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [734 C D] (iii) Section 10A provides for acquisition of surplus area by inheritance. The scheme is to see that no person held in any excess of his permissible area is conditioned by the permissible limit. If after the Act, April 15, 1953, any such person acquires land by succession or bequest, he may acquire lands in excess thereof.

The plaintiffs claimed the Zamindari of Amarshah under the will of Amarzart. The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to the Zamindari on the death of Amshah upon the death, of Amrari. The claim was resisted by the defendants on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation as the suit had been filed within two months from the date thereof and the plaintiffs were not entitled to claim compensation for the estate acquired by them. The Compensation Officer held that the claim was barred under section 14 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the Compensation Officer was contrary to the customs and law governing the Zamindari; and the decision of the Governor in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be the successor on the deceased Amarshi was not binding on the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the decision was instituted within two years from that date. [334 B] (ii) The High court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded by the Compensation officer. [340 C] (iii) The question regarding the pro priction of mesne profit awardable to the plaintiffs was a question of fact and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date, and the High Court was in wrong in not interfering with the decision on the question of mesne income. [341 D] (iv) The decision of this Court in M/s. Ram Gopal vs State of Rajasthan, ; , relied upon. (v) The claim for compensation made by the plaintiffs under section 15 of the Land Acquisition Act was not barred by the decision in M.P. V. Sundararama Iyer vs State, A.I.R. 1951 Mad. 853, distinguished.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that he had let out the premises to one Mr. M. V. Desai, who was the tenant in respect of which the suit was filed. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions contained in section 12(3) (a) of the Act do not apply to the suit as the suit is governed by the provisions of section 12 (3)(b) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay High Court had taken a contrary view and held that the dispute as to standard rent was to be raised within one month from the service of notice under section 12. [610C] 2. Section 12(1)(a) is an inclusive provision which provides for the application of the provisions in respect to standard rents in certain cases. The provisions contained therein are as follows: "12(3)(a). Where a landlord makes an application to the Court under sub section (3) of section 11 and thereafter pays or tenders the amount of rent or permitted increases specified in the order made by the Court, the Court shall pass a decree for eviction in any such suit for the recovery of possession. " [611D E] 3. Section 13(1) (b) provides that where there is a dispute as regards the amount or permitted increase, the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section(2), he makes an applica tion to the court under sub sec. (3). The provisions of sections 12(4) (c) and (d) are as follow: "In any case where there has been a dispute, as to the amount, of standard rent or allowed increases recoverable under this Act, the court shall pass such decree for ejectment in any suit for eviction whether with or without a claim for possession of the premises. " The Bombay Rent Control Act, 1958 was enacted by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers conferred on it by section 12 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947. Section 11(4)(c) provides for an application made to the High court under section 11(3). Sub section (2) of that section provides that if there is any dispute as regard the amount payable by the tenant, he shall be entitled to make an application before the Court within one year from the date of service of the notice terminating the tenancy by raising a dispute. The appellant landlord had filed a petition under section 13(3), (4) and the respondent tenant in the High Courts for eviction on the grounds of non existence of the dispute. In the High courts, the question was whether the provisions relating to standard Rent were applicable to the case. The High Court held that since the dispute was not referred to the trial court under s.11(3); (4)(a), the suit could be filed within one months from the expiry thereof on one month; and (b). In the appeal by Special Leave, it was submitted on behalf for the appellant tenant that the Bombay Rent Act did not apply in view of section 13 (3), and (4A) of it was applicable to a case where the suit had been filed within two months from its commencement. Dismissing both the appeals, ! HELD: The provisions in sections 12 (4), (c), (d), (e) and(f) are not applicable to cases where the dispute is raised at any time prior to the expiration of one year after notice under s 12(2). [612C] In the instant case, the appellant landlord was entitled to raise a dispute in regard to standard tenancy. The Act does not provide for an appeal against the order of the trial Court.

The respondent company was incorporated in the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant was a director of the respondent company and he was appointed to vote for him in respect of the shares held by it in the respondent Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the Respondent company. The respondent company issued a notice under section 21(1) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, requiring the appellant to pay the tax on the shares of the company and also to furnish a statement of account showing the amount of the dividend received by it from the respondent. The Income tax Officer held that the directors of the appellant company were not entitled to any share in the shares but only those shares which were held by them as trustees and therefore, they could not be said to have "a controlling interest" in the company. On appeal the Appellate Tribunal held that there was no question of law referred to it under section 20(1)(c) of that Act and that the appellant had failed to prove that the shares were held as trustees. The High Court on reference answered the question against the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The finding of fact recorded by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was correct. The Tribunal was right in holding that there could be no question as to whether the directors had "a control" in a company when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority of the capital which under the articles of association of the Company carry the right to vote. [193 H] (ii) The word "control" in section 2(21) of Excess Profits tax Act means "to exercise, on behalf of the person or persons who hold the majority or any of the voting rights in that company". In the present case, the directors were not acting in breach of their duty and they could only be sued to have the shares as trustees, but they did not do so. The word 'control ' in section 20 of the Act means 'to exercise on behalf and direction of the persons who held the majority shares. [194 D E] (iii) The words "a person" in sub section (1) are wide enough to include a person who holds the majority and is not subject, directly or indirectly, to his will and ordering, and therefore he cannot apply either of the tests mentioned above.

The respondent was promoted as Accounts Superintendent on the basis of seniority cum merit. The appellant, a Junior Assistant in the Board, was promoted to the post of Accounts Superintendent by an order dated 30th December 1966. On 1st October 1957, the respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. The respondent opted for the service under the Government and continued to function as an Assistant Accounts Superintendent till he was promoted on his having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. On 30th November, 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed the S A.S., examination while promotion was denied to the appellant. The Board by a resolution dated 5th January, 1970, decided that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the principle of senioritycum merit and not on the ground of delay and laches. On 10th February, 1971, the Board issued a circular stating that the post was to be held by promotion from the cadre of I division Clerks on their being found suitable for promotion to that post with effect on the date of their joining in the service. The said circular stated that the vacancies were to arise only after the first year of recruitment and that the promotions would be made on the result of the examination. On 2nd October, 1971 the Board by its resolution dated 19th May 1969 decided that promotion from I Division Clerk to I Division clerks should be made in accordance with the seniority cum Merit list prepared for the purpose of earning increments and for promotion. The Government issued a notification dated 30 th December 1966 under section 79(c) of the Board 's Regulations, which provided that the existing vacancies would be filled up by promotion on the recommendation of the Selection Committee. On 19th October, 1972, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said resolution and the notification dated 10th January 1969. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was exempted from passing the Departmental Examination before qualifying for the promotion. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board was not in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that it would be applicable only when the vacancies arose in the cadre and not in the case of allotment to the cadre. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The resolution dated 20th May, 1969 is not intended to cover the case where allottees were excluded from the operation of the Resolution the inference that the allottees were exempt from passing 'of the Departmental examination before qualifying them for promotion was not justified. [512C] 2.1 In the instant case, the High court has rightly held that the resolution dated 30.11.1966 was not intended by amending the Regulations. The effect of the judgment of the High Courts cannot be upheld as the binding nature of the regulations passed by the Board under section 80(c). [513D] 2:2 In view of this circumstance, the plea of the respondent will have to fail on the grounds that the Regulations framed by the appellant under section79(c), has not been relaxed by amending Regulation No. 79(a) and (b). The High court was right in holding that there was no reason for excluding from the applicability of the Regulation any further delay and that it was not possible to infer from the Resolution that the allotment was exempt from the passing ' of the ' examination.

The petitioner, a retired employee of the respondent No.6, filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation to be paid to him in respect of violation of fundamental right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to compensation for contravention of fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 21. In appeal, this Court held that the State had not only the power and jurisdiction but also an obligation to grant relief in exercise of its powers under Articles 32 and 226 of the Consti tution. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts are not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights under the Constitution, which enable the award of monetary compensation in appropriate cases, where that is the only practicable mode of redress available. [608C D] 1.2 The relief of monetary damages as exemplary damages in proceedings under Article 226 of India or under Article 227 of the Supreme Court can be granted only once it is established that there has been an infringement of the fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. [613D E] 2.1 In the instant case, the High Court was not helpless because it was not available as a defence in private law for damages under Article 22 or 226 of this Constitution. The relief claimed by the petitioner in the writ petition is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages Under Article 21, which alone can claim compensation for the tort committed by the aggrieved party where that was the only mode of redressal available. This Court and the High Courts have not only their power and authority but also the obligation to award monetary compensation under the private law in an action based on tort.

The petitioner, a prisoner under the Prisons Act, 1894, was sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by him to the President of India for commutation of sentence were rejected by the President. The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the said Act in this Court. The petition was dismissed by the Supreme Court on the ground that the provisions of the Prisons (Amendment) Act, 1976 were not applicable to Delhi because there was under section 161(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, which includes the freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of that Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of the Press, to have an unrestricted access to means of information. In the instant case, the right was sought to be exercised only subject to the rules and regulations governing the interviews. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 161 (2) are not applicable in Delhi because, for example, rule 552A provides for a search of the person who wants to interview a prisoner. If it is thought necessary that such search should be taken, a person who desires to interview the prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules. [1187E F] 2. The right claimed to express an individual view or views on the rights of other citizens and which does not violate the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order, decency and morality. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore we do not see any reason why the petitioner should not be allowed to interview him. [1103B] 3. The fundamental right to freedom of expression is not an absolute right but merely a right to liberty guaranteed by article 21 of the Constitution which includes freedom of press, freedom of the press and the right freely to speak and to speak. It is not a matter for us to decide. If such an application is made to the Superintendent of Jail he will be free to consider the same on merits and in accordance therewith. [111D] 4. The Superintendent of the Tihar Jail shall allow the petitioner, if it is felt necessary that his request should be considered by him on merits. [112F G] 5. The President of the India rejected the petitions for commutation and the petitioners were given the liberty to make a representation to the State Government against the rejection of their petitions filed in this court.

The respondent was the Receiver of a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but the High Court set aside the decree and directed that the damages awarded to the respondent be recovered from the appellant. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended (1) that the respondent was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire; (2) under the terms of the bond the appellant was not liable for the losses caused to tea garden because the Receiver had failed to perform his duties in respect of the tea gardens and as such he could not be sued for the same. HELD : (1)(a) The surety bond is executed both by the surety bond and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District Judge of Agartala". [360 F] (b) The sureties bond was executed both be the Receiver and the respondent. The surety bonds were executed both for the purpose of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond. stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. [360 G] (c) The appellant was put in possession of the Tea garden in his capacity as a Receiver and not as a partner in office or office of the District Magistrate. The sureties bonds were not executed by the appellant as he was neither the successor nor the successor in office nor the assign of the district Judge. The bond was a part of the proceedings pending before him and on transfer of it to the Subordinate judge under the Tripura (Courts) order of 1950. [361 B] (d) The agent bond was not executed either by the Receiver or the appellant, but only by the successor. The agent was put into possession of tea garden in the capacity as Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea estate was managed by the receiver economically and efficiently. [362 C] (e) The bond is a part and parcel of the proceeding pending before a District Judge and on that basis it cannot be enforced against the appellant to the extent to which it rendered itself personally liable under the conditions of the bonds. [363 D E] (f) The order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver can be executed against the appel lant to the amount to which he has rendered himself personally liable.

The appellant was a dealer in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller, Lucknow. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants at the time of their purchase. The appellant challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that the goods were not sold by them to the State Government and that the transactions of supply did not result in sales, and that there was no sale within the meaning of the U..P. (Central) Sales Tax Amendment Act, 1959. The High Court held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was nothing in the Act which prevented the assessee from selling the goods to the Government by way of sale. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sales made to the regional Food Controller under the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh (Central Sales Tax) Amendment Act 1959 were sales within the definition of "sale" in section 2(h) of the Act and therefore, the transactions could be regarded as a sale. HELD: The High court was right in holding that there is no contract between the assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods are sold within the ambit of the definition. [512 B] Ram Bilas Ram Gopal vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. Ram Bilasram Gopal vs The State of U. P., ; , referred to. (i) There was nothing on record to show that the transaction of supply of sugar was a sale within section 2 (h) and therefore the transactions were not exigible to sales tax. [506 B] (ii) The High Courts erred in holding the transactions as sales within section 3(h). The Sales tax Officer had no authority under the Act to impose tax on such transactions. There was no contract of sale between the parties but in the statutory order. The tax payer was under the control of the State and it could not be said that there were any contracts between the appellant and the respondent.

The appellant was in jail for a period of three months. He was released on June 23, 1986. The Advisory Board submitted its report to the State Government on April 24, 1986 stating that there was sufficient cause for his detention. On May 26, 1986, the State Govt. issued an order under section 3(1) of the Act directing that no person shall be detained in any place beyond three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of two months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause. The appellant was arrested on May 26 and was released from prison on June 24. 1986. On June 23. 1986, he was served with an order of detention under section 11(1)(a) of Act No. 1 of 1986. He challenged the said order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The State filed a Letters Patent Appeal against the said judgment and the Division Bench allowed the same on the ground that the appellant had not been detained in accordance with law. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The report of the Advisory Board is more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order of the detention though it was within three months from the date of the second order of his detention, where the earlier order is revoked and a subsequent order is made. [206B] 2.2. In a habeas corpus proceeding, it is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date on which the report or beyond three month from the first order of conviction is passed. The fact that the report of such an Advisory board has to be obtained before the expiry of three weeks from the last date of detention does not mean that the reference, though not made within three weeks, was made before the hearing of the case. If the report is not made in three months, it would be a question of prejudice to say whether there was adequate cause for such detention. [207C D] 2:3. The question to which the Advisory board had to apply its mind is whether on the date when the report was submitted by the Advisory Committee, there was enough cause for the detention of the person. That inquiry neces sary involves the consideration of the ques tion as to whether there is sufficient cause or not. [208D] 2 4. The procedural requirements are not complied with when the order is passed but the report must be obtained within three days, and it is no answer to saying that the representation, thoughnot made within 3 months, was disposed of before the day of hearing and therefore, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three month after the date o f detention. If a reference to an Advisory Boards is to be made within two weeks, it will be open to the detenu to make a fresh representation against the order on the basis of such fresh facts as may be available in law. [209E F] 2 5. The Court was not confronted with the present situation at all. It could not say that there had been sufficient cause to say so. If, the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it was no answer t o say that, the report though not obtained within 3 weeks, is disposed of.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for specific performance of an agreement to sell dated 18th January, 1977. The appellant contended that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and the respondent had agreed to such entrustment. The respondent applied on 20th June, 1977 for filing the award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the Act. The trial court rejected the objections filed by the respondent. The High Court dismissed the revision application holding that the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the Award. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties to refer the disputes to arbitration and that the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there is an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed that the dispute should abide by the award dated 20th January 1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the arbitrator himself. [539C] 2. The fact that the respondent has agreed to refer disputes to the arbitration of the named arbitrator is not a proper arbitration agreement in terms thereof. It is clear from the narration of facts that the appellant had agreed upon the reference to the respondent and that he made an award. This letter of 14th August, 1978 was replied in the form of a letter dated 4th September, 1978 addressed to the petitioner by the arbitrator. The award was signed by the parties about which there is no factual dispute. [540D E] 3. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case it is clear that the conduct of both the respondents that there were an arbitration agreements and by sign the award they could be regarded as a proper Arbitration agreement in accordance with section 2(a) of Act.

The appellants were the mortgagees of a mortgage debt in respect of certain properties. The mortgage was executed by the mortgagee in favour of the appellants on January 2, 1941. On January 30, 1939, the sub mortgaged property was sold to the appellants and they were put in possession thereof. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from them on the ground that the mortgage debt was not an absolute interest but an absolute right and that the mortgagee had no right to recover the amount. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sub mortgage was not a sale within the meaning of section 2 (22) Of the Act, and that it was not liable to be set aside on the grounds that the appellants were not the mortgagees in possession of the mortgaged property. On appeal by the appellants the High Court held that the decree was not one which was passed in a suit to which this Act applies and that as the sub mortgagee had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of section 28, it was open to him to have the mortgage redeemed on payment of the debt. The question for decision was whether the respondent as sub mortgagee was an assignee within the definition in section 2(22 Of the Indian Act. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that a sub mortgage is not a transfer of an interest in the original mortgage and that a mortgage is a sale of property by the mortgagor to the mortgagee for the recovery of a loan advanced before or after the commencement of this Act. The words "all the rights of the mortgagee" used in section 28 are wide enough to include all the rights which the mortgagor had in the suit to enforce against the original mortgagor and that, therefore, the respondent was not entitled to recover any amount from the original mortgagee.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided into two equal shares by metes and bounds. The partition deed provided that the properties should be partitioned in accordance with the provisions of the Madras Hindu Law. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 15, 1946, were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the transfers were not supported by any consideration and were invalid. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree in respect of the two other items. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfer was made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the respondent in view of past illicit cohabitation. The High Court held that the transactions were not vitiated by any considerations of public policy and were therefore void. HELD: (i) The transfers were without consideration and are by way of gifts. [46 B] (ii) The transfer was without consideration by way 'of gift and as such was invalid. [47 C] (iii) The properties gifted under exhibit A 1 and exhibit A 2 were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras School of Mitakshara law by which Venkatachallulu was governed, he had no power to make a gift of the joint family properties to his concubine. The gifts were not hit by section 6(h). [47 D] (iv) The transactions in question were not void as they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubines for her past services.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, was carrying on business as a dealer in gold and silver. The Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to the appellant, claiming that the amount due from him had been paid by them to the respondent. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the said amount was due to the Government as it was payable only to the assignee and not to the defaulter. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that the liability of the appellant to pay interest for the period after the date of maturity of insur ance policy had been fully discharged by the respondent, and that the appellant was entitled to claim interest for such period. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High Court erred in holding that there was no liability of interest on the amount of compensation paid to the respond ent. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether a person is liable to pay the interest for any period prior to the date fixed by the statute or not has to be decided on its own facts and circumstances. [114F] 2.1 In the instant case, the award of interest was made much later on 5th December 1975 in pursuance of the Court 's order to enable the appellant company to make the payment due against the policies to the respondents. The operation of the notice under clause (vii) of sub section (3) Of section 226 of the Act by the I.T.O. is not governed by Section 244 of the Indian Income Tax, 1922. [115G] 2(a) The question of revoca tion of the amount demanded by the notice issued under section226(3)(vi) of Income Tax is a matter which falls within the ambit of section 244 of that Act. [116B] (b) The High Court was in error in holding so. [117D] 2.(c) The delay in making the requisite statement on oath under clause(vii) thereof raising an objection on the basis of the registered assignment is a serious lapse and it cannot be said that writ petition when the appellant had made the requisite statements on oath before the IICC was not maintainable. [118E F] 2 (d) The time for making the statement under section 227(3), 1961, by the 1.T.,O.P. has to start from 5th January 1975 and it is only after the L.I.C. made the necessary statement on affidavit that the same was filed in pursuance to the Court "may" notice under Section 226(2) of Act, 1962. [119F] 3.1 The question as to whether a party is liable for any default or not is a question which falls outside the ambit and given to section 244. [120G] 3(a). In the present case, since the award was made by the LC.O., in the present matter, it was incumbent on the L C.O to make an application under Section 245(3). The appellant had not filed any affidavit on oath of the LCIC. [121B] 3 (b).

The appellant was the owner of certain lands in which he had a house. He filed a suit for possession of those lands on the ground that the respondents were not entitled to recover possession thereof. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the first limb of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act was applicable only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law; and that the second limb of sub section (2) will also apply to an appeal under the Representation of the People Act. HELD: The first limb is concerned with the effect of the provisions contained in section 29 of the Indian Limitation Act. It is not necessary for a suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the First Schedule. [143 E] (i) The second limb is applicable only to proceedings under special orlocal law for which a period is prescribed in that Schedule. The first part of sub s.(2) is concerned only with proceedings under the special or Local law for the time being in force and not with any other matter connected therewith. [144 F] (ii) The first clause of section 30(1) of Act, 1951, provides that a suit appeal or an application for an order of the Tribunal shall be filed within three months from the date on which it is made. The second part of s.29(2)(a) is not attracted.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He challenged the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate, Mathura on the ground that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a bus stand under section 76 of the Act. The High Court held that section 76 was not applicable to the case and quashed the order made under section 77 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the State Government had no authority to appoint an area as bus stand in the town Area, Baldev (Mathu ra) as well as the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses at the bus stand fixed by the State Transport Authority. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The District Mags trate has been authorised by the state Government under section 78 of the , to pass an order fixing the Municipal Bus Stand as a Bus stand for purposes of stopping their buses in accord ance with the order issued by the Regional Transport Authority, Baldev. [707D] 2. Section 76(2)(r) of the is not applicable in the case of a bus stands which was a sort of radiating centre of all the bus traffic in the Town Area. The Municipal Council had passed the impugned order in question with the object of establishing a bus Stand in the area in question. This Court held in T.B. It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by any authority, and therefore, rules could be framed by the Government regarding the said subject under section 68(2) (r). [708E F] 3. The State Transport Appellate Authority had passed an order in accordance with law and that order was open to revision under section 64 A by the appellant. Such a power should be given specifically by the statute and that the power to compel persons in charge of motor buses to stop only at certain places for the pur pose of taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a composite scheme of road transport. [808F G] 4. The provisions relating to parking places and halting places have no application to a permanent bus stand which is a sort or radiating center of all other bus traffic. [909G H] 5. The power under section 82 of the cannot be exercised only by the Municipal Council having jurisdiction over the area and therefore the order dated 22.5.1986 passed by District Magistrate could not be equated with the Regional transport Authority constituted under the Act.[808H; 810A B] 6. The decision of the High Court in TB. is set aside.

The appellant was charged with the offence of attempt to commit theft. The prosecution case was that on October 19, 1961 he had entered into a conspiracy with one M and others who were partners of Messrs. In the course of the conspiracy M was found in possession of paddy and truck No. P.N.U. 967. The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the . He was sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 250/ and in default to undergo imprisonment for one month. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellant and acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there was an attempt on the part of the prosecution to transport paddy outside the State of Punjab in this case. HELD : (i) The fact that the appellant had entered the premises at Delhi after the incident did not make any difference as to whether he was carrying the paddy outside his premises or not. [667 E] (ii) There is no evidence on record to show that the appellants were engaged in the business of transporting paddy within the State. It is also not disputed that the possession of M was taken by the appellant from M and the bags of paddy were seized by the police. The fact remains that the goods were found in the truck which was loaded with 75 bags of rice and the truck was intercepted at the spot. The appellants were therefore guilty of an attempt to export paddy outside their premises. [666 G] (iii) There has been no attempt on behalf the appellants to commit the offence. It must be shown first to have had an intention to commit it, and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the actuates that the act was done by the appellants and thirdly to have do an actwhich constitutes the offence is different from attempt to committing it.

The appellant was the Managing Agent of a Company which was incorporated in 1950. The Managing Agency Agreement provided that the Company would be liable to pay to the Company for the entire year 's remuneration on the termination of its agency and that the company would not be liable for any loss or damage arising from the termination thereof. The Company was to receive the Managing Agency commission at the end of the calendar year and became a debt due to it under the terms of the Managing agency Agreements. The appellant claimed that in the absence of any agreement between the parties, the Managing Agents were entitled to receive remuneration for the whole year 'as they had not earned any part of the profits or gains from the business. Held, that the Managing Agencies were not liable to tax in respect of the entire income of the Company and the High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not liable under section 10(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year in question was the calendar Year. The agreement between them did not create any liability on the company but only created a liability to pay commission to the Managing agents and not to the appellant. The remuneration received by the Managing agent from the Companies under the agreement was merely an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire profits of the business carried on by the Company, when as a fact he stepped into the position of the managing Agent only on some date in the course of the year by virtue of the assignment. The liability of the appellant could not be said to arise out of the transaction between the company and its employees, because, the agreement did not provide for any remuneration or commission to be earned by the company from the companies under the Managing agencies agreements. Held further, that in computing the taxable income of a person on the date when the managing agency agreement was entered into, the profits and gains of the company must be taken into account as part of its business and not as part thereof.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be so in the case of a statement in writing, there could be no difference in principle in the cases of oral evidence; (2) the prosecution had failed to prove the motive for the murder and (3) the deceased and the accused had some quarrel on the Janmashtami day in the evening. HELD : (1)(a) The High court was right in holding that a statement made by an accused admitting guilt is not an admissible piece of evidence but only as a corroborative piece of substantive evidence. [708 D] (b) The circumstances found by the High Court, which are as follows: (i) the accused admitted his guilt; (ii) the appellant was overheard muttering to himself,f, if otherwise than in his sleep, is admissible against him, if independently proved. [809 E F] (c) The evidence of the witnesses examined by the prosecution shows that the deceased had gone out of the house at about 6 a.m. on that day and he was not in the house. There were no other circumstances which would justify the conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder. [909 G H] (d) The fact that the appellant had been overheard, does not necessarily lead to the only conclusion that he should have committed a murder. It is true that the evidence of PW 11, 13 and 15 was not sufficient to prove that the solar lantern was burning in the room where the deceased was sleeping and thereby finished the daily quarrels. But, at the trial the said statement of the appellant could be proved as a confession made by him. [1009 G] (e) The circumstance found by both the High Courts, which lead to only one conclusion that it is corroborated, does establish the guilt of the person making the murder; and even if so much was established, prudence and justice demand that such evidence cannot be made the sole ground of conviction. It may be used only as corroborative piece or substantive evidence, but it can be used merely as a corroboration to its contents. [1110 G H, 1112 A] (f) The prosecution has failed to establish the motive of the murder by leading cogent and reliable evidence. The circumstances proved by the trial court were found to be not sufficient for conviction.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary employee in the respondent Corporation. He was confirmed on the post of an Assistant Engineer in the Respondent Corporation. The appellant was promoted to the post on June 30, 1976 and he was confirmed with effect from July 1, 1977. In the meantime, the appellant was transferred to the respondent corporation. On August 3, 1977, the respondent was appointed by the appellant Corporation as an Assistant Executive Engineer. He continued to remain in service till March 31, 1980. The respondent challenged his termination on various grounds including that he had been terminated without giving him a notice or pay in lieu thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the order of termination was arbitrary and void offending Article 14 of the Constitution of India. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The respondent has the right to dismiss an employee under Rule 8 for misconduct in the manner prescribed in the Rules. [224D] 1.2 The expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee 's service whether permanent or temporary which shall be decided by the Board" is susceptible of two interpretations. The one interpretation put up by Sri Ramamurty is that the Board may unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there is no need for the services of a particular employee, in given facts and circumstances, though the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving one month 's notice or paying in lieu thereto. The other view capable to be construed from the language employed would be that the respondent has not yet been appointed. [225E F] 1:3. In view of the fact that the appellant had the right of dismissal under Rule 5, for misconduct, in the matter of misconduct, the Board of Directors have to take a decision whether the need to continue the employee ' s service subsists which would be based on the relevant material.

The appellant was a licensee of a shop in Orissa. The respondent No. 1, the Excise Inspector, issued a notice under section 22(1) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 to the appellant for re auctioning the license. The appellant challenged the said notice by filing a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the licence was not granted for an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the grant of the exclusive privilege under section 21 of the Act because the Collector had no authority to issue such a notice in view of section 6(a) of that Act. In appeal by certificate, the appellant contended that the High court erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector was not for the grant or renewal of an exclusive right to manufacture liquor and that it was not necessary to issue any public notice under that sub section as the power of the State Government in that respect had been delegated to the Board of Revenue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State has the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor. [814 B] 2. Section 6(1)(a) is a provision for the levy of excise duty on excisable goods. It does not confer any power on the State to issue a notification under section 29(2). The power of State Government to issue notifications under section 5(1), is subject to the provisions of the Constitution. [850 E] 3. Section 2 to 5 of the Amending Act of 1970 provides that the State has exclusive right, and privilege, of manufacturing or selling liquor, and that the power to grant an exclusive licence under section 6 is subject only to the restrictions imposed by the Act. The power to issue licences is subject also to the limitations imposed by section 6. [852 E] 4. Section 3(1A) of Amending Act provides that no person shall manufacture or sell any liquor except in accordance with the conditions specified therein. The expression "excise" has been defined in section 2(d) to mean any liquor which is not a intoxicating drug. It includes any article which is capable of being sold as such. [851 B C] 5. Section 4 of the Amendment Act provides for the imposition of excise duties on excisable articles and reads: "4. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that all or any of the provisions contained in this Act shall apply to any class or classes of goods specified in the Schedule. " [852 C] 6. Section 5(a), (b) and (c) are not made retrospective in operation. The effect of section 3 is that the amount realised by auction was illegal and that section 6 was therefore ultra vires the powers of the Legislature. [853 D] 7. The word 'excise ' has been used in the Act to mean "any article which contains any intoxicating drug". It means "any substance which is ordinarily capable of producing a intoxicating substance". The expression 'exact ' has not been defined either in the Bihar Excise Act or in the Amending Acts. [865 E] 8. Section 7(1 A) of this Act provides, inter alia, that no liquor shall be sold except as such by the State or its authorised officer. It is not necessary for the State Legislature to issue the notification under sub section (2) of section 29 of the amended Act. [864 F G] 9. The words "exact" in section 6 are wide enough to include within their sweep any article including articles which contain alcohol, but do not include articles which have been made out of a medicinal or toilet preparations. It cannot be said that the expression "in accordance with law" has not acquired any special meaning. [874 G] 10.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar in material particulars in regard to the connection of the accused with the crime and in regard thereto the prosecution had failed to prove that there were sufficient corroboration of his evidence. HELD: (i) The High court rightly came to the conclusion that there is no infirmity in the evidence. [601E] (ii) There was no corroboration of evidence of the eye witnesses. The evidence of PW 2 and Dinkar was that he had seen the piece of cloth which was found in the tailor 's shop. He did not say that the cloth was given by accused No. 2 to him. He also stated that he used to wash the clothes of accused No 3. He was a witness to the recovery of the articles from the house of Dr. Nanavati. The fact that the tailors were found dead in the room of accused no. 2 and the evidence showed that the blood stained clothes of the deceased were taken out from his pocket and he had been asked to produce the gunny bag which he did. The witness was not cross examined on behalf o the accused No 1. [625E F] (iii) There is no corroboration in material details in regard the connection between the accused and the crime.

The appellant 's land was acquired by the Town Planning Officer under section 23(1) of the Gujarat Urban Development Act, 1961. The appellant ' s land was declared surplus on the basis of the declaration made by him under section 32 (1)(iii). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said declaration and also the notification issued under section 31(1)(iv) of that Act. The High Court held that the declaration of intention to make a scheme was not appealable, and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the decision of the Town planning Officer determining the amount of compensation in the appellant 'S case was not an appealable one. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Town Planning officer under section 63 (1) has a duty to determine the compensation payable to the owner of any property or right injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions of section 69. [876C] 2. The object of the Act is to provide for the development of urban areas and to provide that the cost of acquisition of land shall be determined on the principles laid down in the Act. Under section 67(1), the owner or occupier of any land injuriously affects by the use of such land, his property being estimated at its market value at the date of declaration of the intention to take a scheme without reference to improvements contemplated in the scheme other than improvements due to the alteration of its boundaries. [886D] 3. The provisions of sections 66 and 67 are as follows: (i) If the owner is not provided with a plot in the final scheme or if the contribution to be levied from him under Section 66 is less than the total amount to be deducted therefrom under any of the provisions, he shall be entitled to obtain compensation in respect thereof from the local authority or from any person benefited or partly from the Local Authority and partly from such person as the Town Plan Officer may in each case determine. (ii) The owner of an original plot who is not providing a plot for a public purpose or purpose of the local authorities which is beneficial partly to the owners or residents within the area of the scheme and partly to that general public, shall be liable to pay compensation from the market value of such plot at the rate of Rs. 1/ per sq. metre. [896D E] 4.
