The owner or the occupier of an existing plot who has been allotted a plot under section 66(1 ) is entitled to get compensation from local authority in cash or in such other manner as may be agreed upon by the parties. The amount of solatium payable to an owner for loss of land has to be determined by the local Authority under section 69 and not by the market price of the plot at which the plot is situated. [906E F] 5. The principle for determining the compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not; compensation is payable on the value of the plots at the time of declaration. [916G H] 6.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama. The first respondent was the daughter of Seethama. She had a brother and two daughters, who were minors at the time of his death. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Madras, on the ground that the gift was altogether void for uncertainty, and that the appellant had no male issue but left two daughters surviving him. The trial court held that the property was not capable of being divided as it was not intended to be divided by selection made by the legatee, but only in the legatees. On appeal the High Court held that there were no express words in the will which showed that the testator intended that the daughters should get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. Held, that the language of the will was clear and unambiguous and it could be inferred from the circumstances that the intention of the testator was clearly to select but the word "he shall give to the female children". The words "he may give to any person a right to choose in such circumstances as he chooses to select" were not intended by the testator. The will was not a mere instrument of gift and it was intended to make a gift which could be made certain by selection of the daughters and not for the daughters to make the selection. The words used in the Will were "he will give to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legateees making the selection in the order in which they were named".

The plaintiff appellant, a co sharer of the land in dispute, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the plots in dispute. The defendants contested the suit on the ground that the defendants were in joint occupation of the lands and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff 's name was clearly recorded as a co co sharers with the defendants and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The District Judge, however, held that there was no evidence on record to prove that the defendant was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the respondents were in separate occupation of land or plots in question and the appellant had absolutely nothing to do with them; and that the suit was barred by section 49 of the Act. The first appellate court found that there were no evidence to prove the fact that the appellant was prevented by operation of law from filing any petition under Section 9 of U. P. Consolidation Of Holdings Act or that he had become entitled to be protected by the trustees. In second appeal, the High Court held that the trial court had come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to extinguished. The High Court also found that the District Judge had come into error in holding that some sort of fraud must have been committed by the respondents and continued in possession of any proceedings that may be instituted. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in law in holding the suit to be barred by Section 49 of U P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, as the defendants had not filed any petition for setting aside the decree of the trial Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the District judge on this point is not sustainable in law and the judgment of the High Courts cannot be allowed to stand.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Haryana. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as Deputy Prime Minis ters in the Punjab Legislative Assembly on various grounds including that he was not eligible for appointment as Deputy PM at the time of his election and that he had been given an opportunity to make a representation against the appointment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was still functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Minister is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Ministry of India. [312E] 1.2 The prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. This Court has held that the prescribed oath must be divided among the Ministers. [412F] 1:3 The prescribed form in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirement of Article 75(4) is only for a Minister of the Union and there was no separate form even for the Prime Minister. [512G H] 1.:4. In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers, he takes the same oath as the other ministers are required to take. He maintains that yet in view of his clear statement, he describing himself as Prime Secretary and this practice is in vogue eversincely 1950. [506F G] 1 :5. The prescribed Oath should be split into two part, one for descriptive and another for all purpose he is an oath or affirmation. He also states that describing the Minister as DeputyChief Minister is composite only and there are no 3 Constitutional sanction for this post of Joint Prime Minister along with his other submis sions. [ 506F G; 506A] 1 Whether the petitioner is still functioning or not, is a question of fact. The requirement of article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India and the Indian Independence. [504H; 506B] 2.1 In viewof the clear admission made by Respondent No, 1, there is nothing on record to show that he has been appointed as Deputy Director of the Punjab Vidhan Sabha when the affirmation was administered. He cannot be said to have been appointed in any manner whatsoever. The expression "in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution" is merely descriptive and not a mere descriptive one.

The appellant was a public utility industry. The management of the appellant 's factory carried on a strike which resulted in the closure of the factory. The workmen were paid wages for the period during which they had worked. The appellant challenged the validity of the strike on the ground that it was illegal and void under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act, 1948. Held, that the action of the management was not justified as a result of the closure on 1st November, 1948, but only because the workmen were allowed to work for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounts to an illegal strike and the workers were entitled to wages for such period. The question whether the stoppage of work on 1 st November, 1949 amounted to a strike was not to be decided by this Court as it was not a case where the management had acted mala fide or with a view to deprive them of their rights under the Act. The action of a management in refusing to work on the night of 1st December, 1948 was not one of the acts of misconduct and therefore could not be regarded as a strike so as to amount to a break in the continuity of service of the workman concerned. Held further, that it is well settled that if an employer has acted mala fides or with the intention of making a false statement or giving false information which he knows or believes to be false, then the employer cannot be said to have committed any misconduct and consequently the action taken by him was illegal. The fact that a very large number of leave applications were put in for various reasons pointed to the concerted action and that the mills had been closed on 1th November,1948, does not affect the validity or otherwise of the action.

The appellant was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious or any material to quash the proceedings, set aside the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the Act, there is no justification for its display thereafter, and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 of the Penal Code, the public exhibition, circulation or distribution or the production of the film, even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence under section 293 I. P.C., notwithstanding. Section 79 of that Act, the Board certifies a film as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292 1.P.(1A) of the Act to punish such exhibition unless the ground covered by the two laws be different. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The trial court when itars the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under section 5A(1A). [5B] (2) The High Courts in exercise of their appellate jurisdiction under article 136 of the Constitution cannot interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the trial court. [5C D] (3) The finding is based on the combined operation of section 5 A and section 79 I.p.C.. [5D] (4) The expression "public exhibition" in section 80 of the Code means a certificate granted under it by an authority competent to grant it. It does not mean that the certificate granted by such authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence punishable under section 3A(I A).

The petitioner, a retired High Court Chief Justice, was appointed as an Advocate General in the Patna District. He was appointed by the State Government to perform all or any of the functions expressly imposed by this Code on the Government Pleader and also any pleader acting under the directions of the Government pleader. The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the Bihar Judicial Service (Appointment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1976, as violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court rejected his petition holding that he was not a legal practitioner for seeking lucrative practice of a single government Pleader. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that his client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legally cover for seeking offers of law offices, and that his clients are entitled to be considered for appointment as well as for promotion to the post of Additional District Judge. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Court cannot sit in appeal over the decision of the High Court on the question whether the petitioner is a legal representative or not. [775C] 2. The Government Pleader, Madras is only an agent of the government Pleader and his duties are only to the Government who are his principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a Public office. [764D E] 3. The State Government has a number of other duties to discharge. It is only in an independent and responsible character, that Government does not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number one of them. [753E F] 4. The fact that the Government Pleaders of this Court are employed by the Government on remuneration paid from the public exchequer and having regard to the various functions and duties to be performed by him in the due exercise of that office, most of which are of an independent or responsible character is the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [758E F; 776A B] 5. The learned Advocate General has a very limited role in a lawyer who has a higher responsibility for his client and has a high responsibility for the conduct of the cases even as any client, who has an independent legal profession, to calculate income on a speculative basis, as this Government Pleader has done in the instant case. [759E F G] 6. The duty of the State Pleader is not only to conduct in courts cases to which Government are a party but also to perform. He owes no responsibility for this duty. [761F G] 7. The duties of the Govt. Pleader, Chennai are duties of a public nature. They are only those who have a high dedication to the people. They must be hold to be public offices within the meaning of a protected right under article 19(1)(f) of the constitution. [762A B; 762B] 8. The appointment of a number is not an appointment for the holder thereof but for the lost briefs through the 'writ ' route. When there are several thousand cases in the High Courts and elsewhere, it is difficult to subscribe to the U.S. situation on which the President and the Chief Justice have pronounced. [763C] 9. The Advocate General is only a agent of Government Pleader who has no higher responsibility to calculate the cost of litigation by not appointed a number. He has a large number of others as his principles, and practice inside the Secretariat or outside the Court. [765D E; 777A B C] 10. The time has come to examine the quality of the product or service, control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the beneficiaries who are the third world clients, and practise internal distributive justice oriented on basic social justice so that the profession may flourish without wholly hitching the calling to the star of material amassment immunised by law from the liabilities of other occupations.

The Mills purchased 5,000 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Mills held on May 6, 1948, a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the Company to Rs. 100 per share for every three shares held by it in this company. The shares were distributed among the shareholders as dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income Tax Act. The Mills exercised the right to take over only 66 shares out of the shares offered and resolved that the right of the remaining 1,600 shares be distributed amongst its nominees. The mills accordingly made a resolution increasing the capital of Rs. 200 per share. The appellants contended that the distribution of the right was not a distribution of dividend within section 2 (6A), but an independent and separate definition of "dividend" in section 2 of the Act, and that the High Court was wrong in holding that the distributed by the Mills to its shareholders amounted to a distribution within the extended meaning of that expression in section2(6 A) of that Act. Held, that the decision of the High court was correct. The definition of 'dividends ' in section 3(1)(a) of Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1948 did not apply to the present case because the distribution by the mills amounted to distribution of "Dividend". The word "dispute" in the definition of a "dopt" in Section 2(5A) was an inclusive and not an exhaustive definition. The expression "dominate" in s 2(1) (a) was not an inclusive one, but an exhaustive description of the expression. The word 'dominates ' in the context of that definition is a comprehensive definition and not a complete definition.

The appellant was the returned candidate. The election petitioner filed an application under section 86 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for examining his witnesses who were kept present in the Court on the date fixed for recording their evidence. The respondent contested the petition and denied all the allegations made against him. The trial court rejected the application holding that the names of the witnesses were not mentioned in the list filed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI. The High Court dismissed the election petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had failed to mention the name of the witness in the List as required by sub rule(1) and that the name was not mentioned therein. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub Rule (1), of Order XVII is in respect of witnesses to procure their presence before the Court without the assistance of the Court. If it was implicit in Rule 1A that it only enables the party to examine only those witnesses whose names are mentioned in sub rule 2 and yet the party is unable to produce him or her on his own under Rule 1 A and in such a situation the party of necessity has to seek the assistance by issuing summons through the Court or otherwice which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring the attendance of a witness whose name is not shown in the lists filed under Sub rule (I) of Order XVIII. [539C D] 2. The requirement of sub rule 1A is that the party may bring any witness to give evidence or produce documents without applying for summons under R Rule 1.

The appellant was appointed Principal of the College in the year 1981. He was appointed as Principal of an institution in the month of April, 1981. The Manager of the Institution issued a letter to the appellant informing him that the Committee of Management had no power to make any appointment and that the committee of management had no authority to make such appointment. The appellant challenged the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the date on which appellant was made as Principal, the Committee had the power to appoint the appellant and therefore the Committee was not competent to make the appointment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order dated April 27, 1981 contained in the radiogram was communicated to the Manager of Institution. If the order was valid and power to pass any consequential order was withdrawn or suspended it would not be open to the Selection Committee to make and select appellant nor the Manager on behalf o the Committee could issue appointment order dated May 1, 1981 to the petitioner and the appointment of the appel lant would be by a body not authorised to make appointment. [982C D] 2. The power to frame appointment is conferred by the regulations. It is an enabling provision which confers power on the State Government without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind any regulation as also make such other order consistent with the provisions of the Act as it deems necessary and in particular may by such order modify or cancel such appointment and pass such consequential order as may be necessary. [8982D] 3. The Committee of management has no power under section 9 to make appointments on May 1. 1981. If it is satisfied that any person has been appointed as head of an Institution in contravention of the provisions contained in this Act, the State Govern ment shall after affording an opportunity of being heard to such person cancel such appointments and pass consequential order accordingly. [90E] 4.

The Delhi Cloth Mills (Control) Act, 1941 was passed by the Central Government in exercise of its powers under section 3(1)(a) of the Act. Section 3(2) of that Act provided for exemption from sales tax on "goods" and "goods". The petitioners challenged the validity of the said Act on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it was not a law relating to trade, commerce or intercourse within the meaning of article 19(1) (g) of its Constitution. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The word "goods", in section 3 of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, is used in the sense of "goods"; it means goods which are capable of being bought and sold by a person either directly or indirectly. It does not mean goods which have been purchased from another person. [503C D] 2. The expression "goods " has been defined in section 2(g) to include "goods which are ordinarily used in relation to the manufacture of any goods, but does not include "any kind of fabric". Therefore, the word "textile" is used for the purpose of defining "goods ". [504D] 3. The definition of "textiles" given in section 4(1), however, is wide enough to cover all kinds of cloth including rayon "fabric", and not any kind of fabrics. Therefore, it cannot be said that the word 'textile ' has been used in a sense which would mean "a textile". [505E] 4. The question whether the tyre cord fabric is an exempted commodity or not must depend on the facts of each case. It is not necessary to decide whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption. [504F G] 5. The words "totton" and 'goods" in section 5(2)(a), (b) and (c) of section 3, are wide enough and have been used for different purposes. It cannot be held that the legislature intended to exclude from its purview the goods which were not "goods ", the use of which alone would make them liable to tax. [506F G; 506A] 6. The fact that the tyre fibre fabric may be the end product for the Delhi Cloth Mill, the crucial question is: Does this product constitute a fabric which is a textile? If the answer to the question is in favour of the appellant, it would not arise. [403B C] 7. The language of section 4 (1) of Act clearly shows that it is meant for "tseeds" and not for any kind or fabric. Therefore even if the tyre fabric may not be the part of the fabric, the relevant question is whether the goods under consideration constitute a fabrics entitled to exemptions. It did not, therefore, seem propel. for the High Court to finally decide on merits, that the taxing authorities had committed error apparent on the face of the record. [ 506E F] 8. The view taken by the High Courts that the goods in question constitute the "end product" which they sell in the market is not correct. [312F G].

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The respondent workman was a Senior Supervisor in the Company 's establishment at Dhanbad. On the basis of an enquiry conducted by the management, the respondent was appointed as a supervisor in the factory. After the completion of the work, the appellant company transferred the case to Labour Court Patna. The Labour Court held that the transfer was illegal and directed the reinstatement of the respondent workman with full back wages. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant Company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workman and transferring the case from the Labour Court, Dhanbad to Labour court Patna should have given an opportunity to the management to transfer the case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Government was misled by the representation of the workmen and transferred the matter to Labour Courts, Patna. [294G] 2.1 The Government had no power to refuse to give an opportunity of being heard to the workman. The order of transfer in that case was quashed for non consideration of the representation made by the workman, and without affording a reasonable opportunity of representing his views on the question and the reasons of the order are reduced accordingly. [295B] 2(a) In the instant case, the Government was wrong in transferring the appellant 's case from one Income Tax Officer to another without hearing the assessee. The impugned order of the Government is therefore set aside.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. The respondent company was a registered trade union of the Hotel Imperial, New Delhi and its workmen were employed by it as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi. On October 7, 1955, the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, issued an order referring the dispute to the Additional Industrial Tribunal, Delhi including the terms of reference. The appellant company challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that the reference was incompetent and two grounds had been urged in support thereof; one was that the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , as the union had no knowledge of the nature of the dispute, and the other was that it was not a living person. The Tribunal held that the dispute was incompetent because the union was not represented by an officer of the trade union and therefore the reference did not become incompetent. On appeal by the appellant company to this Court, HELD : (i) The reference which is otherwise valid does not become competent merely because it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the dispute. [481 B] (ii) The fact that in the order of reference the word "as represented by" has been added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent. The fact remains that the disputes which were referred for adjudication were between the employer and its employees, which were mentioned as its workmen. [482 C] (iii) The word " as represented" has a technicality upon technicality and it does not affect the competence of the order. The nature of dispute is also specified in the terms and conditions of reference, and therefore, the reference which was otherwise valid did not became incompetent merely because the workman was entitled to be represented through some officer, such as its president or secretary and it was that officer who will really represent the workmen before the tribunal, [482 D] (iv) The words "as representing by the hotel Workers ' Association, Katra shahanshahhi,Chandni Chowk Delhi " have been added. It is in this sense that the convenience of informing the tribunal to whom it should send a notice on behalf of the workmen whose number is generally very large.

The appellant imported a consignment of rod bushes and camshaft bushes, which were assessed to duty under Heading No. 84.06. The Assistant Collector of Customs held that the goods were classifiable under Heading 84.07 as they were parts of the engines referred to in Heading No 84.6. He also held that Heading No . 84.63 was applicable to the goods imported by the appellant. In appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that since the bushes and bearings are not identical articles but they are distinct and separate, yet there is no material for holding that the bushes, imported by them were parts thereof. The Revenue filed an appeal before this Court against the order of the Tribunal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification grants exemption in part from payment of Customs duty in respect of the rod bushes, and not under Heading 8.06, which is a residuary item. [84D] 1.2 In view of the fact that the trees are not mentioned under Heading Nos. 8406, 84.08 and 84.09, the appellant is not entitled to claim any exemption for the bushes even if they are parts of such engines. [85E F] 1:3 The Notification does not contain or refer to the parts of internal combustion piston engines, but only refers to parts thereof, and therefore, it cannot be said that the parts imported by appellant are parts thereof.[85G H; 86A] 1 4. In view Of the fact, that the Notifications do not contain any indication that they have been imported by a person other than the owner of the goods, the Notification will apply to parts of those engines and not to parts which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines. The Notification would apply to the items of the engine, such as, parts of machinery, engines, etc., and not as parts thereof; but, even assuming that the tree is part of such engine or engine, it will not get the exemption as provided in the Notification. [86B C] 1 5.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that they were not entitled to any right in the management or share in the offerings in the Dargah and also prayed for a decree declaring that their father was entitled to the management of the Dargah. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove ouster of Fathima Bee from the fight or management of Dargah and that they had not acquired any right by birth in the said offerings. In appeal, the High Court held that the defendants were not debarred from claiming any right of Mujawar as the right was given only to the male members and not to the females. The plaintiffs filed an appeal before this court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiffs are claiming through Fathita Bee as well as the plaintiffs. They have claimed through Fatima Bee that they have asserted hostile title and possession of the offerings made by right of succession and possession. [526C] 1.2 In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathina Bee or the plaintiffs, it was neces sary for the defendants to plead that they asserted hostile ownership in the offering. The defendants were claiming through the Fathila Bee as their father and mother. They had not at any point of time received a share in their offerings nor had they claimed any right till their death in 1957. [525D E] 1:3 In order that the rights of Fatina Bee may be denied, and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through fathima Baksh, should be impleaded as defendants to the suit. The defendant respondents are claiming only through Fatha Bee and not through Fats. They are claiming right in their possession or share over the offerings. [506F G] 1 4.1 In order for making out a claim of ouster from the right or claim of any share in management or offering to the knowledge of FATHima Bee, it is nece sary that title was denied and as a matter of fact, the plaintiffs were claiming only to have acquired right by virtue of the alleged gift. [504F G; 506A] 1 5.1 There has been an express denial of Fats ' title at the time of the judgment of the High court in 1909, if she did not have a title according to Muslim Personal Law that title is denied and she was expressly ousted out from the enjoyment of any shares in the Sheba gors. [ 506B] 1 6.2 The plaintiffs were entitled to claim through FATHita Bee for the right of Jokina Bee as per Muslim Personal law.

The appellant was a tenant of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy the quarters, he filed an application under section 15(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for a house rent allowance. The Authority appointed under section 14(2)(b) of that Act allowed the respondent 's claim for house rent allowances on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from the respondent. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the 1st respondent that the terms of the contract between the parties included the rule quoted above and therefore the position in law is that there is no absolute right in the 1 st respondent to claim the house rent Allowance. HELD : (i) The rules which must be included in the terms thereof are inconsistent with some of the terms and conditions of the definition of "wages" contained in section 2(vi) of Act. [1348 C] (ii) The rule is consistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Act. It does not make the grant in such absolute terms. The rules do not make it a part of the term of the agreement between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one of those places would be entitled to house rent, allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation, he ceases to be so entitled. [1448 C D] (iii) The Rules which are framed under section 7 of the , do not create any absolute right or interest in the employee to the house Rent Allowance and that as far as possible, there is a condition subsequent to the definition contained in sections 7 & 11 of Act that the employee should be posted at a place where he has no accommodation offered to him. [1548 C E] (iv) The provisions of section 23 of the are inconsistent therewith with some other terms of contract. The rule which requires an employee to vacate the quarters offered to the employee is not the same thing as the value of any house accommodation referred to in the Act, and that is, it does not affect the rights of the employee. [1648 C F] (v) The scheme of the rules framed under the Act is consistent therewith with the various provisions of the . The rules are consistent with sections 7, 11 and 11 and do not affect any right or obligation in the employees to house Rent allowance.

The detenu was detained under section 3(1) of the (3) and (2) of The . He was served with a notice dated March 14, 1980 under section 4(1)(a) of that Act. On February 18, 1980, the State Government issued an order under Section 3(2) directing the detention of the detenu. On March 25, 1980 the detenu made a representation to the Advisory Board which rejected the same on April 3, 1980. The detenu filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the said order and also the order of detention. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The detaining authority without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies of which were asked for by the detenus, mechanically refused to supply the copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated February 14,1980. [352B] 2. The grounds of detention were as elaborate as possible, that the substance of the statements, of which copies were asked was more than sufficient to enable him to make an effective representation against his detention. There was thus an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply of the grounds of the detention, all the basic material relied upon or referred to in those "grounds" must be supplied to the detenu with reasonable expedition to enable he to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. [353C D] 3. The supply of copies of statements and documents to the detenus was an integral part of the right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. [354D] 4. The right to make representation is a fundamental right and it is not open to any person to make representations against his order of preventive detention. [355E] 5. The representation made by the detenu is not a mere formality but an empty formality. It is only after the detenu makes a representation that he can make a representation. If the representation is made, the same has to be considered and disposed of in accordance with law. [356F] 6. The detention order must be communicated to the detenue within three days from the date of receipt of the representation by him. It was on receiving a direction from the Central Government that the copies were supplied.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a joint appeal against an order acquitting several accused persons, convicted only on the question of sentence and not to interfere with the judgment of the Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was wrong in holding that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 of the Criminal Procedure Code did not in terms cover the case of an appeal by the State against several accused person jointly tried and convicted by one order at a joint trial. [447 D] (2) The question whether a joint appeals by several accused are maintainable under section 419 or not is essentially a question of fact to be determined on the facts of each case. It is well settled that in an appeal against acquittal by the High court, the State has no right to prefer one appeal against all of them. [427 D] The High Courts were wrong in upholding the maintainability of a joint application for revision by the state against several persons convicted at one trial. The question of competency of a Joint appeal by several persons acquitted at a common trial is confined only to a few accused persons and not against an accused person who has been acquitted.

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in foreign territory. The income tax authorities treated the income as income of the assessee and assessed it to income tax under the 1918 Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. In further appeal, the Tribunal held that the foreign business of the appellant was charged under the provisions of the 1918 and therefore the foreign income could be deemed to have been charged under section 3 of the Act. On reference, the High Court held that in the case of business carried on in foreign country the business as such is not liable to tax under section 2(2) of 1922 Act because the assessee had no right to claim relief under Section 25(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was applicable only to income on which the tax was payable under the Act and not only income on whose foreign business the assessee claimed relief under the 1922 law. HELD: (i) The assessee was entitled to exemption under section 10(3)(iii) of that Act in respect of interest on securities as well as for income from house properties owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. [912 B] (ii) Under the provisions Of the 1918 Acts, the charge was made on the receipt of income in British India and as the income received by the assessee is derived from the foreign partnership and not from the Indian business itself, it must be taken that there was an assessment to tax on the foreign profits. [936 C] (iii) The question for determination is whether the foreign company was entitled under the 1961 Act to relief of section 25 (3) in respect Of interest on security on securities. It is manifest that by section 3 Of the 1922 Acts, income tax was levied by virtue of section 14(2). [936 D] (iv) Under section 3, the tax is payable by an assessee but the assessment of the tax has to be made under the head "Profits and gains of business, profession or vocation". The expression "profits and gains" in section 2 (2) means income derived from business. It does not mean income which is earned on behalf of the foreign partner.

The respondent company entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said Department for construction of the Capital Project, mahalhinagar. The appellant company supplied the bricks in accordance with the agreed rates. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department was a works contract" The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court was wrong in holding that the transaction contemplated by the contracts entered into between the applicant and the Public Work Department of Government of the State of Gujarat was a work contract. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The contract in this case is a works Contract. It is not a works contracts. The contractor shall have to pay the same himself, Clause 24(1) of the contract provides that the contractor shall give notice to the Executive Engineer or his Assistant of his intention of making delivery of materials and on the materials being approved by the Executive engineer or his Asstt. of his Assistant. Clause 23(2) provides that in case of any dispute arising between the parties, the matter shall be referred to the arbitration of a person appointed by the Government. The arbitrator shall have power to refer such disputes to the Arbitrator. The agreement in this regard is not an agreement of sale and therefore the contract in question is a contract of sale. [163B C] 2. The High court has rightly answered the questions in favour o the assessee. [164C D] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, who was a member of the Lok Sabha and elected to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, filed an application before the President of India under Article 32 of the Constitution for a direction to the President to declare his election as void on the ground that the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President on March 25, 1971 had ceased to be in operation on April 1, 1972. The petitioner contended that the proclamation of emergency was not validly issued and that the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were invalid as they had been duly issued in accordance with law and that since the two proclamments had been validly issued, the Proclamation could not be challenged. The President passed an order on March 29, 1977 declaring the said Proclamation to have been in operation from April 1. 1972. On March 30, 1977 the President promulgated the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1976 which was replaced by the Constitution of India (Amendment) Act 1976. The validity of the said Act was challenged before this Court by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the constitution. This Court held that the Presidential Order dated March 25. 1977 had ceased as it stood during the period when the House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act 1975 was passed and therefore, the proclamation was not valid. The Court further held that even though the said Proclimations had been issued by a competent authority under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 352 of the Consti tution, the President acting as the President by Proclamation dated March 27, 1977 had continued to be the President and the Proclamation was revoked by him by the Proclamation dated 21st March, 1977. The petitioners contended that since no such proclamation was issued in terms of the provisions of clause (4) of article 352 of Constitution, the Presidential order dated March 29. 1977 could not have been declared invalid on the basis of the Proclamation. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The two Pro civiations of emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions passed by the Houses of Parliament approving each of them had not been published in the official Gazette. [439C] 1.2 The proclamation of Emergency was issued on March 27. 1977 and the President 's Order of the President dated 29th June 1975 was revoked on March 30. 1977.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the premises No. 29 South Masi Street, Madurai, which was originally constructed by him as a temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951, were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The Trial Court held that the property belonged to the Thoguluva family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf of the family. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court and found that the appellant had not paid court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the properties belonged to Thogaiahva family. [156 B] (2) The property was a private property of the appellant and he had no title or interest therein. He could not have claimed any share in the property under 0. 1,126 6 0 in 1950. [157 C] (3) The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application for setting aside ex parte decree. He was therefore entitled to contend at the time of the leave application that the said property belonged exclusively to and was an alienable private property. [158 D E] (4) The appellant 's case was accepted by the Trial Court but was rejected by the High court and the High Curt held that it was not open to him to raise a question of law as to whether the property was private or public temple. [159 G H] (5) In the present case, the suit in which the appellant claimed that the respondent had been in management of the properties for andon behalf of family, was one of the trustees of the said family. The suit was therefore not maintainable.

The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of re employment. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant and they urged that the practice started by the respondent was not justified as it was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiffs. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiffins, but the Tribunal directed that the clerical staff should be paid Rs. 1/ per day and the subordinate staff as well as the subordinate employees should be allowed Rs. 2/ per month. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance of t he respondents. The appellant 's claim for cash allowance was not pressed and the matter was left to the discretion of the Tribunal. The fact that the re employment of retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations, did not justify the view that the problem did not call for any consideration at all. (ii) The appellant had throughout been making provision for tififfin allowances in addition to the wages and dearness allowance, a provision for thiffin arrangement for t ernment of its employees and in fact when after the award was pronounced in the proceedings of 1956 and this question was left open to the decision of the High Court on the ground that the Tribunal had overlooked the fact that it was a case of reemployment. The question whether the appellant should be awarded cash allowance at the rate of Rs. 3/ per days or not, was a matter which was within the discretion o f the Tribunal and the High Courts in dealing with such matters. (iii) The High Court erred in holding that the limited direction issued by the award is either improper or unjustified. The High Courts have failed to appreciate the fact as to whether the Tribunal has overlooked the facts and circumstances of the case. The decision of this Court in M/s. Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869, relied on. (iv) The question posed by the High court was not a matter within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Labour Court. The finding of the Industrial Tribunal that the respondent had been under an obligations to provide certain cash allowance to its employees is erroneous in law. The award of the industrial tribunal is set aside and the case remanded back to it for fresh decision on the question whether as a result of the demand made by it, the appellant would be entitled to cash allowance.

The respondent, a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund, was a subscriber of the State Bank of India. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, which were framed under the , and the Reserve Bank of England was the agent of the Railway Administration. The respondent applied for removal of attachment on the ground that he had ceased to be a member of the Provident fund. The application was rejected by the Central Government. On appeal by the Union of India, the High Court held that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was not liable to attachment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amount represented provident Fund money and therefore the attachment could not be made until the money was converted into sterling and was transmitted by the Reserve bank to Browne, and that in any event the money representing provident fund moneys which by section 3 of the , was immune was exempt from attachment. HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the Money represented Provident Fund money. When the amount lying with the ReserveBank as the agent was attached the Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal and not till then. [1413 C] (ii) The Union of Indian was a trustee for Browne and it had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into pounds and to remit it to Brownee. The payment was required either under the first intimation at Liverpool by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the bankers of Browne at Birmingham. The Reserve Bank was, as already stated, the agent for conversion of the amount into sterling. [1513 C D] (iii) The Central Government was a Trustee for the subscriber of money. It was not the agent or of Browne to receive payment on his behalf. So long as the money remained under the control of the railway administration as provident fund Money, it was exempt therefrom from attachment and sale.

The appellant was a contractor. The respondent workman was employed as a contractor in the appellant mill. He was paid wages for the period from 1st April, 1966 to 31st March, 1971. On his failure to pay the wages he filed an application under section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 before the Labour Court praying that the order of termination be set aside and the respondent be directed to reinstate him with back wages. The Labour Court held that the appellant had merit on his side and that the respondent was entitled to reinstatement with back salary. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held (i) that the question whether or not the employer had lost confidence in the employee was essentially one of fact aadmissible in law; (ii) that it had been established beyond doubt that the employer was efficient and the workman was efficient; (iii) that there was no evidence with regard to the misconduct alleged by the respondent. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Labour court is set aside. [505C] 2. The question whether the employer has lost confidence or unfair labour practice is essentially one matter which can be determined only on the basis of the social conscience and judicial interpretation of the law in this branch of discharge simpliciter. If it comes to the conclusion that the termination was a colourable exercise of the power or was a result of victimisation or unfair Labour practice, the employer must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. [500D E] 3. The management has passed the order in such a case and it is not open to the court to interfere with such termination. [506F G] 4. In the instant case, the workman did not even file a counter affidavit and the counsel for the Union agreed that the orders of termination were not a camouflage to cover up what really was an order (1) of dismissal. The fact that the workman had not filed a counter statement and the Labour Appellate Tribunal had considered it judicially, would not vitiate such a finding. [504H] 5.

The petitioners, who were the beneficiaries of a scheme for the benefit of the disabled persons, filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the constitutional validity of the provisions of the , and the right to receive the additional payment under the scheme. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State would be entitled to take up the matter with the spirit of the Government against whom the inquiry was conducted by the Deputy Director (Eye Treatment) and the Sub Divisional Magistrate, appropriate follow up action is contemplated by the Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the provisions in the , are not applicable to the case as they were not covered by the scheme of the . Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The State would approach the matter not with the sense of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. [245C] 2.1 The State shall take up this issue and process the claims of the victims for such other bene fits under any of the existing schemes now in force in the State, their cases shall be considered for such benefit. [246D] 2(a) The State will not be entitled for any benefit of pension under any other scheme now in existence in the state. [247E F] 3.2 In the course of his counter affidavit, the respondents have stated that they are willing to render help to the victim within the constraints of their resources. They have also stated that the victims entitled to receive a further sum of Rs.5,000.

The Assam Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over management and Control) Act, 1984 was enacted by the Legislative Assembly of Assam. The Act was amended in 1984 and section 1 sub clause (ii) of this Ordinance provided that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asom Rashtra bhasha prachar Samiti had its jurisdiction immediately before the commencement of the Ordinance by a Notification No. F.1(2)/84 dated 1.10.84 issued under Section 3 of the Act. The State Government promulgated an Ordinance called the Assam Rationalisation and Control (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984 which was published in the Assam Gazette Extraordinary dated 15.12.1984. The said Ordinance was replaced by the Assam Act No. XXIII of 1984. The petitioners who were members of the Board of Management of the Rashtra Bhashaprabhashi Sabha filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said Ordinance and also the notifications issued under the Ordinance and the Act and also praying for a direction to the State Government to restore the management of the Samiti. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Act was not enacted by Parliament in exercise of its power under Article 246(2) of the Constitution of India, but it was made with the assent of the Governor of Assam and published in Assam Gazette dated 15th December 1984. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Assam Panchayat Samiti Act, 1964 are not inconsistent with the provisions of Article 246 (2) and (3) of Schedule I to the Constitution. [176B] 2.1 The Act and the notifica tion issued under it take over the management and control of the affairs of the Parishad.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the respondent, married her daughter in law to Kamala Devi on May 10, 1938. The marriage was performed on May 11, 1938 and the gift was made some two years after the marriage. The appellant 's father died in December, 1938 leaving behind his wife and children. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties which were decreed by the trial court. The High Court affirmed the decree but it held that the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband to her daughter was not valid. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant had no right to dispose of the property in dispute and the respondent could not be said to have been competent to execute any deed of gift except with regard to a reasonable part of the Estate of her deceased husband at the time of the marriage ceremony. The gift was not made in fulfilment of the moral obligation flowing from the ante nuptial agreement made by the appellant, but it was made after the death of the widow and the son in law. The fact that the respondent had the limited right of disposal did not affect the validity of the gift as it was not a valid gift. Held, further, that there was no consideration for the alienation from the point of view that the marriage of the daughter was a religious duty and the promise to make a gift to the daughter as her marriage portion created a moral or religious obligation in fulfilment Of which it was competent for the father to execute a deed of gifts in favour of the son of a reasonably proportionate portion of his estate.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice alleged by the appellant were clearly proved and that the appellant had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the allegation of corrupt practices committed by Tej Singh in the present case was not established; (ii) the evidence adduced by the parties showed that the margin between the votes secured by Tej singh and Avtar Singh was only 123.5% and (iii) the poster which contained the appeal purporting to be of Ruplal was a false one. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The allegations of the corrupt practices alleged are clearly proved. [417C] 1.2 In the instant case, the allegation that the respondent had indulged in corrupt practice is clearly established. It is also clear from the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by parties that Tej Singh was known to him. He was not collected with the printing of the posters. The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubts that Tej singh had indulged himself in corrupt practices particularly when the printing was done by him and he was not collecting any work for the poster. [416D E] 1:3 In view of the very narrow margin of votes between the defeated and returned candidates, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of section Tej Singh will be deemed to have been cast in my favour, is that Tej Kaur had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collect any money from the printing. [414F G] 1 4. The allegation of the respondent that the payment of the vouchers was made by him is clearly proved by him.

The appellant was the Chief Minister of the State. He was a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. The respondent, who was the President of India, was the Secretary to the Government of Punjab and Haryana. In his application for contempt, he alleged that one Devinder Sharma was a forest Minister in his Council of ministers headed by him. The appellant alleged that he had been a Forest Secretary in the council of Ministers consisting of Shri Bhajanlal and Shri Bhajan lal. He also alleged that the respondent had been making preparations to commit criminal contempt against him. In the application for Contempt, it was stated that the Chief Secretary had made an order or decision in his favour. The High Court dismissed the application holding that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have jurisdiction to punish for contempt of itself. [893C] 1.2 In other words, the High Court derives its jurisdiction to impose punishment for contempt. When no punishment is imposed by the High court, it is difficult to say that the High Courts had exercised their jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution. The jurisdiction of the High courts is to punish a person who has been punished for contempt and not for any contempt. [884C] 2.1 In other cases, the Supreme Court derives their jurisdiction to punishing for contempt from Article 215. [876D] 2:2 It does not mean that when the HighCourt acquits a contemnor guilty of criminal contempt, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without remedy. The power of the high courts to punish is not available to the petitioner because he has been deprived of his liberty by the impugned order. [896E] 2(a) In view of the fact that no appeal is maintainable under section 19(1), as there is no exercise of jurisdiction or authority by the Court, it cannot be said that the decision of the Supreme court in not exercising its jurisdiction or powers to punish the petitioner for contempt is made in the exercise of its jurisdiction. [906F] 2 (b) The High court exercises its jurisdiction and power under Article 215 which confers jurisdiction or right on the High Curt to punish an contemnor for contempt but does not include the jurisdiction to dispose of the case either by punishing the contemnor or by acquitting him. [916G H; 91A] 2.(c) The jurisdiction to convict for contempt includes also the jurisdiction of a court to decide whether such punishment should be imposed or not and when the Court is conferred with the power or jurisdiction to act in a particular manner, that is to say, by imposing punishment for Contempt. [92D] 3.1 It does no mean that where the High Commission has acted in excess of its powers or authority, it can impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor. The order of the Court cannot be challenged as arbitrary or illegal. [93F] 3(a). In the instant case, the appellant was interested in keeping a watch over the dignity and integrity of the courts will not he without remedy.[92H; 93A] 3.(b) There is no scope for interference with the order of punishment for such exercise. The appeal is incompetent and is accordingly dismissed.

The appellant was the owner of certain lands in Bombay. The rent note was executed by the respondent landlord in favour of the appellant and the rent note had been duly stamped. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he had failed to pay rent within the time prescribed under section 111(g) of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of section 111 (g) were not applicable in this case and that the notice as required by section 111 had been given. HELD : (i) The provision in sub section (g), which is a general rule of justice, equity and good conscience, or whether it is merely procedural and technical rules introduced in the section by the legislature and was not based on any principle of justice equity or good conscience and cannot govern leases made prior to the coming into force of the Act. The provisions of sub section(g), as they stood before 1929, were intended to apply only to leases made after 1st April, 1930, and not to leases executed prior to 1st May, 1930. [1023 D] (ii) The provisions in sub s.(g) are not exhaustive and do not deal with any particular provision of law which is applicable to a case where the tenant has failed to establish that he was going to avail of the forfeiture and that can be done by the filing of a suit as in English law.

The appellant was appointed as a driver in the respondent 's factory. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been found guilty of misconduct by the Enquiry Officer and the enquiry was held against him. The Labour Court upheld the dismissal order but the High Court confirmed the punishment of dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the Arbitrator had power to interfere with the punishment in the instant case having to the facts and circumstances he was not justified in setting aside the dismissal of Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan; (ii) the High court erred in holding that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to enter into the merits of the case or interfered with the penalty of dismissal; (iii) the award of the Labour court was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the respondents of showing cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. 17; and (iv) the interference with the quantum of punishment in respect of Rama Shanker and Barmajripradan was erroneous while another writ petition filed by the Management was allowed and the High Curt quashed the order of dismissal on the view that the enquiry had been vitiated because the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the first part of the Standing order deals with several punishments and requires finding of guilt in respect thereof. [366C] (2) The second part of Standing Order deals with two different stages concerning disciplinary proceedings against a delinquent, first holding of a departmental inquiry into the charges where principles of natural justice must be implied and second the infliction of graver punishment before awarding which opportunity to show cause has been provided for; but the plain reading of the standing order read as a whole does not warrant any such assumption. [367E F] (3) The first part is in the nature of an exception to the general rule that where the enquiry is held by an authority competent under the Act, it shall be deemed to have been conducted by such authority and the inquiry has to be held according to the procedure prescribed by the statute. [368F G] (4) The third part of sub section (2), which deals with three stages in respect to disciplinary proceedings, is not intended to apply to a case where the Enquiry officer has no jurisdiction over the matter or interfered therewith. The second parts of the sub section deal with two distinct stages concerning the disciplinary proceedings and require finding of guilty in respect thereto. [369F G; 369A] (5) The word 'may ' occurring in the first clause of sub sec. (2)(b) is not to be given a restricted meaning so as to include even an appeal or revision against the order passed by the authority concerned. It is only when the enquiry officer has acted without jurisdiction that he can interfere with it and if he does so, he cannot have recourse to the provisions of the Act. [370A B] (6) The words 'any other sufficient reason ' in sub sec.(2)(a) are not intended for the purpose of giving a restricted interpretation to the word 'shall '. It must be remembered that the expression 'may" is used in the context of the first and the second part.

The appellant was in occupation of a land for not less than ten years. The respondent landlord filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the land on the ground that he had occupied the land for more than ten y years and that he was in continuous occupation of the said land for a period of ten years, and that the appellant was entitled to be deemed tenants under section 52 or any other provision of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent landlord had not acquired any right to possess the land as he had no right over the land in question. In appeal, the High Court held that the Explanation to Section 7D of the Act was applicable only to a person who had occupied land for less than 10 years within a period specified in section 52 and therefore the appellant could not be deemed to have acquired any rights under the said Explanation. The High Court also held that since the respondent tenant had surrendered the land, he could not claim possession of it as he was not entitled to possess it. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the interpretation of Section 7 D of the Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 was erroneous and that section 6D was applicable to a tenant who had been in occupation for more then ten years within the period specified therein. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Explanation to section 7D is not attracted to a case where the land has been occupied by a person in occupation on the basis of an oral permission or an unregistered deed purporting to be a lease deed granted by a competent person to be continued in possession of such land till the commencement of the [112F G] 1.2 The Explanation does not apply to a landlord who is in occupation as a tenant for morethan ten years before the commencement date of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1970. The Explanation applies only to persons who were in occupation at the commencement when the Act came into force and not those who were not competent to lease the land. [112G] 1:3. The expression 'tenant ' is defined in section 2(1) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act 1949, as meaning a person holding land less in extent than the ceiling area. The definition of tenant in section 3(2)(a) of that Act includes a person continuing in occupation after the commencement thereof. [113A B] 1 4. Section 6D of Kerala Land Reform (Amendment ) Act, 1968 provides for a right to cultivate any nilam after the 11th day of April 1957 and was cultivating the nilam at the time when the said Act came in force. The proviso to section 6 D(2) is not applicable to such a person as he has been in possession on the date of commencement of this Act, or which had not actually transferred possession of land to the landlord before the date the commencement. [114F G; 115A B C] 1 5. Section 7E of the Karnataka Land Reforms and Ceiling Act, 1964 provides that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law or in any contract, custom or usage or in the any judgment, decree or order of court, any person who is In occupation of land for the purpose of a period prior to the 11 th day of May, 1957 shall be deemed tenant if he or his predecessor in interest occupied such land on that date. [115E F] 1 6.

The appellant was prosecuted under Section 135(a) of the . The goods were seized on 21 4 1967. The appellant pleaded that the goods were smuggled and that he had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under Section 136(a). On appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant knew that the boxes were smuggled goods and therefore he could not be said to have been smuggled or imported into India without an import licence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the evidence showed that the respondents had placed a box there, and that the statement made by them to show the place from where they came, was not voluntary and that there were no circumstances which could enable the appellant to know where the goods came from or when the goods went. HELD: (1) The possession of the goods on 21st April 1967 there is no evidence to support the contention that the appellants had been in possession of such goods without knowing that they were illegally imported or smuggled. [557H] (2) The mere possession by the accused of such a goods could not enable the prosecution to apply Section 106 of the Evidence Act when the appellant could not know where he was an innocent receiver of such evidence without knowing what the goods actually were, and writing on boxes in which they were found. [541A B] (3) The fact that the person who had taken delivery of the boxes was not examined by the prosecution witnesses shows that the contents of the box were not produced before the Court. It is immaterial whether the appellant was found in possession or not. If he could have succeeded in explaining satisfactorily how he was a witness to show where the articles came from, or when they were imported, were questioned, he may have had a chance of getting the benefit of doubt. [542C D] (4) The word "evidence" is used in connection with the prosecution evidence and it has been used in relation to matters which are relevant under section 123(2). It is not necessary that the accused should be examined by a Court to prove the fact from which he was brought into India. In any case, there was some evidence to enable the Courts to come to the conclusion that the articles must have been known to the appellant. [543D E] (5) The words "evidence of the person in possession" in section 123 (2), are not relevant for the purpose of proving a fact under section 106 read with section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act.

The appellants were partners of a firm which was dissolved in February 1948. The firm was dissolved on June 26, 1946 and the accounts were to be rendered by the Registrar of Firms. On July 1, 1946, the firm was registered under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The appellants filed a suit for accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar from April 1, 1947 to June 26. 1946, and claimed that the suit was not maintainable by reason of the provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa Act. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs had no right to sue in respect of the profits made on the sale of bales of Gwalior cloth and that the claim for accounts was barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court held that the suits were not maintainable because the provisions Of section 4 (2) Of the Rewa States Companies Act 1935, did not apply to the suit as the suit had been filed within the period of limitation prescribed under section 4 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that by reason thereof the suit for accounting of the cloth Association was dissolved and the provisions in section 4 were applicable to the case. HELD : (i) The suit was barred because the suit filed by the plaintiffs was not one for accounts but for accounts. [403 B] (ii) Section 69(3)(a) of Act, which is a general provision, provides that no company shall be formed for the purpose of carrying on any other business that has for its object the acquisition of gain by the company association or partnership or by the individual members thereof unless it is registered as a company under this Act. [404 C] (iii) The provisions of the section are not applicable to cases where the suit is filed on allegations which on the face of them show that the contract of partnership on which he sues is illegal, the only course for the courts to pursue is to say that he is not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the courts cannot adjudicate in respect Of contracts which the law declares to be illegal.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 9(1) read with section 5(2)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that on 8.6.1986 at 2.0.1986 the respondent along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 1 of the compartment No 1 of a train. On 8.4.86 at 2 P.M., the respondents along with three others were charged for offences under sections 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471 read with Section 34 IPC. The trial court found that the respondent was guilty of the offence under section 5 (2)(a) readwith section 5 of the Act and ordered issue of process against him. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed issue of a process against the respondents. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the publication of an article attributed to a judicial officer was not cognizable in contempt jurisdiction by virtue of section 50(1), of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; (ii) the notification dated 8.5.1986 issued under section 4 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1973 was invalid as it did not contain any provision for investigation and issuance of process; (iii) the High court had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings in exercise of its powers under section 482 of the Cr. P.C.; (iv) the complaint was barred by limitation; (v) the trial court acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offences and ordering issue of summons against the accused; (vi) the order dated 1.7.1986 passed by the Judicial Magistrate, Chaibasa, was not a nullity as it amounted to an abuse of the process of the Court or not; (vii) the proceedings were vitiated because the complaint did not disclose any offence under the Act, and that the High Courts had no power to quash them in exercise thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "any offence" is a well settled principle of interpretation of statutes that when two interpretations are possible, one which would lead to an absurd result or absurd consequences, the other which would render the provision nugatory. [463C] 1.2 In the instant case, the complaint does not disclose that the allegations made in the article constituted an offence under Section 499 of IPC and at the same time constitute an offence Under Section 500 read with Sections 34, 468 and 471 read alongwith 50(l) of Cr.P.C. The High Court was therefore justified in quashing the proceedings of the Judicial Magistrates on the facts of this case. [464D] 1:3. In view of the language of the sub section which uses the words "where such contempt is an offence" and does not say 'there the act alleged to constitute such contempt, is an offences '. [466E F] 2.1 It is well settled that if a person commits a criminal offence under certain circumstances, he must be punished with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The expression 'abetment ' has been used in the context of Section 5(3) of Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1974. [467F G] 2:2 In view thereof, the ingredients of an offence punishable under section 499 IPC are not made out and the High courts have rightly quashed the proceedings against the respondent. [468H; 468A] 3.1 There is no merit in the contention that the complaint has been filed by the respondent with a view to harass him. The allegations made therein are vague, indefinite and vague. It is difficult to appreciate how the complaint can be said to have been filed with a mala fide intention as an exercise of power under section 50 (1) of Act, in its ingredients and content.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of fine.
