In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the High Court had no power to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State; (ii) the Magistrate has not given any reasons for rejecting the surety because the Magistrate does not spell out the details of the bail, and so the magistrate ordered that a surety hl be released on his own bond without bail. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The law is brought out in the Report: "The evil of bail system is that either the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties for providing bail or suffer pre trial detention. [343C] 2. The practice which is now being followed in the United States is that the accused should ordinarily be released by the court to further the ends of justice and nothing in Sec. 389(1) which reads: 389 (1) Pending any appeal by a convicted person the Appellate Court may, for reasons to be recorded by it in writing, order that the execution of the sentence or order appealed against be suspended and also if he is in confinement, that he be released from justice. [344C D] 3. The procedure which is being followed by the magistrate in the instant case is not the money tag. The evil of the accused has been brought out by the Magistrate, lawyers, members of Parliament and other legal experts. It is imperative for the magistrate to release the petitioner on his personal bond without sureties. [345D] 4. The duty of the magistrate is to release a surety if he has one or more sureties. If he has two sureties, he may be released in favour of another surety. But if he does not have sureties, the court can direct that the surety should be released. [346E F] 5. The discretion of the Magistrate to release on his self bond is not a judicial function. It cannot be said that an under trial is worse of than a convict or that the power of the court is less than a sentence of imprisonment. [347F G] 6. The magistrate should always bear in mind that monetary sureties, especially when risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not its very essential and there are other factors which are sufficient deter mination against flight. [348A B] 7. The Magistrate must always bear the mind that financial hardship is one of the considerations for granting bail. If a Magistrate is Satisfied after making an enquiry into the condition and background of the applicant that the applicant has his roots in the community, he can safely release the accused on his request to appear or on his behalf to support himself and his family with the result that burden of his detention falls heavily on the innocent members of the family. [349F G; 350A B C] 8. The court should always keep in mind the need for liberal interpretation in areas of social justice, individual freedom and indigent 's rights, and no hard and fast rule can be laid down as to what would be the appropriate remedy. [350C D].

The assessee, a registered firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 52. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle Amritsar, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that the business called 'Castle ' at Bombay was a branch of the appellant. The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner held that the assessee had no business to carry on its business and directed the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court for decision. The Tribunal, however, did not give any direction to the Tribunal as to how the income of 'C'astle should be computed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The finding of the Tribunal that the income from 'C 'astle was not computed and included in the assessment of the respondent was not conclusive. [431 E] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax officer in the assess ment in question of the income. [427 G H] (iii) The Tribunal had erred in not giving any direction for the purpose of section 66(2). [435 A B] (iv) The decision of the Appellate Tribunal was based upon a misconception that in the previous year to the year of assessment 1951 52, 'Cantle ' had carried on business and had earned income. It was not open to the Court to ignore other relevant matters on which the Appellate Tribunals relied.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was appointed as a Secretary to the Government of Punjab. He was also directed to file his affidavit. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 confirming the earlier seniority list. The respondent filed an appeal against the said order before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that he had not been impleaded as a party in the writ petition. In the appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that since the Minister concerned might give a personal hearing to the parties, and thereafter pass the necessary order in the matter, the Minister should be impleaded as an intervener in the Writ Petition filed by him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in directing that the Minister be impleaded in the petition, as in the view of the Judge allegation made against the Minister. [972C] 2. The direction for impleading of the Minister as a respondent in the present case is given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the affidavit and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. [993D] 3. The order of the High Courts directing that Minister be added as a member of the Public Service Commission should be set aside. [1004E] 4. The directions for impleading the Minister in the case of Duggal respondent should also be set at liberty.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. He filed an application under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that he had been in arrears of the rent due from him under the lease. The Magistrate held that the amount was due as arrears of land revenue and directed the eviction of the respondent. On appeal the High Court confirmed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the view taken by the High court that arrears of rents due under a lease cannot be recovered under section 258 of the Act is erroneous. HELD: The provisions of section 259 are not applicable in respect of rent of land or buildings under the management of the Cantonment Authority. [347 B] The words "claimable by a Board" in section 259 must be read as meaning that the proceeding before the Magistrate was not one under the Code of Criminal Procedure and, therefore, neither could a reference be made by the Sessions Judge to the High Commissioner under section 438. [348 C] The provisions in section 258 are applicable only when the rent is recoverable by a board or a Military Estates Officer under the Act or the rules made thereunder. Therefore, the proceedings before the magistrate were not one contemplated by the Act and the Rules which empower the Board to let out the land or building upon the ground of arrears. [349 E] The two cases on which reliance was placed before the High Courts arose under section 81 of the Code.

The appellant was in the service of the respondent company as a Section Salesman. He was terminated from service on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. The respondent company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the termination of the appellant by the respondent Company. The High Court held that the appellant was not a workman within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's services were terminated, and that the reference was incompetent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Labour Court has given findings on the nature of the work being part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promoting salesmen and local travelling salesmen appointed in the area of his operation. [474G] 2. The finding of the Tribunal that the respondent was not an "workman" is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour Court. It is seen from the records produced before this Court that the Tribunal further observed that the appel lant was required to supervise the work of local salesmen, and local traveling salesmen were appointed in place of the petitioner. The supervising work of the other local salesman was part of the same work considered for the purpose of showing publicity and advertisement and of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. [476B C] 3. The question whether the appellant is a workman or not is a matter of fact. It has to be determined by the evidence adduced before the Tribunal. The Tribunal has given reasons for coming to the conclusion that the termination was illegal. The findings of the Tribu nal on the question whether it was illegal are binding on the Labour court and the High Courts. [477C D] 4. In order to come within the definition of workman under the Industrial Dispute Act as a result of which the appellant has to pay an amount equivalent to three years salary at the rate he was drawing when the respondent 's Service was terminated, in addition to what amount they were paying during the pendency of the appeal under orders of this Court. [478D] 5. The appellant was required by the Labour Courts to supervise and promote sales of the company. The supervision of the others local sales manu factured by it directly through their wholesalers who in their turn sold the product to various dealers appointed by the company in the areas where they were working. The inspecting work of other local Salesmen was part and parcel of his duty as skilled, unskilled, unskilled and/or clerical in nature. [479G H] 6. The workmen covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within their definition of workmen under the industrial Disputes Act. The management has given a finding that the appellants were employed to do canvassing and promote sale of the product of the Company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company, and deposited the same in the company itself. [480G H; 481A] 7. The work involved the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study is carried out of the market condition.

The Company was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The Company was incorporated in 1950 with the name of the State of Madhya Pradesh. In the year 1951, the Company was formed and registered as a Company under the Madhya Bharat Co operative Societies Act, 1950. The company was incorporated on 1.10.1956. The Government of Madhya Bharat issued a Notification dated 1.9.1977 under section 182(2)(i) of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (Act No 66 of 1950). In pursuance of the said Notification, the company was granted a lease of the land in question for a period of five years from 1.4.1956 to 31.3.1957. The lease was renewed from time to time by the State Government on 1st October, 1977. The respondent Company filed a suit against the Company for eviction of the Company on the ground that the Company had not been holding over under the old lease and that it had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act 66 of 1951. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the company did not enjoy the status of a Gair Maurusi tenant and that the respondent Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant. The High Court, however, held that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the Government and the Company continued to remain in possession of the same as a lessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that there was no 'phakka ' tenancy within the meaning of section 181 of the Code. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression "pakki" is defined in the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue & Tenancy Act. [180G] 2.1 The word "phakk" has been used in the sense of a term which includes a right to occupy land for purposes of agriculture and also to include a right of occupation for purposes connected with agriculture. It is not and cannot be disputed that subsequent to the withdrawal of the appeal from this Court, fresh terms were agreed upon between the Company and the Government to enable the Company to remain In possession of land as a lease. [179A B] 2(a) The word 'pokka ' has been defined in section 2(i) to mean a person who holds land from the State or to whom a right is granted by this Act or the Collector and who is not entitled to hold land as such. It means a person holding land from a State Government and not from a private owner. [183B] (b) The expression 'pankka ' in section 182 of the Madhya Pradeshik Cooperative Societies Act is defined under the M Bharat Cooperation Society Act, 1951. In view of the definition of 'pakhk ' in the M agna Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 1964, the word 'Pakki ' has to be read as a whole and not as a part of it. [184C] 2.(c) The term 'pachka ' is defined by section 2 (i) which defines a 'khatka '. It includes a land held under the State. [185D] 2 (d) The definition of "pakhka" in section 185(1) of Madhya Pradehshik Cooperative Society Act 1951, is wide enough to include any land held by a person in accordance with the provisions of that Act. The word `pakk ' has not been defined either in the Code or in the Rules made thereunder. [186F] 2:2. The definition given in section 3(1)(a) of Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 is wide and includes a person whose land is held by him as a Bhumiswami. [187G] 3.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1950 was enacted to provide for the acquisition of land in an estate and for certain other purposes. Section 1(3) of the principal Act provided that the Act shall come into force on such date or dates as may be specified by notification. By section 1(4) of that Act the State Government made a declaration under section 3 of the Principal Act, which was published in the Gazette on July 1, 1949, that the land in question was needed for public purpose and that the provisions of Ch. IV of the Act were applicable to it. The appellant who was the owner of the land filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 1 (3) Of the Principal Seventeenth Amendment Act, 1964 on the ground that it was inconsistent with or takes away orabrashed any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Legislature had no power to enact a law in respect of land which was within the ceiling limit applicable to the holder under any law for the time being in force. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The right to compensation which is not less than the market value under any statute providing for acquisition by the State of any estate and where the land is within the Ceiling limit applicable, under any other law for a time being, in force, cannot be questioned because section 1.(3), proviso 2, and is not attracted to the case. [337C D] (2) The power to bring into operation the provisions contained in Ch. III of Part III is not an absolute power but only a power to make provision for compensation for the property so acquired and either fixes the amount of the compensation or specifies the principles on which, and the manner in which, the compensation is to be determined and given. The right conferred by section 1 is not a law within the meaning of article 31 A. [437D E] (3)(a) The word "law" in Ch IV of Part I of the Schedule to the Constitution means any law made under the authority of a law which provides for the compulsory acquisition of any land or building or structure standing thereon, and includes any order made by a competent authority under section 4. [427D E; 427E] (b) The expression "law", in Ch III of Schedule I of Part II of the schedule to the Act means any act done or purported to be done in pursuance of a legal duty imposed on it by law which is required to be performed by a person having lawful authority to do so. [535G H] (c) The words "law and order" in section 1 of the Orissa Land Reform Act, 1951 are not restricted to laws which provide for compulsory acquisition but only those which are within the legislative competence of the State. [ 427A B] (d) The provisions of the Ch. II of Part 11 of Schedule 1 of Part 111 of the , are not applicable to them because section I(3)(b) is merely a power of making an order under section I (3). [427B C] (e) The Act was passed in exercise of the power conferred by Ch.III of Part 1 of Schedule II of that Order and therefore, it could not be said that the impugned notification issued by the Government was ineffective. [ 428C D]. (f) The State Legislature has no power under section l(3). proviso 2 only provides for compensation to be paid to the landholder for the loss sustained by him in consequence of his interest in the land. The Act is a law relating to acquisition of lands and not to acquisition by private persons.

The widow of her husband 's estate was in the hands of her son who died in 1947. The widow filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that she had no interest left in her, and that the widow had no right to recover possession of it from the widow. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the appellant 's mother was entitled to claim possession of her property on grounds of equity, justice and good conscience. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The widow 's title to the property during her lifetime could not be surrendered to the reversioner. [355 D] (ii) The right of a prior alienee from the husband 'Sreeramu vs Kristamma, I.L.R. , referred to. (iii) The fact that the son had died in 1950 and the widow was in possession of only the property left by her would not make any difference. [356 F] (iv) The appellant ' s right to challenge the right of the widow under section 6(1)(a) of the Hindu Law is a voluntary act on the part of the husband and she is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. [358 G] (v) The mere fact that a son has died in 1949 would not by itself make him a coowner of the estate. It is only when the widow becomes entitled to possession of property that he acquires title from the wife or his spiritual benefit. [359 B] (vi) The position of a person who has acquired by adverse possession the limited interest of a Hindu widow is exactly the same as that of an alienee and if the title of such person has been completed already, it could not therefore be defeated by a surrender made by the widow in favour of the reversionary heir.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Cotton Mills Company was formed on January 1, 1956 and it was registered as a public limited company under the U.P. Industrial Development and Regulation Act, 1948. The appellant company had been running its mills for the purpose of manufacturing cotton yarn. The respondent No. 2 who was the Managing Director of the Cotton Mills company, was appointed Receiver in respect of the said shares. The respondents Nos. 1 to 3 were also appointed as Receiver in their place. The appellants filed a suit against the respondents Nos., 4 and 5 for recovery of the amount due from them on account of the purchase of the cotton mills by the Cotton Mill Company. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant company did not have any right to participate in the meeting of the Board of Directors of the Mills Company, and that the order of the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares in question and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the Cotton mills Company had lost its right to vote at the meeting. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton Yarn Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member under section 169 of the Act and that there being an appointment of a Receiver in favour of the Government of Uttar pradesh, the order passed by the Collector was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment of the shares of the Polytex Company held by the cotton Mills Company had not deprived the holder of the share whose name is entered in the Register of Members of the company the right to voting at the meetings of the Company or to issue a notice under section 170 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. [875C] 2. The order passed on February 1, 1985 by the collector was an order within the meaning of section 169(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act read with section 190 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [820F] 3. The fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged in favour the Government is not relevant Sections 172 to 178 A of the deal with the contract of pledge. In view of the foregoing the pawnee in the instant case i.e. the Government had become the member of the polytex Company by reason of the appointment of the Receiver in his place and to call the meeting in accordance with the notice issued under section169(1) (a) thereof. [821C D] 4. The finding that 3.50, 000 shares have not been pledged is a finding of fact based on no evidence. It is also not possible to accept the contention that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was no legal or other equitable right to interfere with the order. [822D E] 5. The mere appointment of an Receiver in the name of the appellant does not make any difference between the contract and the sale of shares. It may be that a Receiver has been appointed in respect thereof but it is not possible for him to have a legal or beneficial interest which would override it. [823F G] 6. The question whether the order was an illegal one or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [825G H; 879A] 7. The sale of the goods in question by the appellant is not a valid sale. It has been held to be a valid transaction of a person who had no legal interest in the goods. [828C D].

The petitioners filed a suit in the representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure for a declaration that they were owners in possession of the land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur had no sort of right in the suit land and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that they had been owners in posses sion of the suit property along with others, and that they could not be dispossessed without following due process of law. In appeal, the District Judge held that since the question involved in the case was merely one of title to the suit lands and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit would be maintainable before a civil court, and accordingly dismissed the revision petition. The petitioners filed an appeal before the High Court which came to the conclusion that the issues involved in this suit were not triable by a civil Court by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 and therefore they were not entitled to file a suit for declaration that the land was shamlat deh. The High Court held that the issue involved in both the suits was merely a question of title and it did not lie in the mouth of the plaintiffs to raise any question of fact or law. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The trial Court had rightly dismissed the plaintiff 's suit against which this petition is filed. [833C] 1.2 In view of section 11 read with section 13(1) of the Act, it cannot be said that any person claiming right, title or interest in any land vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under this Act or in respect of any matter which the Commission or the State is empowered by or under the provisions of the , or in any original suit, application or execution proceedings. [820F G] 1:3 The High Courts have not been able to interfere with the judgment of the trial court on the ground that the jurisdiction of the civil courts had not been taken away by virtue Of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation). Act, 1962. [821F G; 834H] 1 4.

The appellant Board was constituted under the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply Act, 1978. The Board was established under the Act with effect from 1st April, 1979. The appellant Board had been supplying electricity to the respondent company on its own account and had also been paying interest thereon. The respondent company was also supplying electricity at the same rate as applicable to other consumers. The supply of electricity was governed by the Andhra Electricity Supply (Regulation) Order, 1948. The tariff for the supply of electrical energy was fixed at Rs.1.50 per unit. The rates were revised from time to time and the appellant had been paying the bills for the period from 1.4.1979 to 31.3.1980. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the demand on the ground that it did not contain any norm of guideline with regard to framing of terms and conditions for supply of electric energy by the Board as well as the conditions on which it was supplied being statutory, the provisions under the conditions of supply that the Board shall not pay interest on the security deposit had statutory basis and accordingly could not be struck down as arbitrary. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no order of this Court adjudicating the rights of the Board on the consumer in respect of the validity of consumption security deposit being condition precedent for the Supply of electricity by the respondent. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the fixation of tariff under the terms and condition of supply of Electricity is a statutory function and therefore cannot be struck as arbitrary on the basis of a commercial transaction governing a bank deposit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the Board is bound to pay interest or not arises in respect thereof. [278C] 2.1 The fixation of terms & conditions for the purpose of supply is a condition precedent and therefore it cannot be said that the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19 (1) (f) and (g). [278D] 2(a) The Board has been conferred statutory power under section 49 (1), of the Act to determine the conditions for supplying electricity. It is not correct to say that if there is a revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in consumption security deposits since it has direct bearing on the operation of the Electricity Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. [279E] 2 (b) The condition of Supply requiring a consumption security Deposit has a direct bearing upon the operations of the respondent which are required to be maintained in such an event. [280F] 3(a). The conditions of supplies providing for non payment of interest on security deposit are not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. No.

The petitioners were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre in the same posts and discharging similar duties. The Recruitment Rules were framed by the President under Article 309 of the Constitution of India. The recruitment to various cadres in the service was made under the Sect ion of the Indian Telecommuni cation Service Group A and Group B. For the first time the Union Public Service Commission advertised for the recruitment of 10 Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I, namely Assistant Director and Deputy Director. The petitioners were also included in the list of officers eligible to be promoted as Executive Director. In the writ petitions filed by them they challenged the validity of the Recruitment Rules on the ground that the said rules were violative of Article 14 and 16 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong are not given any Special Pay in these grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is paid for the arduous and special nature of the functions to be discharged in the Telephone Communication Centre. [1010B] 1.2 The Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and the transferred officials and that the transferred official had to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay. It was paid for t he arduly and special character of the function to be performed in the telephonecommunication Research centre. [102C D] 1:3 The petitioners belong to the Indian Telephonecommuni ty Service Group B and they have been working throughout in the said Telecommunication research Centre. They are not entitled to any Special pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Communications Service who are selected by the Union public service Commission after a rigorous competition examination need to be given special Pay. [103D] 1 4. The question relating to denial of promotional opportunities to the petitioners according to the Recruitment rules is left open to be agitated before the Central Administrative Tribunal.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent 's factory. He was dismissed from service on account of misconduct. The respondent filed an application under section 42(4) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 for relief under section 7 8 (1) D.A.R. and for consequential reliefs. The Labour Court held that it was not necessary for an employee to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4). The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending that the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application within the period prescribed under section 43(4). On appeal, the High Court held against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the second respondent had not complied with the provision of law and that the order of dismissal was illegal. HELD: (i) The provisions of section 42 are intended to enable an employee who has been dismissed or discharged or retrenched or Whose services have been terminated from employment on account thereof, and to see whether it is possible to come to any agreement and an application to the labour court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute. [707 D] (ii) The scheme of section 7 of the Act appears to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Labour Court. [808 E F] (iii) The object of the Legislature is to provide for the settlement of industrial disputes in respect of certain matters specified in Schedule 11 of which item 3 reads "Dismissing of any employee except as provided for in the standing orders applicable under this Act". Under section 79(1) proceedings before a Labour Court in respect thereof must be commenced on an application made by any of the parties to the dispute etc. and under sub section (2) every application under sub s.(1) has to be made in the prescribed form.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were occupying the property under a registered lease for 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. The respondents resisted the suit contending that the appellants had not vacated the premises after 31.07.1971 as tenants from month to month and further contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that in absence of a month 's notice under section 12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsif, and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The first appellate court held that in view of the expiry of the period of lease the appellants were entitled to continue in possession after 31st July, 1971 as tenants. The High Court dismissed the second appeal holding that the respondents had no right to remain in possession even after 31 st July,1971 and that the entire proceedings was misdescribed. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant appellants that the courts below were wrong in holding otherwise. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether a landlord after the expiry or not is entitled to move the Court by an application under section 11 of the Act is wholly inapplicable in the facts and circumstances of the case as the respondents by their notice, did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. [775C] 2.1 In the present case, it is the Civil Court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or making an application Under section 12 of the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1947. The view taken by the High Court that in no event the landlord after 31 7 1971 would be entitled to file a suit and in any event section 12 is wholly irrelevant in the case of the present respondent, is not correct. [750D] 2(a) In the instant case it is not disputed that the appellant had filed an application for eviction under section 13 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 before the Civil Judge Ranchi. The suit was filed by the appellants as an application to be treated as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. [751E] 2 (b) In view of section 12, the proceeding has to be held as a suit. It is the same court before which both a suit under section11 and an application thereunder are to be filed. In the case in hand it is only the Civil court, Ranchi who is the proper court either by way of appeal or revision. The jurisdiction of the civil court is not barred in the fact of the matter. [753C] 3(a). The question does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy was concluded by the first appellate Court in favour of the respondent. The occasion for filing an application u/s 12(3) can arise only where the matter is covered by section 12 and as such, there is no point in asking the appellants to file such an application. [764D] 3 (b). In the facts of the instant cases, it cannot be said that the respondent has not sought an extension or a suit within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The fact that the suits are filed by two different persons does not make any difference in the matter and the question is whether the petition which was filed before the civil Court was one under section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. [774E] 3.2 In the absence of any specific provision in the Act, it can be said to be a suit as contemplated by section 11 (1)(b) of Act. It cannot be held that the application which was made by the appellant was not one under Section 12 of Act at all. The respondent has no right or interest in the property as the dispute was concluded on the expiry date of the lease and, therefore, there was no question of limitation.

The appellant, a registered Society, filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the court of District Judge, Jaipur City. The suit was decreed by the trial court on 4.9.74 and the appellant 's application for withdrawal of the suit was made by one Laxman Das Swami. The appellant ' s election petition was dismissed by the High Court on 5.9,74. The appeal against this order was also dismissed by a Division Bench of the High court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the trial Court had committed several serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the elected Secretary of the Society and had therefore full authority to withdraw the suit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The trial court has rightly held that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Proce dure was not maintainable. [237B] 2. The High Court in C.W.P. Beyond pointing out that even according to the impugned judgment of the trial Judge the errors in the judgment were serious, it ought to have been rectified. But if a party makes an application before the court for setting aside the decree on the ground that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the order if it is satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree. [238C D] 3. The courts below were right in holding that the applications of the appellant invoking the inherent jurisdiction of the Court were not maintainable, and the High Courts were not right in dismissing the appellant's application as not maintainable because the trial judge had failed to exercise his revisional power on the assumption that it had no jurisdiction to do so. [239D] 4. The court has been clearly wrong in dismissing a suit under its inherent powers. [240E] 5. In view of the finding of the courts below that Hari Narain Swami was not the elected secretary and was, therefore, not authorised to withdraw his suit, the prayer for withdrawal was not made on behalf of the appel lant at all and the impugned order was passed as a result of the court being misled. [241F] 6. The question whether the trial courts had jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of suit under their inherent power is a matter which has to be decided by the Court having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case. [242G H] 7. The Courts below were clearly wrong, in dismissing appellant 'S ' application as barred by limitation. If a party making an application for setting it aside on the grounds that he does not give its consent, he is not authorised under law to withdraw such suit. [243H; 244A] 8. In this case, the High Curt has held that there was no jurisdiction in the Court to cancel or withdraw the plaint under its general power and the only remedy to the party is to institute a suit. The Court has also held that in the exercise of inherent powers under section15 1 of Code of civil Proce edure, a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. [244B C] 9. In such circumstances, the courts have been clearly right in dismiss ing the appellant application as non est. [245C D].

The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but on appeal by special leave, Held, that the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" in section 72 of the Act were omitted from section 72 during the period specified in section 3. The words "for the space" used in section 2(a) of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, were intended to be read with the omission of the words ' for the time being in force ' in section 7 of the said Act, viz., June 27, 1940. The word " for a period not more" used by the Legislature was meant to have a retrospective effect and the intention of the legislature was to give a retrospective operation to the section as it originally stood. The fact that the Ordinance had been promulgated on April 1, 1946, did not affect the continuance of the Ordinance in force until April 1. 1946 when the Act came into force. The appellant could not be convicted under the provisions of the Constitution for any period beyond April 1., 1946. The Ordinance having continued in operation even after April 1,. 1946, the said notes continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India and therefore the Ordinance having been promulgated by the Indian Legislature without any limitation on its duration was to continue in force till it was repealed. The effect of such omission was not to continue the period of the Ordinances which had been passed between June 27 , 1940 and April 1 , 1946, but was perpetual in its duration with the result that it continued in force immediately before April 1 1, 1947, when the Ordinance came into operation.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., for murder of a young boy, and sentenced to death by the High Court. The High Court confirmed the death sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the death penalty should be awarded or not. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the decision cannot be construed as laying down a ratio decidendi. [1065 H] 1.2 In the instant case, the High Courts have not considered the question whether the death punishment should be imposed or not must, in my view, be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such cases. If the general observations on sentencing jurisprudence made in Rajendra Prasad 's case (supra) are to be regarded as 'law declared by this Court ' within the meaning of article 141 so as to bind all Courts in the country, then the observation or the so called guideline as to the effect "special reasons" necessary for imposing death penalty must relate not to the crime as such but to the criminal". [1066 H 1065 A] 1:3. The question whether a sentence should be passed or not should be left open to the Judge who tried the accused, and if he is satisfied that the extreme penalty is awarded, he should pass the same inference as drawn in the earlier case one way or the other. If he is of the opinion that the capital punishment should not be imposed on the offender, then he should have recourse to section 302 of the Indian Penal Code read with Section 354(3) of Cr. P.C. [ 1066 A C] 1 4. The sentence of death passed under Section 302 I. P., C. is a rule of universal application and it cannot be said that the award of death sentence should relate, not to a crime as yet but to a criminal. [1167 D E] 5. In the present case, there was no special reasons for imposing the death of the two appellants. The judgment of the High court is set aside and the appeal is remanded to the trial Court for its disposal in accordance with law.

The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with misconduct in the discharge of his duties under the Indian Railway Establishment Code, and was dismissed from service on 30th September 1953. The order of dismissal was confirmed by the Appellate Authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the departmental proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to produce nine witnesses in defence, all that is suggested is that these witnesses could only state what opinions they had formed about the work, efficiency, and integrity of the appellant. [583 F] (2) The High Court did not deal with a number of submissions made by the appellant which could have had that effect upon the departmental proceeding. It was for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental authorities, which had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he had suffered some injustice which to be set right. [584 F] In the instant case, it was not open to the appellant, at any stage, to raise a plea of a revocation of special leave at this stage after hearing arguments. The question as to whether the departmental inquiry was null and void could not be raised in the present proceedings. [585 G H] (3) It is true that the charges were framed against the appellant under the provisions of the Indian Railways Establishment Code. But, it is possible that the appellant may have been emboldened by the failure of officers to report earlier that charges should be framed and tried. In any case, this could not stand in the way of the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed and fully inquired into by Officers whose integrity and sense of justice are not challenged.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The sales tax authorities levied tax on the appellant under section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 on the sale of manganese ores in the State. The appellants contended that they were not the last purchaser but the M.M.T.C. was the last seller within the state and therefore the M/s. T.C., was liable to pay tax. The High Court held that there existed a bond between the parties and the sales were inter se between the appellant and the M,M. T.,C. and the foreign buyers. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the contracts between the appellants and the respondent were similar. HELD: (1) The contract between the two parties is not identical. [445B] (2) The contracts between them are different contracts and it is the S.T.,C., which entered into independent contracts with their foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis. Under the contracts, the seller 's duty is to place the goods "free on board" a ship to be named by the buyer. This is not in the course of export. [444D] (3) The fact that the contract between M and the S was one of sale within the Sate does not make it clear that the goods were different from the contract of sale. [44C D] (4) The High Courts have held that the transactions between the seller and the buyer are different transactions and it has to be found out whether the contracts are integrated or the contract is different. If they are different, then the purchase by the State Trading Corporation from the appellant would not make the two contracts either inte rated or the contracts in question to be export. The fact of the case that the sales are inter se within the territory of the State does not render them separate and independent contracts in the sense that property in the goods passed from the appellants to the M and, therefore, the purchase is the last purchase in the state. [45C D; 46A] (5) The normal presump tion attaching to F.o.B., contracts is that property therein passes only when they are put on board the ship. In the instant case, the goods are not inter se outside the State and therefore, there was no privity of contract between them from the S t.C.; and the sale by the appellant to the respondent. [46E F] (6) The sales in question are different. The purchase by S. T./C. is an independent one between the Corporation and its foreign buyers and, hence, the purchases by the respondent are different from those of the appellant.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. He was terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. The respondent filed an application under section 25B(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 before the Labour Court for reinstatement and compensation in lieu of back wages. The Labour Court held that the termination of service of the appellant was illegal and inoperative and directed reinstatement of the respondent with full consequential benefits. The appellant challenged the order of the Labour court by filing an appeal before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the respondent did not hold any temporary post in his employment as he had been working for a period of one year from 8.12.1973. The High Court held against the appellant and dismissed the appeal. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that (i) the termination was illegal because the termination order was bad since it did not give any notice to the respondent before terminating his services; (ii) the respondent had been given a notice in writing under section 10(2)(a) of Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1970 and (iii) the discharge of the Respondent was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The termination of the service of a workman is abruptly illegal and void. [532B] 2.1 The termination is not illegal merely because it is in contravention of section 25F of the Act. It is enough if he has worked for 240 days in a period Of 12 months. It means that he has been given notice of termination of his service under section 11(2). If he has, he would be deemed to be in continuous service for a further period. [506C] 2(a) The termination was not illegal because it did take place on the date of termination. The fact that he had not rendered uninterrupted service for one year does not mean that he must have been in continuous employment for a certain period. If he had, he might be deemed, to be an employee for a specified period, but if he had failed to do so, he could not be said to be a casual worker within the meaning of section 2(oo) and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 10, his case would be governed by sub section (1). [533C D] 3.2 The termination order is bad because it does not give him any notice of retrenchment or retrenchment. It merely gives him a notice of one month 's pay in lieu thereof. It does not provide for the termination without giving him an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken under section 20(1). If the termination is illegal, inoperative or a lockout or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the workman, he cannot be said that he should have been given an opportunity of being heard. [504D E] 3(a)(i) The word 'retrenchment ' in section 2 (oo) of Act means termination of employment for any reason whatsoever. It includes a termination of a temporary employment which is for a definite period or months, but does not include a termination for a short time. The word "retrenchment" has been defined in the Act to mean "to be in existence for a continuous period of 12 calendar months or six months, as the case may be". [534D E; 505E F] 3 (b) The expression 'retrenched wages ' means all remuneration which is paid by the employer to an employee. It implies that the payment must be made by way of compensation for termination of services. If the workman has been in service for more than one year, he shall be deemed not to have been retrenched from service for any period of two calendar months.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet on the ground that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and bad demanded Rs. 30/ as bribe from him. The Enquiry Officer found that the appellant had received a sum of Rs. 200/ as unlawful gratification from the Darbara singh and had demanded Rs, 30/ for making illegal gratification. He also held that the charge sheet was not signed by the Inspector of the Settlement Officer and that he did not record any statement of witnesses in support of the charge. The appellant filed an appeal to the State Government which dismissed it on the grounds inter alia that the order of termination of employment was in contravention of article 311(2) of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order was at all given. On appeal, the State contended that the enquiry was vitiated by the fact that the Deputy Commissioner had not acted in exercise of his authority under section 3 of the Act and that the impugned order was not a valid order. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the dismissal from service was in violation of article 14 of the constitution as no opportunity to prove the charge against the appellant was at least afforded to him. It was not necessary for the State to show that the inquiry was made by the Settlement officer on charges of misconduct or inefficiency and it was only when the enquiry officer found that there was a misconduct or incompetence, that he could be removed from service without holding an enquiry. The order of dismissal was passed in contravention Of article 311 (2) as no such order is found on the record, and it appears that witnesses in the case were examined before the Settlement Commissioner. Ram Narayan Das vs State of Bihar, ; , followed.

The appellant was appointed as Professor in the Medical College of Jammu and Kashmir. The Commission recommended that the selection should be made by a Committee consisting of three members, namely, Dr. B. R. Sharma, Dr., M. L. Gupta and Dr. D. C. Gupta. The Committee recommended that a panel of four persons should be prepared for appointment to the posts of Professors in the colleges. The appellant was selected and appointed as such. On November 15, 1968, the Government of Jammu & Kashmir issued an order appointing Dr. Sharma as Professor. The appointment was challenged by the appellant on the ground that the Committee had not been consulted either in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the State Government was not consulted in regard thereto, and that the Public Service Commission was consulted in accordance with its requirement. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Commission was not consulting the Commission either in respect of the principles which were to be applied in making the promotions to the post of Professors. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The State Government at first framed rules on November 15. 1968, for selections to posts of Professor and transfers therefrom from one Service to another and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. The rules were made quite clear that the Government was consulted by the Commission in regard the principles for making promotions to civil service and posts. [875C D] 2.1 The State has not been able to support that contention. It is not disputed that the appellant had not ventured to take a plea to the contrary, but it is also not disputed, that the commission was consulted on the basis of the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969, which makes it quite clear, that it consulted the Commission under section 133 of the Constitution and as the writ petitioners have not venturing to take any plea to such a plea, the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. [820E F] 2:2 The State is an authority competent to appoint persons to civil posts and posts in the service.

The petitioner was elected to the Bihar Assembly from the State Legislative Assembly. The Speaker of the Assembly, after a discussion with the Chief Minister of the State and the House of Commons, passed an order removing him from the office of the President of India. The petitioner challenged the said order by means of a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Speaker had no power to remove the petitioner from his office as the President was not competent to remove him from his post. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The powers, privileges and immunities of a House of the Legislature of a State are only those of the House or Houses of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and of its members and committees at the commencement of this Constitution. [636 B] (ii) The power, privileges, immunities and immunities conferred on the Legislature by article 194(3) are not expressly made subject to the provisions of the Constitution. The powers privileges and immunity of a member or committee of a Legislative Assembly are only such as may from time to time be defined by the Legislature in this behalf. [536 C] (iii) The House of Lords has no power under article 194 to prevent the publication of its proceedings or portion expunged by the Speaker in respect of the proceedings. [506 D] (iv) The petitioner 's fundamental right under article 19(1)(a) is preserved because, as a result of the provisions contained in article 194, he is entitled to succeed. [504 E] (v) The privileges conferred on a House are not those of a house of the legislature of a state and of the members and the committees thereof.

The appellant was appointed as Reader in the College of Behrampur. The Government took over the management of the College on March 9, 1971 and a formal agreement was executed between the Management and the Governor of the State. The College after the take over was administered as a Government College. The appellant was working as Readers in different faculties in the said college on the date of taking over. He was drawing a salary of more than Rs.600/ . On July 30, 1970, each of the respondents was drawing an amount of Rs.60/ . The appellant 's writ petition challenging the appointment of the respondent as Reader was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the Government had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Reader and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the takeover, their names should be referred to the Public Service Commission for consideration against those posts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The condition of draw ing of Rshome/ or more on the dates of takingover is completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible, on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment as Readers. [707C] 2.1 The condition regarding draw ing up of Rs,600/ or less on the basis of the date when taken over, is arbitrary and discriminatory. [778D] 2(a) The condition relating to draw ing the salary of a Reader on the last day of taking charge is completely defi ctive to the amount of pay which is paid by the Government servant to the post. [784E F] 3.2 In the instant case, the appellant was promoted as Reader on 4 9 1969 and was drawing Rs. 600/ . [774F G] 3(a). The condition in the letter dated July 30. 1970, which took recognition of the service in the private college in the case of two (1) ; , is completely erased to the effect that they would not be suitable for selection for the post of Reader and later for consideration of their suitability by the Public Services Commission for appointment to the posts as Readers, is a seriously grim issue. [777F G; 778A] 3.(b). The conditions of drawin of Rs.,600/ , or more are totally effaced from the date on which the takeovers are taken over by the State Government. [779D E] 3 (c) The conditions in the order of July 19, 1971 alone were in dispute in the High court. [780E F; 779A] 4(a)(i). The appellant is entitled to be referred for consideration under the Public service Commission for the posts in question. [781F G].

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 A) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority granted temporary permit to the appellants on the ground that they had not completed six years of service as required by section 68F(1A). The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order granting temporary permits for the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date on which the approved or modified scheme was published. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Transport Authorities had no power to grant temporary permit for the entire route, and that the appellants were not entitled to obtain a temporary permit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that in respect of the route a scheme has been prepared and published under section68C of Chapter IV A of the Act and the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, it would be squarely attracted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The permits will have to be temporary permits because the scheme has not been published in respect thereof. If the Corporation does not apply for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permit, and section 68 G(1) would be attracted. [985C D] 2. The permit will have only to be permanent permits because it has been issued in respect to the route under section 69C. If a scheme is published in any area or route or part thereof, the remaining permits will also have to he granted to any other person willing Jo obtain temporary permit which may have to his prejudice. [89 E] 3. The scheme has to be published in accordance with law and not otherwise. It is open to the State Government to grant a temporary permits to any one else if the Corporation is unable to provide service by obtaining all requisite temporary permits, the balance of convenience will have been in favour of the few. But if the corporation does not applied for all of the permits, but only on some other person, willing Jo obtained temporary permit then it would have to grant permit to any person who has applied for the permanent permit and ply vehicle because in respect o the remaining number of strength there would be no application by the corporation and section68 F(I A) would not be attracted if such applications are made under section 63 F(l A). [89 H; 89 E] 4.

The appellant was the son of a grandson of his maternal grandfather. He had two sons, one of whom was the daughter of his father and the other of his wife. The first son died in 1947 leaving behind his widow, the appellant and his mother. The second son died on November 1, 1948. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the property which was decreed by the trial court. The High Court held that the property inherited by the appellant from his maternal grand father was not ancestral property as he had no right to transfer it in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the suit was not properly valued and that the appellant had no locus standi to institute the suit. [1101 D] (ii) The decision of the High Court is wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of law which has been consistently followed by the community since 1895. It is not possible to say that the decision of this Court in Narotam Chand 's case was erroneous. [1202 C] (iii) The question whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral or not, must be confined to the property descending to the father from his male ancestor in the male line. It may be that the son has a right to challenge his alienation of the said property. But it does not mean that he can claim any right to bring the suit on behalf of his paternal grand father. [1302 C D] The decision in Narottam Chand vs Mst. Lehna, ; , relied on. (iv) The appellant contends that the High Courts had erred in not following the earlier Full Bench decisions on this point and it is urged that the decisions of the first Full Bench are wholly unsustainable. [1404 G H] (v) The view taken by the High court was erroneous as a result of the Privy Council decision. It was not suggested that the custom differed from the Hindu law on the issue before their Lordships. [1505 C D]. (vi) The decisions of this court in Narhatam Chand and Narotham Chand ' case, relied on by the respondent, were not correctly decided.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under section 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, he had a number of persons including Matiullah and others who were armed with dagger and Ebber Ali, armed with spears, lathis, spears etc., assaulted him and some of them. The appellants were convicted under section 302/34 Indian Penal code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but acquitted the appellants on the ground that they had not committed any offence punishable with death. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The prosecution evidence was reliable and there was no reason to disbelieve the testimony of the witnesses who were interested in the commission of the crime. The evidence was corroborated by the medical evidence. The injuries found on the body of Haji E brar Ali were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature. The offence under section 448 read with section 34 of the I.P.C. is not a serious one and it is not necessary that there should be any intention or knowledge as to the commission thereof. The words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 of the Code but also in the two succeeding sections, 450 and again in section 454 and section 457 of the Criminal Procedure Code. (ii)The conviction under section 114 read with Section 34 of I. P.C., is not sustainable in law. The conviction under Section 114 readwith section 34 is not warranted in law as it is based on no evidence.

The appellant was the son of one of her sons. The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the properties in dispute were ancestral and not self acquired property of her father. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the parties were governed by Hindu Law and not by Hindu law, and that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial within four degrees, and therefore, could not succeed to the estate of her deceased father. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent had failed to prove that the property in dispute was ancestral and that there was no custom which required the appellant to establish that the family was governed by the Hindu Law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit for declaration of title as collateral was not maintainable in view of the provisions of the Indian Succession Act, 1925; (ii) that the trial court had erred in holding that there is a custom which requires the plaintiff to prove the fact that she was entitled to succeed to non ancestral property of the father and that it was necessary for the appellant in order to establish her claim that she should be given a declaration of her title as a collateral; (iii) that there were no special custom in favour of the daughter of Gurdial, and (iv) that even if the presumption as to the correctness of the Riwaj i am be weak it was sufficient for the Court to say that irrespective of whether the properties were ancestral or self acquired properties of her husband she had been excluded from succession to the father. HELD: (i)(a) The High Court was right in holding, on a proper construction of the relevant provisions of Indian Succession act, that there must be a custom and not one which is binding on the parties. [153 D] (b) The appellant has failed to establish the custom as required by section 3(1) of the Act. The appellant had proved her case that she had succeeded to the property of Gurdial in preference to collaterals. The High court was right, in holding so, because the appellant had not produced a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collaterals from succession. [154 D] In the present case, the appellant has not produced any single instance or evidence showing that the collateral of one Harnam Singh who was also a Sarswat Brahmin of the Gurdaspur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway in 1913 and which have been discredited in judicial proceedings and held to be incorrect cannot be regarded as reliable or trustworthy document. [155 D] The appellant 's case is not supported by any evidence. It is true that the High Courts have taken a contrary view of law, but it is equally true that in the last case, it was enough for the court to say whether the custom should be proved by the appellant by producing in evidence the Rwsav i am of 1913 and 1893. The statements in a Riwraj i amalina are beyond the fourth degree and it is sufficient for them to prove their special custom. [156 D E] (c) The evidence adduced by the respondent was not sufficient to establish his claim that he had succeeded in preference over the collateral, but the High court has erred in law in holding otherwise. [157 B C] (d) The fact that the Rivaj i Amalina is a Sarees of Gurdaspur District prepared by him and does not contain within its four corners contradictory statements of custom and in the opinion of the Settlement Officer is not a reliable or credible document and cannot be ignored. [158 D E; 159 A] (e) The statement in a case under section 3 of the Evidence Act, which was not proved, was admissible in view Of the provisions contained in section 3 (1) (a), and that section 3 was not applicable to the present matter. [159 B C].

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company which was carrying on business as managing agents of several companies. The appellant, who was the managing director of a limited company, was the sole proprietor of a firm and was the principal officer of the company. He was also the managing agent of the firm. In the course of his business he had been managing agents for some of those firms. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant on the ground that the two firms were not liable to pay any tax under section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 and that the instrument in question was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the instrument was not chargeable with a single duty of Rs. 1,000 and as such the instrument could not be split up into separate instruments; (ii) the document in question is a power of attorney and it would fall under article 48(d)(1) of the Schedule to the Indian Stamps Act, 1908, and as the instrument is chargeable with aggregate amount, the instrument must be construed as a single power of Attorney liable for a single levy under section 4 of the Act; (iii) the instruments in question cannot be split into separate deeds and that therefore the instrument did not comprise distinct matters within section 5. Held, that the words "distinct matter" in article 48 (d)(i) of Schedule I to the Act are wide enough to include all distinct matters which the donor is capable of performing; (iv) the words 'distinct matters ' in article 49(a) do not mean any thing more than those specified in the instrument, and that it does not mean anything more than what is specified in a particular instrument. The word "distinction" in section 5(1) means something more than one. In order to constitute an agreement between two persons, the words must be read as meaning something more or less than one which is specified. The words "transfer of property" in the context of article 48 are not intended to include a transfer of property within the meaning of article 49 (a). The word 'distinction ' in section 3(1)(c) means that it is used in relation to a transaction which is not a single instrument but consists of several matters and thus requiring to be stamped with the total amount of the duty payable. In other words, the expression "transfer" in clause (d) of article 54(a), includes both the transactions of sale and transfer. The expression "distribute" in cl. (c) of section 5 is not intended merely to include both the transaction as well as the transfer of the property. The instrument in issue does not comprise separate matters but consists only of different matters, thus requiring a separate agreement between the parties. The question whether a power is exercisable by an attorney or a combination of several of them depends upon the terms of the instrument and the nature and extent of the authority conferred thereby. In this case, the document did not contain distinct matters but consisted of one matter only and that matter was the execution of a general power of power by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the doneeations his attorneys to act for him in all the capacities which he enjoys.

The assessee, a firm carrying on business in cotton textiles, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that the depreciation should have been allowed as a proper claim for allowance under section 10(5) (b) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, if it had been in force at the time when the assessment was made. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the assessee because the depreciation which could have been and would have been allowable under the Act had been allowed by the Indian income tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the words "or which would have be allowed" in section 13(5)(b) did not permit the Income tax officer to make any deduction under this he was not entitled to claim such allowance. In appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that no deduction should have be made on the strength of the words which would be allowed if proper claim had been made. Held, that the expression "or who would have otherwise allowed" occurring in section 10 (5)(b) is not intended to cover a case where the depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income taxes and super tax or any law relating to tax on profits of business which was law of a part B State, would come within the first portion of the clause. The words "any law relating thereto" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order are not intended for the purpose of express and give effect to this intention.

The petitioner, a contractor, was awarded the contract by the Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd. (K.P.C.) for supply of certain items of materials to various parties. The contract provided that the contractor would be entitled to supply the materials at any time before the date fixed for completion of the work and if the contractor failed to do so within a period of three months, he would be liable to pay the balance amount of Rs.1,00,000/ . The petitioner was also informed that the contract would be terminated by giving one month 's notice in writing. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award of the contract and also the order of termination of the agreement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner had not been able to supply any materials at all before the tender documents could be supplied to any intending contractor. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the K.P.(M.C.), which was a party to the contract, was not entitled to tender for the contract. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have consistently taken the view that in cases where there is no dispute about the genuineness or otherwise of the documents, the parties are bound by the terms and conditions of the NIT. [236C] 1.2 In the instant case, the contract was not a contract for supply at all. It was for the KPC to assess the value of the certificates furnished in this regard and if it considered them sufficient to warrant the issue of a tender form to the applicant, the Court will decline relief. [237D] 1:3. The question whether there is any difference between the requirements in paras I and V of the N.I.T. and the rest of the information were intended to verify the fulfillment of the three conditions set out in para I. The more harmonious and practical way of construing the N,I. T. is by saying that before the tenders are supplied, an intending ten derer should satisfy the K P.C., by supplying such of the materials called for in para V as are material in assessing the fulfilment of the condition in para 1. [238D E] 1 4. The very object of the Act is to provide for the supply of essential commodities and the provisions of the . are not intended to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply. It is only when a party comes to Court saying that the applicant has refrained from applying for the tender document only because it thought it would not be able to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. The requirement of para I is that before an application can be considered, the applicant must satisfy the authority concerned that he fulfills the three condition set out therein as are relevant in assessing his value of certificates furnished by him. [239D E; 240E] 1 5. In view of the fact that the lacuna in furnish ing the information has been set right subsequently by the tenderer before opening of the price documents, it is not possible to accept the contention of the petitioner that it had refrained from doing so. The mere fact that there are some other requirements in the N.,I.G. and other details called for vide para I(c) of the letter dated 5th September, 1989 would not make any difference to the question whether the requirement is satisfied. [240E F] 1 6. In this case, if a party does not strictly comply with the requirements of paras III, V or VI of the National Building Code, it may be open to the KPs.

The appellant was a displaced person. He filed an application under section 38 of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947 for confirmation of his order of detention against him on the ground that he had been detained in pursuance of the orders passed by the Custodian and that the order of confirmation was not subject to appeal or revision and it was specifically declared to be final and conclusive. The Custodian General rejected the application holding that the appellant had no jurisdiction to confirm the order under section 37 of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order. The High Court held that the orders of confirmation were not subject matter of appeal or reference and that there was no question of any revision by the Government against the order passed by him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the Custodian General is final and binding on the appellant. [1139 C] (ii)The order of confirmatory could not be challenged in a writ proceeding under article 226 of the Constitution. It was not open to the High Courts to interfere with the orders made by the authorities under section 27 of the Central Act XIV Of 1947. The order passed under section 35 of the , is an administrative order and it is not subject only to appeal, revision or review but becomes final and finality.
