[1239 C D] (iii)The appellant 's contention that the application for confirmation pending on the date when the office of the custodian General was set up and he was clothed with powers of revision under section 25 of the . , is not correct. The orders passed in 1952 would clearly be subject to the revisional power of the Government of India under section 6 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947. [1339 C E] (iv)The High Court was right in holding that there could be no revision by an order of any authority under section 5 A of the Punjab Act XII Of 1950. The appeal must therefore fail.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of workmen employed in the establishment. The dispute between the employer and employees was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. " The Tribunal held that the demand was not maintainable because it did not provide for those categories of bonus and confined itself to profit based bonus, or did not fall within the provisions Of Bonus Act, but only related to bonus. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that the claim pertaining to customary bonus was barred by the general principles of res judicata; (2) that it was not a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees; (3) that in any event, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the dispute as it did. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the demands pertaining to practice or customs prevailing in these establishments before 1966 were not such matters as have been adjudicated and therefore the Tribunal made a short shrouded one for adjudication and so there was no question of any customary bonus. [608 D] (ii) The fact that the workmen had been given notice of termination of their services by the employer shows that they had been paid wages at a uniform rate throughout to justify an inference that the payment at such and such a rate had become customary and traditional in the particular concern. The fact, however, does not detract from the claim of customary bonus or those based on conditions of service. [613 D] In the instant case, the question whether the demand for bonus was justified as it was raised by the workmen was not raised before the Tribunal. It is true that if the Bonus Act is a complete Code and is exhaustive of the subject, what the statute prohibits is to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner. [508 D E] (iii) The question whether a particular dispute falls within the purview of bonus or not must depend on the content and terms of that custom or the practice on which the claim for bonus is made. If it does, then it would be violative of the rule of resjudicata. [595 F G] (iv) The Bonus Act was enacted in 1965 and the Industrial Disputes Tribunal relating to the claim, which had not been put an end to, and so this Court took the view that so long as the award stood, the same claim under a different guise (the Shops Act) could be subversive of the principle of resjudi cation.

The petitioners were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana by promotion. The Governor of Haryana amended rule 12 by the Haryana First Amendment Rules, 1972 providing that seniority of members of the service whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by the length of continuous service on a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said amendment by way of writ petitions before the High Court contending that the rules governing seniority between direct recruits and promotees appointed to that Service were governed by a rule of quota only and not by the rule of rotation; that the rule was ultra vires the Constitution as it violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it conferred power on the Governor to frame rules regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed, inter alia, to the Judicial Service. The High Court rejected the contention of the petitioners and held that the Rules governing seniority were not applicable to the direct recruits; that Rule 12 was ultra virus the Constitution because the rule had been framed in consultation with the High Courts and that the amendment made by the Governor of Punjab did not violate article 14; that it was not open to the High court to give an arbitrary date of appointment to the promotees. The State Government filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the validity and validity of Rule 12. Allowing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were not justified in applying the rule to the Rules of seniority of the members of service. [1038C] 1.2 The High court was not justified on the question whether the Governor had the power to frame Rules regulating the seniority of judicial officers of the State. [ 1039D] 1:3. The rules of the Superior judicial Service have been amended by the State Government in exercise of its powers conferred by Article 309 of the constitution and the power of control vested in the High courts under article 235 is thus expressly, by the terms of that Article itself made subject to the law which the State legislature may pass for regulating the conditions of judicial service of the persons appointed to it. [1002D] 2.1 Rule 12 of the Rules framed by the High Commission provides that seniority shall be fixed with reference to the dates of confirmation and not any other date. The rule is a rule relating to seniority of officers in the judicial service. It is an exception to this rule. The proviso to Article 309 provides that the Governor may, if he thinks fit, make rules regulating recruitment and service conditions of persons so appointed by promotion or transfer from one State to another or from any other State or to any class or classes of posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State. Rule 12 is not an exception thereto. The power of the Governor under Article 309 is thus specifically made subject only to the rules which the Government may pass. [1013E F] 2:2 In view of the provisions contained in Articles 235 and 309, it is clear that the HighCourt was not right in applying rule 12 to the facts of the case. The decision of this Court in Punjab & Haryana vs State of Haryana, ; , relied on.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G.A.R. Rao were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board on a temporary basis for a period of one year. The respondents Nos., 4 &5 were appointed to the post of Assistant Engineer in the A.P. State Electricity Supply Corporation Ltd. (APSEB) on a regular basis. The appellants, who were working as Assistant Engineer, were promoted as Assistant Executive Engineers and were confirmed as Assistant Superintending Engineers. On their promotion as Assistant Divisional Engineers, they were transferred to the Andhra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (APCC). The respondents No. 4 and 5 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of transfer on the ground that they had been appointed as Junior Assistants for a long time and that they were not entitled to be confirmed as Executive Engineers. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellants were appointed by the APCC under Rule 3(1) of the Andhra Electricity Supply (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Rules, 1956 and that the respondents Nos 4 & 6 were appointed on a permanent basis for one year and that their appointment was not in accordance with the rules. The State Government preferred an appeal to this Court against the order passed by the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants for different parts of the State is illegal, contrary to law. [573B] 1.2 The power to organise class or classes of posts of civil servants of the APSEB is not an executive function but is a legislative function. It is a statutory function which is entrusted by the Constitution to the Executive and it is not open to the Legislature to delegate that function to any other authority. [574C] 1:3 The power conferred on the State Government under proviso to paragraph 3(2) of Order No. 1, is only to organise a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts in any department where more than one cadre in relation to such category exists in each department and so that State Government may organise one cadre when more than two cadres in respect thereof exist in each Department; so that the State Govern ment can organise one Cadre when morethan one cadre is in respect for such category. [575D E] 1 4.

The appellant was the auction purchaser in execution of a mortgage decree. The respondents contended that he was the lessee in possession of the mortgaged property and that the Patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage, it was not binding on him. Held, that the question whether the mortgagee had power to grant a permanent lease of the mortgage property so as to bind the mortgagor was rightly decided by the trial court. The appellant could not claim any right in the property which he had acquired under the mortgage decree and that he had ample opportunity to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise his right of redemption. The question whether a mortgagee in possession has power to lease the mortgaged land or not was one of fact depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. The mortgagor could not be allowed to take advantage of the position that he held the property in the usual course of management. The mere fact that the appellant had no right to redeem his mortgage if he so desired, did not mean that he could not have any interest in the mortgaged properties. The mortgagee could not therefore be permitted to take benefit of the situation arising from the provisions of section 65 A of the Transfer of Property Act and the crucial test was whether the mortgagor in possession having the authority to deal with the property, in the ordinary course of administration could be said to have exercised his right in making a lease for a term. The fact that a mortgagee had no power to sell the mortgaged lands or to take any other steps which he might have taken under the law did not make him entitled to disturb the graves of those who had been settled with them before he granted the mortgage. Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumar, I.L.R. , referred to.

The petitioner, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for the supply of electrical energy to the respondent. The respondent supplied the electrical energy at the rate of Rs.1,000 per annum. The petitioner sent notice on November 28, 1989 to the respond ent for reference to arbitration. The respondents filed their objections and contended that since the petitioner had legally invoked clause 68 of the Contract, it was not entitled to leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the limitation Act would apply to arbitrations as it applies to actions in the High Court and the making, after a claim has become statute barred, of a submission of it to arbitration, does not prevent the statute of limitation being pleaded. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the petitioner that the provisions of the Limitation Act would not apply to arbitration proceedings as they are applicable to actions under the High Courts and the make, after the expiration of a specified number of years from the date when the cause of action accrued, that is to say, from the commencement of the arbitration runs from the time when the right to sue or a right to require that an arbitration takes place upon the dispute concerned. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of section 14 of the limitation act would apply in cases where there is no express provision in the contract to the contrary. [366C] 2.1 Section 14 of Limitation Act applies to arbitrations and not to proceedings under the Indian Law. [367D] 2(a) The Court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to the parties to rescind the arbitration clause and declare that the arbitration shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference or dispute referred to in the notice of the petition. It is, therefore, open to the Parties to plead in the proceedings before him of limitation as a defence. [368E] 2 (b) The provisions in the Limitation act would not be applicable to arbitrations which are governed by the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 and the Indian Administrative Law.

The appellant, a tenant of the land in dispute, filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the decree was barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the decree and directed the executing court to proceed against those lands. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the objection as regards the executability of the decree pleaded by the judgment debtors is barred by the principles of res judicata and (2) the bar of section 4 (d) pleaded is not tenable. HELD: The provisions contained in section 4 of the Act are applicable to the proceedings under the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1951. [1104C] The provisions of section 16 in regard to the scaling down of debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under section 3. Therefore, in construing section 4, it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the enactment do not fall within the protection of the statute and again at page 578. [111D E] The words "any suit shall lie" in section 6 which provides for transference to the State of the interests or tenure holders in land and of the mortgagees and lessees of such interests are wide enough to include all suits and proceedings for recovery.

The appellants were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ' and who had appeared in Civil Services Main Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal. The respondents were not eligible for promotion to the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) and were within the permissible age limit and have succeeded are to be given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of C.S.(E). The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the C.P.(E.E.) Rules, 1989 on the ground that they were not entitled to sit at the main examination as they had been allocated to any of the Central Services, Group 'B ' or I.Ps. and who have appeared in civil services Main Examination for competing for IAS, IFS, IPS or Central Service Group 'C ' and which was within the permitted age limit. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the first proviso to rule 4 of CSE Rules, 1988 was not applicable to the case of the appellants as they were entitled to have their success in the main Civil Services Examination. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A candidate who has been allocated for IAS or Central services Group 'D ' and whose name is on the basis of the previous examination or the subsequent examina tion will be eligible to appear in the next Civil Service Examination subject to condition that they must be within the eligibility limit and without having to resign from service to which they have been allocated. [512C D] 1.2 The High Courts have used their expression "may be allowed to sit for the main Examination but it did not restrict it only with regard to the preliminary examination as now contended by the learned Additional Solicitor General. In view of the fact that the appellants had been allotted to the Indian Administrative Service Group B, they were within their permissible age limits and without any prior notice to them, they cannot be given benefits of their failure to resign on the date of the earlier examination or subsequent examin ation. [506D E] 1:3 The High court has used their expressions "may also be allowed" in the subse quent Rule 4. This permission is only for the ensuing examination. The appellants who have been allotted the I A.S., or Central service Group 'E ' and have appeared at Civil Services, Main Examination of a subsequent year under the Interim orders of this Tribunal for the Civil Services Examinations in 1988 or1989 and have failed to resign form the Service, they are to have one more attempt in the Subse quence of Civil Services examination for the services indicated in Rule 17. [504E F] 1 4. The Tribunal has used its expression "shall be allowed not to sit At the next civil service Examination but shall have to be allowed only for those appointments. A candidate, who has already been allocated as a Central Service, Group B or I, may have one attempt in that service examination for a period of two years or more and considered only for such appointments. [ 506F G] 1 5.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by an order dated 25th November, 1986. The Advisory Board after considering the representation of the appellant and the materials placed before it, rejected the detenu 's request to be assisted by a friend at the hearing and for reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of detention on the ground that the detaining authority was represented by customs officers of the rank of Deputy Collector and Superintendent of Central Excise, who were not even parties to the writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ Petition holding that the detenu had no locus standi to file the writ appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of the detaining Board is set aside and the detenu is directed to be released forthwith unless he is required in any other case. [792B] 2.1 In the instant case, the Government merely informed the detenu that he had no statutory right to be represented by a lawyer before the Advisory Board. It did not preclude the Board from permitting such assistance to detenu when it allowed the State to be represent by an array of lawyers. The order was therefore quashed. [892C] 2:2 In view of the position of law and the facts of the case, there is no justification for entertaining the contention that if the detaining Authority or the Government takes the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser before the Board through a legal practitioners, the detenu must be allowed the facility of appearing before the board through a Legal practitioner. [789D] 2(a) The Advisory Boards have, of course, to be careful in permitting assistance of a friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer. [779F] 2 (b) The detaining authority or the State Government cannot be allowed to be present by counsel before the advisory board and the refusal of such assistance would amount to denial of privilege under Article 14 if a similar facility is denied to the detenu. [780G H; 792A] 2.(c) The order passed by the Advisory Boards is set out in paragraph 2(b) of this judgment. It does not preclude it from allowing such assistance.

The appellants were the owners of certain goods. The respondents who were the managing agents of the mills, filed a suit against the appellants for possession of the goods and for damages for wrongful detention and for compensation for loss suffered by them on account of the failure to deliver the goods. They contended that the goods were not delivered as required by r. 75 A (2) of the Rules framed under the Act and that the respondents had no right to claim compensation for their wrongful detention. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree. Held, that the appellants were entitled to possession of certain properties and the respondents were entitled only to possession thereof. The property in the goods passed on September 30, 1946, and not as required under r.75 A (3) of Rules 75 A(2). The respondents had been served with a notice of acquisition on September 29, 1946. The appellants could not claim any right to possession on that date. The notice was served on the managing agent of the Mills on September 31, 1946 and the names of the appellants whose managing agents were mentioned in the schedule. The notices of acquisition were valid and binding on the respondents. The High Court was wrong in holding that the notices were invalid. The order of requisition was not a valid service as provided by r, 75 A. Held further, that under r, 76 A (1) of Order XXIX, r. 1, C.P.C., the property in goods passed to the Government of India on September30, 1946 when the goods had been delivered to the mills and the name of the mill whose managing agent the address was also mentioned in that order. The fact that the mills were served on September 28, 1946 did not make any difference as regards the title to the goods in question. The delivery orders were valid only if they were executed by the mills. The words "the property in them" in r. 76 A(1) meant the property of the owners and not of the respondents and therefore there was no acquisition under r., 75 A of Order XXI C. P.C.

The assessee company was a private limited company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. The assessee claimed that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was a reserve and should be excluded from the computation of capital of the assessee company under Rule 1. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, the Revenue contended that the amount of Rs 4, 50,000 was a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice under Section 23A of the 1922 Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the provisions made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) were indeed a provision and not a reserve. [113E] In the instant case, the assessee had been contesting the proceedings taken against it under Section23A. The question whether the amount was a deposit or an asset is a provision which has attached onaccount of the issue of a show cause notice. [114F G] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , referred to. In the circumstances of the case, it must be held that the provision made by assessee in the Books for meetings the anticipated loss and contingencies are charges against profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L. accounts and the balance sheet.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Engineers on a temporary basis. The appointments were made by the Railway Board, pursuant to the authority given by the President of India, on the recommendations of the Union Public Service Commission. The petitioners challenged the validity of the classification of personnel into those that were recruited on the basis of the competitive examinations and those that had been introduced in the year 1975. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions holding that they were not entitled to equality under Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution, for the reason that they had no right to equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by Articles 14 and 19 of the constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the classification made in the impugned classification was not discriminatory as it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved, which mainly was efficiency of service, and that both the services had started separately and never became one. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification of temporary Assistant Engineers is neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 or 16 of India. [1022C] 1.2 The classification made by Union Public Services Commission on the ground of efficiency has been upheld by this Court with weightage of half the length of service as temporary Assistant Officers subject to a maximum of five years, because of its being questioned elsewhere. It needs mentioning that the appeals now sought to challenge the classification at this point of time to look for a substitution at our end, as that would unsettle a settled position, established more than a decade ago. [ 1022C D] 1:3 The distinction between the two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case (supra) and the important question of equality was once for all settled.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, for offences punishable with imprisonment for life and a charge was framed against him for offences under sections 3 and 4 of the Act. The trial court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the appellant 's petition under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance, which authorised the State Government to direct any class of cases or offences to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the Act, did not violate article 14 of the constitution and as such the notification issued thereunder contravened article 14. HELD : (i) The notification issued by the State of West Bengal under section 3 of the Ordinance was different from the notification dated the 8th December, 1949, issued under that part of the section which authorised it to direct a class of offences or classes of cases to be investigated by the special court constituted under that Act. [445 B] (ii) The language of section 11 clearly shows that it is not permissible for the State government to direct an class of persons to be charged with offences or offences, but only to direct such class of offenders to be dealt with according to the provisions of the statute. It is not possible to say that the notification under section 11 was different than the notification. The notification under s.3 of the ordinance issued by State Government under that section did not contravene article 14 Of the Constitution and as the notification was different, it could not be held to be invalid or ultra vires. [441 C D] (iii) The power conferred on the State to direct offences or class of crimes is a legislative function and the State has no power to make a classification which must satisfy both conditions, namely, that it must be based on some intelligible differentia distinguishing the offences grouped together from other offences and that differentia must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation as recited in the preamble. The Act does not violate any of the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 14 or article 19(1)(f) of its Constitution.

The appellants were convicted under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellants under section 302 I. P.C., but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of P.Ws. 1, 2, 7 and 8 could not be relied upon because they were interested witnesses and their evidence could not have been relied upon by the prosecution. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The High Courts have rightly rejected the evidence given by P.W.2 who admittedly was in the eastern kotha where the main part of the occurrence had taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify, with the help of the lantern which was burning the appellants who were previously known to her and not strangers and she has received as many as 19 injuries during the course of the incident. [975C D] (2) The evidence of the witnesses is corroborated by the evidence on record. It is not possible to accept the evidence that all the appellants were in the western kothas of the house at the time of the crime. There was sufficient moon light at the place of occurrence and it is not improbable that these appellants were seen by P,Ws 1, 7 & 8. [ 975E] (3) The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High Court for rejecting the evidence are not convincing. [977F G] (4) The reason given by both the courts below for rejecting their evidence is not convincing and that the witnesses have been declared hostile. It cannot be said that all these appellants had been in a position to identify any of the culprits. They were in a western kodha where they were found broken open. [978F G; 975A] (5) The circumstances of the case are such as would justify the conviction under section 395 I.p.C.; and that it is difficult to accept their evidence.

The appellant Corporation terminated the services of its employees on the ground of unsuitability. The respondent Corporation terminated their services with effect from 1st April, 1973. The appellant Corporation issued a notice to the respondent Corporation terminating the services with immediate effect. The Corporation challenged the termination by filing writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court held that the termination was bad and set aside the order of termination. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the services having been terminated on the grounds of unsuability, the termination is bad, being violative of the provisions of section 25F of the , and that the retrenchment was bad in law. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The termination of the service of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment '. [794C] 2.1 The termination is not a termination simpliciter but only a termination of service by way of punishment inflicted by way off disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman, retirement of workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. [894D] 2(a) The expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of employment except those not expressly included in section 25FF or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the Act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF. [78B] 3.1 In the instant case, giving full effect to the words 'for any reason whatsoever ' is nothing but a discharge of surplus labour force and therefore does not amount to retrenchment. The expression "retrenchment" must include all termination of services except those which have been embodied in the definition, discharge from employment or termination of Service of a probationer would also amount to termination of his service. [774C] 3(a). In the present case, the order terminating the service was bad because it did not contain any stipulation in the Act that the notice should be given before retrenchment. [753D] 3 (b) The word 'termination ' must be construed as a discharge or termination simpliciter and not an automatic termination of a contract of service. It is not necessary to go into the question whether the termination of an employee on the basis of unsubsity was in accordance with law. [764E F] 3.(c). The expression `retrenchment " must include any termination of any service by an act of employer. 'The word 'terminal ' means the discharge or retrenchment of a person for any reason whatever, but not expressly mentioned in section 2(oo) of the . [795G H; 797A] 3:2. The words 'ret retrenchment ' must mean the termination either by way or as a punishment inflicted on the employee for any reasons whatsoever. The word "termination" is used in the context of the definition of the expression 'termination of service for any other reason whatsoever, and not otherwise.

The assessee, South Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying in the factory. The assessee applied for registration as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax Officer examined the case and found that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sale effected by it was sales under the Act and that the assessee was a "dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Bengal finance (Sales tax) Act 1941. In second appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was carrying on business as a 'dealer ' within the definition of the expression in the Act, and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. The High Court dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The activity of so disposing of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying out business as carrier of goods. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carriers of goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of such so disposing would be regarded by principal activity of carriage of goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern Railways, which is engaged in selling scrap and Tyreable material, that it is an "dealer", for the purposes of the Calcutta Act enabling it tO sell the goods. [778C D] 1.2 The activity carried on by the respondent clothed him with the status of a dealer liable to be assessed under the West Bengal Finance Act, 1942. [781D E] 1:3. The activity is an incidental or auxiliary to its main purpose and it cannot be said that the business carried on in the instant case was incidental or incidental to its carrying on by purchase or sale. It may be a "business" which may not be regarded merely as incidental or subsidiary to its principal activity, but it may also be a business which may have been regarded as incidental to the business as carriage of good goods by that activity. [780E F] 1 4. The word 'dealer' is used in the context of the definition in section 2 (c) and therefore it cannot include a " dealer". It is not an activity carried out by a person for the purpose of carrying on any business, but only as a result of his activity of purchase or of manufacture for sale. [779F G] 5. The expression 'dealer" has been defined in section 3(c). In the instant cases, the assessee Eastern Railway was a carrier of the said goods and it is engaged therein in selling goods and therefore, the Railway is entitled to sell the same. [783G H; 779A B] 6. The question referred at the instance of the Revenue to the High Court at Calcutta is as follows: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Controller of Stores, Eastern Railways is a dealer engaged in the business of selling scrap, and whether the assessee falls within the ambit of the provisions of the West Ben.

The appellant was a Director of the Indian Insurance Company. He had been appointed as an officer of the Insurance Company in respect of certain transactions between the two parties. The appellant was appointed as the officer of that company on September 17, 1954. On September 20, 1954 he made an application to the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the appellant for a direction to the Secretary of the Union Agencies to make the payment of the loss incurred by him in respect thereof. The Chairman of that Board did not agree with the proposal and the appellant was asked to debit the amount of the sale price of those securities to the account of the Bank. On October 17, 1955 he made a demand for the payment on the ground that the amount had been paid to the Union agencies by the appellant. The Secretary of that Agency sent a letter dated September 20. 1956 to the appellant stating that the appellant had no knowledge of the transactions and that the money was not sufficient to meet the losses. The respondent contended that the transaction was in the discretion of the Chairman and that he knew that the securities were sold or pledged and that therefore the amount was invested in securities. Held, that the Board was competent to make a demand under section 409 of the Act for payment of any sum which it had received from the appellant as compensation for loss suffered by him. The fact that the respondent had made a request for the settlement of the dispute did not mean that he was authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf of the company. The Board was not competent to enter into any agreement with the appellant and the transaction could be said to have been done in the course of the business of the Company. The contract for the purchase of securities had taken place on September 20 and the payment was made by the respondent to the Bank as soon as the amount became due. The transactions were not entered in the cash statement but were entered in a cash statement and the entries were to be made in the account books of the respondent. The transaction was not entered into in the manner prescribed by section 409(1) of the , and therefore the appellant could not have been authorised to enter the said transaction.

The appellants were appointed to the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. The services of the appellants were transferred to the Secretariat in the State and they were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the Government of Gujarat under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1956. The appellants were allotted by the Secretariat to the State Government for administrative purposes. The posts in the Secretariat were abolished and the appellants who were holding permanent posts in that department were absorbed in the services of a new State of Saurashtra. The State Government issued an order dated August 19, 1966 under section 115(7) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, directing the State to treat the appellants as permanent employees of the secretariats of the merged States and to forbear from enforcing their order treating them as servants of the Secretariats. The respondents challenged the validity of the order on the ground that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States Secretariat personnel to the Gujarat Secretariat was not open to objection. Held, that the power conferred by section 115 (7) proviso to section 115 of the Act is a legislative power and it cannot be exercised in respect of any matter which has been referred to the Central Government under section 80(7). The power of transfer of an officer from one State to another is not a legislative function. The power to transfer an officer is not an administrative power but is a judicial power. The exercise of such power is subject to the provisions of article 309 and the proviso to article 309. The High Court was right in holding that since the arrangement which was made by the Government was provisional and to enure so long as the Central Govern ment did not make a final decision, it was not competent for the officers of the respondent State to challenge the authority of the government of Gujarat either to transfer officers from the Districts or to post and assign them duties in the secretaries.

The petitioners were dealers in goods sold to the respondent State. The tax was levied on the first purchase of goods and the second purchase of the goods was made liable to pay sales tax under section 5(2)(a) (vi). The petitioners challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that the tax was not at all leviable on the second sale in the case of imported goods. The High Court held that the levy was not a tax at all and that the State had no power to impose it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Act itself did not indicate the stage at which the tax is to be levied and because under section 15(1) of the Central Act there could be no liability for payment of tax unless this stage was so stated in the Act or the rules thereunder. [554 D] (2) The levy of sales tax on the last purchase in the State of any declared goods and such goods are sold in the course of inter state trade or commerce, is not a valid tax under the Central Sales Tax Act. [556 E F] (3) The tax levied by the State Legislature was not only at one stage but also at different stages of the same transaction. It was not necessary for the State to say that a person, who is not liable to tax, must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund at a later stage. [555 F] In the present case, the tax levied on sale or purchase at the very first transaction was not one stage and therefore, it could not be said that a dealer who is liable to payment of sales Tax must nevertheless be paid at more than one stage. The Act does not indicate that a persons, who are not liable under the Act, must still pay it. [557 G H] (4) The State Legislature did not specify the stage when the tax could be levied. It merely provided for the levy of tax on first purchase in respect of declared goods. If the Central Legislature makes it mandatory that the Tax can be collected only at a single stage, it is not enough for the state to say whether a person who is entitled to pay tax must nevertheless, pay it, at more or less than one time.

The appellant was the defendant No. 1 in a mortgage suit and the respondent No. 2 was the mortgagee of the mortgaged property. The decree holder filed an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the decree on the ground that the amount payable by him under the decree was to be settled at Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition under section 48 of the Act. The District Judge dismissed the application holding that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to be paid by defendants 2 to 7. The High Court held that the decree holder could not get the benefit of the scaling down of the debt and set aside the order of the District Judge. Held, that the view taken by the District judge was correct and must be upheld. The question whether a purchaser could get the benefits of the creditor 's Relief Act arose out of the execution proceedings before the District Court. The provisions of section 47 are not applicable to the case because the decreeholder had no right to get the amount paid under the compromise decree as scaled down by the High Court in favour of defendants 2 and 7 only and the amended decree directs that on payment, the entire mortgage debt would be allowed of the mortgage property. In the present case there was no purchaser of the mortgagee 's debt and consequently there was not a question of the purposi tion of the creditors who were not agriculturists. The compromise between the parties arrived at in course of execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release their interest alone in the mortgaged properties would not be liable to be sold.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in question under the first defendant. The first plaintiff was a tenant of the second defendant. In the suit filed by the appellants, the City Civil Court held that the first plaintiff had no right to sublet the premises and that there had been a lawful subletting by the first appellant of the said premises. The City Civil Judge held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no lawful subletting. On appeal, the High Court held (i) that the City civil court could not have jurisdiction to try the suit because there had not been a valid subletting by first appellant and (ii) that there were no lawful sub tenants of second defendant as the provisions of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, did not apply. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by article 136 of the Constitution inasmuch as there had already been a determination of the question whether the first respondent was a sub tenant or not. HELD : (i)(a) The City civil Court could not decree the suit of the plaintiffs unless their claim to remain in possession was established under the Act or any of its provisions. [374 B] (b) The Bombay Rents. Hotel Rates & Lodging House Rent Control Act is a special law and it does not apply to suits for eviction of tenants. It does not deal with the rights of sub tenants. The suit of a landlord against a tenant in respect of a premises under the second plaintiff was one relating to possession of the same premises. [375 C] (c) The suit filed in the City of Bombay, therefore, was one for ejectment of any of the defendants from the premises. It could not be said that the plaintiffs were the tenants of premises in dispute. [376 D] (d) The High Court correctly decided that the suits filed by appellants were one relating only to possession and those filed by them did not admit that the second and third plaintiffs could establish their claim for being in possession of premises. In view of the provisions contained in section 28, it was not possible to hold that the trial court had jurisdiction under the Bombay Rent Act to entertain such a suit. [377 E] (ii)(a). The City of Court could have decreed the suit only if there had existed a valid sub tenancy by the second appellant of premises which were to be determined by the courts specified in section28 and no other. [378 F] (iii)The High Court rightly decided that it was competent to the City Court to entertain and try such a case. The High court correctly decided this point.

The appellant was a director of the company. He was appointed as managing director in his place. The appointment of the appellant was challenged by the respondent on the ground that he had not been appointed as the managing director of a company and therefore, could not be made an assignment of his office to him. The High Court held that the word "assignment" in section 312 of the new Act meant a transfer of office by a director for if the section had intended only to avoid an appointment by a Director of his successor, it would have clearly said so and would not have used the word 'assignment ' in the main part of section 86B. The appellant contended that the words "assign" in the section were wide enough to include "appointment". Held, that the proviso to section 86 B did not indicate that it was intended that the term "assation" in a section would include appointment. It was not intended that there should be an assignment by a person who had no power to appoint his successor. The proviso to s 86B does not indicate any policy in the Act which could be said to be liable to be defeated by the appointment of a successor by a company. The word "promotion" in sub section (1) of section 87A is used in the sense of an assignment and it does not include appointment, but only means an assignment. It is a well established principle of construction that where one finds a proviso to a section, the intention of the Act would be defeated.

The appellants are the tenants of premises situate at No. 6 Kasi Chetty Street, G.T. Madras. They carry on business there. The respondent filed eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence the eviction petition was not maintainable. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop let out to the said M/ s. Adeshwar glass Mart without receiving the rent from the respondent. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the ground established and proved by the evidence on record were sufficient enough to justify the finding of subletting by the appellants. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellants that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction order was passed against the appellant firm and one another partnership firm, M/S Adeshwar glasses Mart, without joining the partners as respondents. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without joining its partners as parties or serving the partners is a matter which has to be decided by the Trial Court. [420C] 2.1 In the instant case, no such objection was raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is always open to the respondent to amend the eviction proceedings and join the partners in the eviction proceeding. [426D] Chhotelal Pyarelal vs Shikharchand, ; , relied upon by Mr. Nayar, the objection to the main tainability of the petition was raised for the first time at the earliest stage and was rightly rejected by the High Court. The High Court was right in holding that it is only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 that a firm could sue and defend the suit. [ 420D E] Chh landlady Pyarelal, vs Shikhachand, I.L.R. , relied on.

The Andhra Pradesh Act sought to impose ceiling on land situate in urban agglomeration and since the concept of agglomeration defined in section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Central Act was an inclusive definition, it was not within the legislative competence of the Andhra Pradesh Legislature to provide for imposition of ceiling on lands situate within such area. The Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Act, 1957 was passed by the State Legislature and came into force on 1st January 1975. Section 2(1)(A) of that Act provided for levy of ceiling in respect of land situate within the urban agglomerations referred to in section 3(j). Section 2 (n)(B) provided for imposition on land situated within such areas as may be specified by the Government. The State Legislature enacted the Andhra Area (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act (Act No. 1 of 1964) which came into effect from 1st April, 1965. The Act was amended by Act No. 2 of 1976. Section 3(1) provided that in respect to land situate outside such area, but before the commencement of the Act, the Central Government would have legislative competence to provide, for imposition and collection of ceiling, on land comprised in urban areas and for matters connected therewith. The appellant State filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the said Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act was not violative of article 14 of the Constitution as it was enacted with a view to provide a ceiling on agricultural lands within the meaning of section 2 (1)(a) of Central Act No 1 of 1965 and since there could be no question of any ceiling being imposed on land in excess of the ceiling area, the entire Act was ultra vires. The appellants contended that the Andhra Act sought the imposition of Ceiling on land under the Act which was not a part of the definition of 'family unit ' in section 4(1), (A) and (B) of Act 1 of 1966. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "family unit" in section 7(2)(A), (B), (C) and Explanation to section 2 of the , are wide enough to include a family unit within the definition in section 5(1). [1157D] 2. The definition of family unit in section 6(a) is an inclusive one and includes a family units which have more than one family unit. It is only in respect thereof that the Central Legislature would cease to have competence to legislate with respect to ceiling on holding of land situated in such area even though it is not an urban aggl PostalCode exercise. [1158E] 3. The word 'family ' has been defined in the Andhra State Act, 1956 and it includes a person who owns or holds land in urban area. It does not include a member of a family. [1259F] 4. The term 'family units ' is used in section 8(1A) to mean a family which owns or held land in an urban area and includes the members of a Hindu undivided family. The words "family units" are defined in Section 2 of that act as meaning a unit which has more than two families. [1059G] 5. The object of the enactment is to provide that the ceiling on holdings of land in such areas should be determined and if there was any surplus it should be surrendered to the State Government. It would not be correct to say that merely because an area may have been notified as an urbanisable area under section 2, the State Act would cease lo have competence. [ 1059H; 1060A] 6. The land obtained by the divided minor son on partition would be liable to be clubbed with the land held by the other members of the family unit and situate within a urban agglomerated area. [1002B] 7.

The appellant company was a public limited company and its workmen were dismissed from service. The Company filed an application before the Labour Appellate Tribunal under section 33(2) of the , for reinstatement of the respondent workman on the ground that he had been retrenched without giving him an opportunity to show cause against his dismissal. The Tribunal held that the appellant was guilty of misconduct and directed the company to reinstate the respondent in service with full back wages. On appeal by the Company, the Labour Court held that there was no evidence of misconduct on the part of the workmen and dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the Tribunal had not given any reasons for its decision; (ii) the respondent workmen did not join duty on October 1, 1953, but were allowed to continue in service without any condition; (iii) the company had failed to produce evidence satisfactory to the Company of their absence as required by the notice dated September 17, 1953. HELD : (i)(a) The Tribunal was right in holding that the respondent 's services were rightly terminated under Standing Orders of the Company. [674 B] (b) The Industrial Tribunal had no power to give compensation for the period anterior to October 2, 1953 and it could not have given any reason for its conclusion. It was not open to the Tribunal to interfere with what really is a finding of fact. If a large number of workmen are arrested by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute, as in this case, the work of the company will be paralysed if the Company is forced to give leave to all of them for a "more or less indefinite period". [674 C D] (c) The finding that the workmen were not taking complete rest as " advised by their doctor but was engaged in doing some " public work" does not amount to victimisation. If on the contrary, the Tribunal proceeded on the footing that the company has decided to terminate the services of Chattoraj there being a suspension order against him, it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial Tribunal should not have interfered with what actually is a charge in respect of which an industrial dispute can be raised.

The appellant Dr. Urea Kant who was a Professor in Botany and was appointed as Professor in the department of Botallore, was selected by the Selection Committee constituted under section 5(1) of the University Act, 1974. The appointment of Dr.Urea Kant was challenged before the High Court by way of writ petition. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the selection committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joined the post, the reserve list exhausted itself. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that once the selected person joins the post he would be entitled for appointment if any vacancy is caused during the validity period of the reserve List. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The selection committee constituted under Section 5(2) of Act 1974 has to prepare a list of candidates selected by it in order of merit and shall further prepare a reserve list in the same order and to the extent of 50% of the vacancies for the post of teachers or officers for which the Selection committee was constituted. [422C] 1.2 The selection Committee constituted shall prepare a select list of persons selected by them in orderof merit and submit it to the Syndi cate for approval. The Syndian Kant who is already selected and appointed as professor in Botshally, shall be considered for appointment on the recommendation of the Selection Commit tee. [420C] 2.1 In the instant case, the High court has arrived at the conclusion that the Committee constituted for the selection of a professor in the University was proper and in accord ance with the provisions of Section Uma Kant was found suitable for the posts of professor in other universities. The Selection Committee in the present case was constituted for selection of Professor in a college which is a non expert body, if it is not a member of any particular university. [416D E] 2:2 In view of the fact that the High Courts have arrived at a conclusion that there is no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve lists alive for a long period of one year, as no person selected for the said post can at all be expected not to join for such a long time, the question of the selection being made in accordance therewith does not arise. [414F G] 2(a) The Selection Commis sion Committee constituted by section 5 of the Act is competent to make its recommendations and it has approved and recommended the name of the candidate for the concerned post. [413D E; 414E F] 3.1 It is well settled that in a matter of this nature, the Court should not interfere with the decision of the High courts unless there are good reasons for interfering. [427F G]. In the present cases, the very purpose of preparing a reserve List would be defeated if the view taken by the High Curt is accepted that once an person selected by selection committee has joined that post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve select list is of no avail and becomes extinct. [527F G; 415A] 3(b) The very purpose and object of preparing the reservelist would be frustrated if the views taken by it are accepted that when a person selected is joined, he will not be entitled to join any other post in his service. [ 415D E].

The petitioners, who were the owners of certain lands in the State of West Bengal, challenged the validity of the provisions of section 9 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on the ground that their lands were earmarked for public purposes under section 7 of the Act. The High Court held that the local authority could easily delay the acquisition of any land designated for a purpose specified in clause (b) or (e) of section 7 and that the provisions Of sections 4 to 16 of the said Act would be applicable only if the local authorities concerned were satisfied with the preparation of the development plan. The petitioners contended that their land was earmarked for a public purpose under section 3(1) of the , and that, therefore, they could not have been deprived of the benefit of section 17 of the . Held: (i) Section 9 of Act No. 1 of 1894 provides that as soon as may be after the coming into force of the ; Act, every local authority shall carry out a survey of the area within its jurisdiction and prepare and publish a development plan for such area in accordance with the provisions contained therein. The preparation of a development scheme is not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authori ty. The draft of a section of the Development Plan for K, P and R Wards was published on July 8, 1961. On July 8. 1964, the development plans were submitted by the Municipal Commissioner to the State Government for sanction under section 10 of the West Bengal Town Planning Act, 1956. The scheme was approved by the State Govern ment on July 9, 1961 and the draft scheme was published in the prescribed manner for inviting suggestions from the public within a period of two months. The final development plan was submitted on July 7, 1964. On August 8, 1964, a notification under section 4 of the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911 was issued by the Government under section 5 of the Acquisition of Land (Amendment) Act, 1964 and the scheme was prepared in accordance therewith. The State Government made an order under section 9(3) of that Act on July 10, 1964 directing the State to prepare a development plans for K P and T Wards. On September 8, 1965, the Municipal Commis sioner issued a notification declaring the area as reserved for public purpose. The petitioner challenged the said notification by a writ petition in the High Court. The main contention of the petitioners was that section 9 Of the Act did not apply to the case because the local body could easily enter into an agreement with the public and that it was not possible to say that the commencement certificate could be given without doing any violation to the development scheme. Held, further, that the notification under s.10 of the Bengal Town Improvement Act was valid and the acquisition was valid. The notification under S.10 Of the Land Acquis tion Act was published by the local bodies on July 11, 1964 in accordance With the rules framed thereunder complied with. The declaration under section 6 of the Bihar Town Improvement (Amendment ) Act, 1965 was not a final scheme but only a final development scheme and therefore the acquisition could not be said to have been made without complying with the development.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the United States of Kutch and Kutch, was carrying on business as a dealer in certain commodities. The respondent company claimed that the territory of the State of Gujarat was a part of India and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions, that the State Government had no power to make laws for the regulation of the relations between the two States and that the Indian territory was not a part thereof. The appellant contended that the respondent company was not entitled to the protection of article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution as it had not been established by the British authorities governing Sind since 1843, and that in any event, there was no question of infringement of the fundamental rights guaranteed under article 19 (1)(f). Held: (i) The State Government could not be said to have acted arbitrarily or unreasonably. The dispute between the appellant and the respondent was one which was a matter of public policy. The State had no authority to make any law in respect of the territory between the boundary shown in the Map 'A annexed to the award, and the boundary fixed by the Tribunal was not binding on the respondent. (ii)The claim of the Government of India to exercise fundamental rights in respect o the territory in that Sector may be entertained only if it is established that the territories are now in different states or areas different from those specified in the State List, and no constitutional amendment is necessary. The award does not purport to nor does it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. (iii)The dispute between two States was one of a public nature and had to be decided by arbitration. The claim of Indian citizens to exercise rights in relation to the territory was entertained only when there were several occasions to demarcate the boundary between Sind and the Rann of Kutch. The claims made by the claimants that in view of the alignment under the award the territory which is Indian, it cannot be implemented without the authority of an amendment modifying the boundary of the state of Kutch in which is now included the Round of Kutch, were not accepted.

The appellant mortgaged the property to the mortgagee in favour of the mortgagor on April 7, 1937. The mortgagor 's right title and interest in the mortgaged property was sold on January 16, 1937, and after the sale the mortgagee became entitled to recover the amount due by sale of his interest in Mauza Bahaldih. The mortgagee filed a suit for recovery of the amount from the appellant on July 12, 1946, and obtained an assignment of the rights of the mortgagees under the two deeds dated June 14, 1922, and August 27, 1922. The mortgage was executed on April 1, 1937 and after expiry of the period of limitation for the suit, she filed a fresh suit on July 13, 1946. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the appellant and held that the suit in respect of the first mortgage was not barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest to extend the period for the purpose of the suit she could still maintain the suit relying on the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 8, 1937 by the auction purchaser who purchased the mortgagor ' s rights in Mauza Muzas Bansjora. The High Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had been dispossessed from Mauza Bahahrih and that the mortgage deed dated June 18, 1922 was not a mortgage within the meaning of section 68(1)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) The suit in question was barred by limitation because it was barred under the law as the mortgage 'was partly one of the mortgaged properties, and (ii) the suit was barred because the mortgagee had lost his interest therein. HELD : (i)(a) The right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the mortgage security or where he is not secured in his possession of the property or where possession is not delivered to him as agreed, the claim maintainable by the mortgagee under section 68 of the Act was at the date of the institution of the action. [675 B] (b) The appellant had not relied upon any other part payment in respect Of the first mortgaged before the mortgagor had parted with his interest and such payment having been made within twelve years from April 14, 1925, the plaintiff 's claim to enforce the mortgage was at that time barred by law. [643 C D] (c) The High Courts have held that a suit under section 69(1) of Transfer of property Act is not barred because it is barred by article 120 of the Limitation Act.

The appellants were engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling motor vehicles. The respondent company was prepared to grant free transport facilities to the employees from Chinchvad Village to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants also averred that they had been paid a consolidated sum of Rs. 2 per month as transport charges for the transport facilities provided to the staff by the company. The company claimed that these amounts were realised by the appellants only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the challenge to the tax sought to be realised was not tenable and the appellants were liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the levy of a tax on passengers carried in certain classes of public service vehicles was illegal; (2) that even if a nominal charge is realised from the employees that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; and (3) that there was no justification why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a public servant vehicle. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [361C D] 2. The word 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules. It is true that the term 'public servant ' has neither been defined nor has ever been defined in the Act. But that does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the Act, it is of a wide and amplitude. [362D] 3. The definition of 'stage carriage ' contained in section 2(7) of the , clearly indicates that the tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public duty vehicle. [363E F] 4. The expression 'public servants ' has been defined by the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958 as meaning a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver who is for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the definition of the 'stages carriage '. [364E F; 362A] 5. In view of the Preamble, the tax can only be levied on passengers and not on persons who are paid for the entire journey or stage of the journeys. The vehicles provided to them by the appellant were reserved for them only and no other member of the Public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that the transport vehicle provided to a employee by the Appellants could be a public servic tion vehicle in any sense of the term.

The appellants, who were the owners of a cinema house, filed an application under section 795 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952 for a licence to establish a cinema. The licensing authority granted a "no objection certificate" in favour of the appellants. The appellants challenged the validity of the said "no objections" certificate by filing a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there was a mosque, and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence had been re opened in the locality. The State Government appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not taken into account the fact whether there was any mosque, or a temple, in the proximity of the site where the alleged mosque is situated. [897G] 1.2 The High court has not considered the further question whether in an appeal filed by an applicant who had objected to the grant of a "No objection" certificate, the local residents, who had opposed the grant, were entitled to be heard and the decision arrived at by the State Government Appeal at their back was vitiated by the non consideration of the objections. [889H; 897A] 1:3. The Act does not confer any right of appeal on a person who might have raised objections before the licensing authority against the grant or a " no objection" Certificate, as the case may be. It is only an appellate authority which has to consider whether there is any impediment to the granting of such a certificate. [891B] 1 4. The provisions of section 6 of the Act do not confer a right of Appeal on a party who might having raised objections against the refusal of a licence, he may have applied for a cinema licence. [997C] 2.1 In an appeal under section 8(3) of the , the local resident, who has objected to grant of the "noobjection" certificate and whose objection had been overruled by the licensing Authority, cannot be permitted to raise objections against grant of such certificate. The appeal must fail. [902D] 2:2. In an application for a "NO objection" under section 6(3), the local inhabitants who have objected to it, are entitled to have their objection admitted in respect of a permanent Cinema licence granted under rules 3 and 102. They cannot be heard to say that in an Appeal filed by a person aggrieved by the decision of the licensing authori ty refusing to grant a " No objection" certificates, the Local residents, whose objections had been rejected, are not entitled to file objections and nor were they entitled to appeal against the rejection of the application for the same. [912D E] 2 3.1 A person who has opposed to the refusal to grant the licence is not entitled, as he may be, to file a "any objection" in respect thereof. The local residents are not required to file any objections and they cannot be allowed to plead a right to oppose the grant. [922D F] 2 4.2 In an Appeal under section 9(3)(a) of Madhya Pradesh Cinema (Regulation ) Act, 1951, the District Judge is empowered to grant or refuse to grant such a licence. The District Judge has no power to grant any licence in respect o the cinema house.

The plaintiffs instituted a suit against the defendant claiming to be in possession of the mining lease. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that the plaintiffs accepted the offer of September 2, 1957 by their plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 and that this acceptance was communicated to the defendant before November 6, 1957. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The plaint in the present case was not an acceptance of the offer but it was intended to be an acceptance. [584 B] (2) The plaintiffs accepted their offer and the defendant was at liberty to revoke the offer at any tune before its acceptance by the plaintiffs. [585 C] (3) The pleadings and issues raised the question whether a contract was made on September 2. 1957 or not, must be held to have been concluded in November 1957. [586 D] (4) The pleading and issues raise an inference that the defendant accepted the offers of September, 2,1957 by their letter dated September 2 and the plaintiffs ' refusal to accept them. [587 E F] Bloxam 's Case(5) referred to. (5) There was no concluded contract between the parties. It is not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint. The plaint was not in any way an acceptance or acceptance of a proposal.

The appellants were owners of agricultural land in the State of Bihar. They had been carrying on business as dealers and selling their produce. The appellants were charged with offences under section 3(1) (f) read with section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The prosecution alleged that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The trial court acquitted the appellants but convicted them under section 4(2)(b). On appeal the High Court held that the investigation was not properly conducted and that the appellants were guilty of offences under sections 3(3) and 7 of Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution had failed in its duty to investigate the same. HELD : The offence alleged is punishable with three years ' imprisonment and as such it falls within the 2nd Sch. of the Cr. P.C. and consequently the appellants could not be convicted under section 7. [655 D] The question whether the cultivation and sale of sugarcane can be regulated under section3 of the Act cannot be raised in this Court. It is true that the Parliament intended to bring under control the cultivation, supply and distribution of essential commodities and trade and commerce therein for maintaining or increasing the supplies thereof or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. But the power conferred on the Central Government by section 3 of the , cannot be questioned as invalid. [676 G] The power conferred by section 4 is not a part of agriculture. It can only be exercised in respect of agricultural produce which has been purchased or sold, and in addition to the Sugar Control Order, 1955 which was issued by the Central Govern ment on 27th August, 1955, it also issued the Sugarcane Control Order 1955.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain lands in Mysore State, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the orders dated 12th January, 1977 and 12th February, 1977 issued under section 3(1) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable to the present case because it was found by the Government of Karnataka that the concessions granted by the earlier order dated 30th June 1969 were being misused and undue advantage taken of the said concession had been taken of by the newly established industries. The appellants filed a writ petition in this Court challenging their validity on the ground that they had started new industrial units in the State on the assurance extended or because of the concessions given to them, inter alia under the said order dated 12 th January,1977. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The doctrine of promissory estoppel is not applicable in the present cases because it is found by this Court that the concession granted by it was being misused by the new industries. [950C] 1.2 In view of the fact that the order of 30th July 1969 did not specify the power under which it was issued, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. The mere fact that an order of 12th Jan. 1977 did not mention the power in the order does not establish that the promise was, in fact, misused. [ 951C D] 1:3. In view thereof there is no substance whatsoever in the contention that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds. The doctrine cannot be regarded as good law now. [977F G] 2.1 There is nothing on record to show that any such misuse was being made or undue advantage took place of the same. In fact, there is nothing in the record to indicate that any action was taken by the State to grant refund. It is clear that the Government had not authority to give the refunds. [978F G; 951A] 2:2 The doctrine is not attracted in the instant case because the benefit of sales tax granted to the new industrial industries is by way of refunds of sales Tax paid to the extent provided in the Order. In effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of salestax or reduction in the sales tax liability to the amount stated in the orders. [980F G].

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegation that they caused the death of one of the persons belonging to the group of the accused.
