The Trial Court acquitted A 1 to A 3 but convicted A 4 to A 6 under Sections 148 and 307 read with section 34 I. P.C., and acquit them on the ground that they formed an unlawful assembly with a common intention to kill the deceased. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 and dismissed their appeals. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.p.C.. [891G] 2.1 There is no question or dispute that A 1 and A 3 were armed with spears, A 4, A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 was armed with knives. The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A 4 had been attacked by the accused party. It is in evidence that all the accused persons were armed at the time of the attack on the deceased and caused his instantaneous death. [892H; 893A] 2:2 There is nothing to show that A 3, A 1, A 3 and A 5 were armed or had any intention to cause the death. The High Court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction of the appellants under Sections 302 readwith 34 I P. C. if the evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of them all. [889C] 2(a) There is a force in the contention that the appellants were not armed with weapons and they were not members of any unlawful assembly. The non applicability of Section 149, I.Ps.C, is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants. [876B C] (b) The High court clearly fell in error in affirming the conviction. [864D] 2.(a) The prosecution story from the evidence that A1 to A3 were armed and there was long standing enmity between the parties. The deceased Madda Lakshamandas was undergoing life imprisonment for the murder of one B. In the absence of any overt act on the part of the appellant, he could not be convicted under Section 302 read alongwith 34 I PC. [851D] 3(a). There is also no evidence that the other accused were armed when the deceased was passing near the field of A 1. It may be that some persons were in a number, but there was some dispute between the two parties. Therefore, it cannot be said that the appellant had formed an offence within the meaning of Section 147 I.PC. [891D E] 3 (b).

The assessee, a registered firm, was carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton yarn. The assessee had purchased cotton yarn from the open market and sold it to its customers. The price paid by the assessee was not included in the assessable value of the goods as on the date of transfer. The Income tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax under section 52(2) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee had failed to prove that the transfer was effected by him with the object of avoidance or reduction of liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains and that the transaction was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(2)(a) of Act. On reference, the High Court held that there was under statement of consideration in respect of the transfer and sub section (2) applied only where the consideration for the transfer is shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by the transferor. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Courts were not justified in holding that the fair market value of capital asset transferred by the appellant as on date of the Transfer was correctly declared by the Income tax Officer and that there could be no question of any addition or deduction under section 54(2). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding the fair and reasonable construction of section 52 sub section(2), read with section 2 (2)(b) of that Act. [645B] 2.1 The High Courts have not been justified in taking a view different from the one taken by the Tribunal. It is well settled that the principles of interpretation of statutes are to be applied in construing a statute and if there is any ambiguity or doubt, it should be interpreted according to its plain meaning. [643C] 2(a) The High courts have not intended to lay down any general rule of construction which would apply to all cases where the full value of consideration received by an assessee is correctly declared or disclosed by him and there is no understatement of the consideration, it would result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to the assessee nor been received by him. [ 643D] 2 (b) The principle of interpretation that a fair market price of the property as on that date should be taken into account for determining the real value of such property is not applicable to cases where actual consideration received for the transferred is under stated or in other words, shown at the lesser figure of that value so declared. [ 644E] 2.(c) The principles of construction of statutes have been applied by this Court in a number of decisions and it would be appropriate if the Courts are satisfied that the true meaning of these provisions is to be given effect to. [545B C] 3.1 In the instant case, the assessee has not produced any evidence to show that the value received by it was not declared or furnished by him in respect thereof. The only thing required is to find out whether the fair price of capital assets transferred by him is shown or disclosed and if so, what is the consideration declared in respect thereto. If the valuation of the assets as on 1st April, 1957 exceeds the full market value, then it would have no application in case of a transfer made after 1st March, 1957. [445C D] 3(a). The High court was right that there should be an addition or deletion of the price paid to the transferor by the transferee as on 31st March 1957 and that such addition or deleting should be confined only to cases when the actual consideration was understated by the assesses or in others. [41B C]. (b). The assessee has failed to produce any evidence showing that the market value received from the assessee is more than what is declared or disclose at a lower figure than the actual value actually received.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 7(i)(f) and 7(ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case against him was that he had only black Tils used for Pooja and not for human consumption. The trial court found that the evidence showed that the appellant had only one black Tills used for the purpose of Pooja after the accused had told him that they were not meant for human use. On appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution was not able to prove that the black Tiller was a food when it was sold by the appellant to the Food Inspector and that the Food inspector 's version was more probable because it was supported by what the appellant wanted to prosecute him if he kept adulterated foodstuffs for sale for human food. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The prosecution has not been able to establish that the accused was guilty of an offence punishable under section 3(i) (f) or 7(iii). [330 D] (2) It is true that the word 'food ' in section 2(1)(f), and the words "food" in section 10(7) are not defined in the Act. But, it is clear from the definition of 'fruit ' in the Prevention Of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 that the term 'fruits ' includes all those who have been found guilty of any offence under the Act or under the . [330 G H] (3) The word 'Food ' has not to be given a wider meaning than what is generally understood in ordinary parlance. It is not necessary that the food should be used for human purposes. It must be used as food when reasonable doubts arise. [330 A B] (4) The definition of "fruit" in the Indian Penal Code, 1860, does not include any article which is capable of being sold or is capable to sell. The word "fruits" in its ordinary dictionary meaning means "a person who has a market for sale or purchase". It is clear that the definition is wide enough to cover all those persons who have a market at the time when they are sold by them. [334 B C] (5) The words 'feeds ' and 'fix ' in clause (b) of section 2 of the Act do not include "feed" or "fix". The definition is not exhaustive. It does not exclude from its purview any article like food, it must be construed as a whole and not as a part of it. [328 B C; 331 A] (6) The expression 'feel ' in cl. (b), which is used in the context of the definition, means "fil" or 'fixed '. It cannot be said that this is so because the word "Food" has not acquired a wider connotation than what it was understood in the sense in which it is used. [332 E] (7) The term 'Fruit ' is defined in section 3 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, as meaning "feel". It does mean "fish or manufactured by a person who is either a manufacturer or a dealer or a trader or a person whose name is mentioned in the list.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th of January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was also dismissed on 31st August, 1967. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the dismissal order dated 13th September, 1960. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order of dismissal was bad and he continued to be in service. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the impugned order of the Divisional Commis sioner was an order prior to the Constitution and, therefore, the High court could not exercise its jurisdiction or was it one pending at the commencement of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is passed. [48B] 2.1 In every such case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of actions shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from the passing thereof, the right to sue shall first accrued. The period of limitation shall be computed from the day when the right was first accrues. [49C] 2(a) In every case only if the appeal has been disposed of by the appellate authority and an order dismissing it is passed by another officer who is subordinate to him, that order must be deemed to have been passed in his own name. [50D] 3.1 The cause for action shall not be taken from the earliest date when a statutory remedy is provided entertaining the appeal. [51E] 2 (b) In each case only where the appeal of the appellate court affirming the decree of the lower authority where a statutory remedies are provided entertaining such an appeal or representations is made and where no such order was made, though the remedy has been availed of, a six months ' period from the said date of preferring of the appeal shall be take to be the date on which cause of Action shall be commenced to have first arisen. [52F] 3(c) In all cases only when an appeal is disposed off, cause or action shall first arise and where the order appealed against or representation was made and if no such orders are made, then the right of sue shall thereafter accrue. The expression 'cause of action ' in section 2(b) means 'a period of six years ' from the end of the period of the suit or proceeding to which the suit is brought; 'and 'a further period ' from 'the date of filing of the application for setting aside the decree '. [54F G] 3 (d) In a case where the appellate Court has no jurisdiction to issue a writ to the appellate Authority it cannot issue a Writ to the original authority. The right to file an appeal against the order passed by the lower authorities is not a vested right in the appellant. [55H; 56A] 4.1 It is not disputed that in the first two cases where the claim has been dismissed on the ground of limitation and the High Courts have set aside the order, the First Appellate Court and the respondent are set at liberty to proceed to dispose of the matter in accordance with law.

The respondent, a member of the family of one R, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of certain properties in his favour. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had failed to prove that R was entitled to the property as he had not been given an opportunity to meet the case against him. On appeal by the respondent the High Court set aside the decree and directed the trial court to proceed with the suit afresh in accordance with law. The appellant contended that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the trial Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as it was barred by section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the decision of the trial Judge was correct and the appeal must be dismissed. The decision of a court on an application under section 34 is not final and conclusive and the decision cannot be set aside unless it is shown that the view taken by the trial judge was erroneous or perverse. In the present case the High court had no power to interfere with the findings of the lower courts. It could not, therefore, have jurisdiction to interfere in a second appeal under section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code. The High Court was right in holding the suit was one of affirmance and this position would be clear from the decision in R. V. D. Parker vs M. P. Seshram, A.I.R. (1938) All. 934, referred to. Held further, that if the appellate decree confirms the decision on the question of value of the subject matter it is not a decree of affirmation and this is not affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is made in favour of the intending appellant and not against him, and whether the variation as to costs is made by the appellate court or the trial as a whole; and if the appeal court makes a variation in regard to the order as to cost such a variation cannot affect the character of the appellate judgment.

The appellant, a Small Cause Court, was constituted under the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The District Judge passed an order directing that the proceedings be stayed pending disposal of the revision petition. The High Court dismissed the revision petitions on the ground that they were not maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in a case arising out of original suits of any valuation decided by the District Court, and that the revisional power enjoyed by the High Courts from time to time was not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The revisional power of the District Judge under section 5, Provincial Civil Courts Act is not amenable only to revisional powers under section115, Code of Civil Procedure over a revisional order made by the district Court under that section. [38C] 2. Section 115 of the Code of civil Procedure, read with section 115, Code Of Civil Procedure, provides that in respect of cases decided before 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising out from original suits or other proceedings of any value decided by District Court. , the High Curt has exclusive jurisdiction to entertain revisional power under section 35, and no question can have arisen of invoking the revisional powers of the Court under section 10, Code. [39D E] 3. The provisions of section 115 are not applicable in case of a revision petition filed on or after that date. [40E] 4. Section 25, Codeof Civil Procedure is not attracted to the present case because the HighCourt has exclusive power under Section 115 to entertain revision petitions against an order of the district court under Section 25 Provincial Small Causes Courts Act, disposing of a Revision Petition. [41F G] 5. The words "any other case decided by a District Judge or Additional District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes" in section 115 Code of Criminal Procedure are wide enough to include cases arising from original decrees of any valuing value passed by the court of Small Cause, and where such a case arises out of an original suit of any description, the High 'Court alone shall be competent to make an order under this section. The Code of C.P., therefore, is not applicable to cases arising in execution of a revisional power conferred on the High courts under section 20, Provincial small Cause Courts (Amendment) Act.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands in Jaipur and wanted to construct a building thereon, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the service of notice under sub section (2) of section 52 was not an integral part of the cause of action and was sufficient to invest the Calcutta High Court with jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the legality of the impugned notification issued under section 51(1). The respondents filed a special leave petition against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The writ petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under Article 226 of The Constitution is not maintainable in view of the provisions of article 226 and the rule nisi on the same. [605D] 2.1 The High Courts have jurisdiction to issue a rule neces sary to exercise their jurisdiction under article 227 of the constitution. [613E F] 2(a) The power and authority of the State Legislature to acquire land under section 53(1), is not an essential part of that power. It is an integral component of the right and authority conferred on the citizens by the Constitution. [505F] 3.2 The High courts have jurisdiction in respect of the exercise of their jurisdiction to deal with the question whether a particular piece of land is needed for public purpose or not. [625H; 602A] 3(b) The High court has jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether a person is required to be given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. If the respondents felt aggrieved by the acquisition of their lands situate at Jaipur and desired to challenge the validity thereof, the remedy of the respondents of the grant of such relief had to be sought by filing such a petition before this Court. [705F G] 3.(c) The State Government has no power to issue any notification under section 54(1)(a) for acquiring the land in question at Jaipur or upon their failure to do so to take immediate steps under sub s.(2) thereof to secure such possession. [600H; 601A B] 3 (d) The respondents cannot be said to have been given an effective opportunity of being heard before the acquisition proceedings were initiated by the Government. They could not, therefore, be deprived of their right to file a petition for quashing the notification dated February 8, 1984 and passed an ad interim order restraining them from taking any steps under section 55(1); [606F] 4.2 In the instant case, the respondents did not raise any objection as to the power and jurisdiction of the Government of Rajasthan to acquire the land under s.52(1 ) of the Act or the legality and propriety of the notice issued by it under section 50(2) for the grant thereof.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in 1968. The landlord filed an application under section 25 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court rejected the application holding that the building in question was constructed in 1968 and that it had been constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to s.2(2) of the new Act. In appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of s.39 of the Act on the date when the revision came to be decided by the High court. The High Court also took the view that the construction of a new Rent Control Act would not apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellant that the premises were constructed in 1969 and that the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the trial court that the buildings were constructed substantially within the meaning of section 3(2)(a) of that Act was manifestly erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the old Rent Control Acts are intended to protect a building from being used for any purpose other than the purpose for which it is let out and not for any other purpose. [334E] 2.1 The construction of the building would be deemed to have been completed on the dates on which the first assessment thereof comes into effect and where the said dates are different, the earliest of the said date. [340F] 2(2). In the instant case, the building was subject to assessment therefore it will be deemed that the new rent Act would apply to the building during the period of 10 years from its commencement. [341H; 343A] 2.(3) The construction would be considered as completed on or before 1st October 1971 and if that be so, the appellant would be entitled to get the benefit under section 39 of the New Rent Control Laws Act. [343B] 2 (4). In view of the fact that the property was subject of tax during the relevant period, it will not be possible for the landlord to get any benefit of section 39 on the basis of the date of the first demand notice. [342C] 3(5) The building was not constructed in 1970 and the landlord 's claim for eviction was barred by section39 of that act. [344F G] 2:3. The question whether the building will be treated as a building after 10 years of the commencement of the Rent Act, is a question of fact. It is well settled that the burden of proving the fact lies on the tenant to prove that he has not been in possession for over ten years prior to the date from which the landlord can claim eviction.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and its Managing Director, was appointed as the sole arbitrator. The respondents filed an application before the Subordinate Judge for setting aside the award on the ground that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the Constitutional provision in force at the relevant time and it was therefore void. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant had no jurisdiction to make the award in terms thereof. On appeal by the respondents the High Court set aside the order of the Subordinate judge and remanded the case for fresh disposal on merits. Held, that the award passed by the Subordinate Court was a nullity and that the High court was right in holding that the arbitrator had no power under section 175 (3) to make an award in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The agreement dated February 6, 1948, was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor General or the Governor, as the case may be, and in consequence there was a valid reference to the arbitration. The High Court had no authority under section 176(3). The award was therefore not void. Held further, that it was the duty of the arbitrator to prepare the award within the time prescribed by the Act and he could not take advantage of his own wrong doing so. The award did not contain any provision for the levy of penalty on the appellant. The provisions of section 175 were applicable only when the agreement had been executed in accordance therewith and not otherwise.

The appellant was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab. He was prosecuted for offences under sections 120B, 420 and 471 read with section 34 IPC. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been convicted by a competent court. On appeal, the High Court set aside the acquittal order and convicted him under section 120B IPC. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the First Information Report against Kailash Nath and the prosecution as against Kailash Narain was not an offence which could be tried in respect of a cause of action which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution, as has been held by the High court to be a rule regulating the condition of service of such a person; (ii) the said rule cannot be interpreted to mean that even if a government servant is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect thereof for prosecution in respectof a cause or action which arises or an incident which tookplace more than 4 years before the institution of the departmental proceedings, as had been held in the case of Des Raj singhal and did not consider other grounds, if any, that may have been raised by him for quashing of the prosecution; (iii) the third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2.2.2 cannot be read as laying down an absolute or general embargo on prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. This purpose can be achieved if the said proviso by adopting the rule of reading down is interpreted to include a provision which has been made in respect to pension of such government servant. The third proviso cannot be invoked by the respondents in support of their interpretation of the third Proviso to clause(b) with regard to pension.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The shares were allotted to the appellant company. The respondent company challenged the validity of the said order by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent company had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23 A of the Income tax Act for any of the three years and on that footing it was not entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares, with no right in the balance of the profits. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which the public are substantially interested, is. It was further urged that the expression "any company" in section 23(2)(a) of the Act means a company in which any public are directly interested and not by shareholders entitled to any fixed rate of dividend. HELD: (i) The Explanation to section 23 (1), as it stood at the material time, no order could be passed in respect of any company in whom the public were substantially interested. [714 B] (ii) The expression "public" is used in the context of a statute which is not defined in the Act. It is well settled that the word 'public ' includes all persons who are substantially concerned with such accumulation. Therefore, the Explanation must be construed as meaning that the public would be regarded as one in which they are substantially affected. [814 C] (iii) The definition of "public company" under section 3(1) is in substance a clause and it matters little to them whether the dividend is immediately distributed to or acquired unconditionally by or beneficially held by the public. It matters little, to them if the public have been substantially interested in such accumulation: it matters not much to them either whether the dividends are immediately distributed or are accumulated. [820 G] (iv) The word "public " in section 3 (1)(a), as used in section 2(2) of that Act, means a public company in whose favour the public is substantially interested and includes a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company is held by a parent company or by an nominees thereof. [821 D] (v) The words "public are substantially different from those used in sections 23(1)(b), 23(3) and 24(4) of Act, are not intended to cover all cases where public are generally interested. It would be wrong to say that the words " public are substantial" in the section must be interpreted in their widest sense so as to include all persons whose interests are substantially prejudiced by the non disclosure of the public interest.

The appellant was the owner of a consignment of cotton. The goods were delivered to the respondent on the same day and delivered to him on that day. The delivery was made by the respondent to the appellant on the next day. On the same date the respondent paid the amount due under the bill of lading. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the goods were not pledged with the respondent and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The delivery of the goods was not made by a person who had no authority to take delivery of them. [107 B] (ii) The fact that the appellant paid the entire amount due from him did not make any difference in the position. It is true that the respondent did not pay the amount but only received the amount as the respondent 's agent. But the fact that he had made payment to the seller on account of the purchaser Shree Kishan & Company does not make it a case of his own showing that he was authorised to take possession of the godown. [108 E F] (iii) The goods left the Mills premises, the property in them had passed and so the first appellant no longer had title to them. The fact of delivery to the buyer was not relevant for the purpose of determining the amount payable under the bills of lading as the goods had been delivered to a person other than the purchaser. [109 E F; 110 A] (iv) The High Court Judges were wrong in holding that the delivery of goods by the appellant was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(g) of the , and that the transaction was not one for sale within section 2 (g). [110 G H] (v) The position at present is as follows: (i)(a) the selling agent has to be in possession of all the goods except those which are delivered by him to the purchaser on account. If the goods are not delivered, the delivery must be made to the person who has paid them. In other words, the sale takes place when the goods have been delivered and the property is transferred to the purchasers. The title to the goods has passed and therefore the first respondent no longer has title to those goods. [110 B C] (b) The appellant was entitled to recover the amount of Rs. 1,000 from the seller. The High Courts were wrong on the view that the sale took place when delivery was given to the vendor. The sale was not by a third person but by a purchaser who had made the payment in advance and therefore could not be said to have been pledged without permission or that only goods allotted to quota holders can be pledged. [111 E F]. (c) The transaction was one for the sale of cotton and not for the delivery to anybody till he was paid. The property in the goods did not pass and so, the first respondents were entitled to claim the amount. [112 G] (d) The sale of the property took place at the time when delivery of possession was made. It was not necessary that the property should be delivered for a period of three years or more. The transaction could only be completed within six months after the delivery was effected and the first two years had expired.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21 Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed an offence punishable under section 161 I.P.C. The prosecution alleged that he had been making preparations to commit offences under sections 161 and 165 I. P.C., and that he was a member of the service or pay of the Government or was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty. The trial court convicted him but acquitted him on appeal. On appeal, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence and convicted him under section 6(1) (d) read with section 5 (1)(e) of Prevention of corruption Act, keeping in view the capacity in which and the nature of the duties which he was Performing as an Examiner of University which it had been found to have no connection with his being a Government servant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that: (1) the words "obtains" in section 5 of the Corruption Act were wide enough to include within its ambit the public servant, and (2) the expression "obtain" in the definition of "public servant" in Section 21 Indian Evidence Act, 1872, did not include within it the element of effort on the part of the receivers to corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public officer. HELD: (i) The abuse of position as an examiner of University was clearly implied. It would be reasonable to put on clause (d), a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of sub section (1). [331 D] (ii) The use of the word "obtained" in clause (e) does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of efforts on the side of the receiver. It will therefore be reasonable and would be unreasonable to put an interpretation which is inconsistent with the main clauses of section 5. [332 E] (iii) The misuse of position would be the necessary ingredient of the offence; the abuse being either by corrupt or unlawful means or otherwise abusing its position as public servant. [328 G] (iv) The definition of 'obtains ' in section 21 of the Indian Penal code has to be read with the context in which it is used and the expression 'obtain ' in the context of that clause must be given a wider meaning than the word 'obtained '.

The petitioners, who were casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the construction Department of the Signal Unit in Northern Railway, filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984. The petitioners alleged that despite the fact that each of them had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, has not treated them as temporary servants and has applied discriminatory rates of wages. They have asked for a direction to treat them at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked the regularisation of their services in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Railway authorities. The Court directed that seniority of project casual labourers should be combined and prepared departmentwise and category wise and in terms of the directions of this Court, steps have been taken to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. In the writ petitions filed by the petitioners, it was contended on behalf of the Administration that since the petitioners had put into continuous service as casual labour they are now entitled to all the privileges as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court HELD: 1.1 The petitioners should be treated at par in the project or in the open line. They should be given full opportunity of placing their arguments and documents before the Railway administration. [144C] 1.2 In the Signals and Telecom Construction organisation under which the petitioners are working, according to the Railway, further privileges of being regularised in permanent service is affirded by giving them access to their regularisation against permanent vacancies which mostly occur in open line, and willing project casual labour are combined for the purposes of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in. This Court changed the existing practice for reckoning seniority and directed that the seniority of projects casual labourers shall be combined with regular scales of pay, increments etc. [145E F] 1:3. The Railway Board has not been given full chance of placing the petitioners at par. There is nothing to show that there was break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. [146F G] 1 4. In view of the fact finding recorded by the Court, it cannot be said that the petitioners have been discriminated against. The writ petitions are disposed of accordingly.

The Forward Markets Commission, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 12(1) of the Forward Markets Act, 1954, framed bye laws for the regulation and control of the business of the commission. The appellant was a member of the said market committee. He was elected to the office of the President of the market committee on March 1, 1956. On January 24, 1956, the President issued a notification under section 12 (1) declaring that the Forward Market Committee had power to make bye laws with retrospective effect and that the President 's powers were exercisable by the Central Government in respect of the matters specified in the said notification. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was beyond the power conferred on the Commission under section 11 (1). Held, that the power of the Central Govern ment to make a bye law with retrospective operation is not an absolute power but is subject to the condition of previous publication and the power to issue such a byelaw is not hedged in any manner. The power to frame bye laws is not a power conferred by the Act on the Central Legislature under section 2(2) of that Act, but it can be exercised only by the State Government or the Central Board. The powers of the Commission are subject to certain limitations and restrictions imposed by the Constitution. The provisions of the Act which are in substance regulatory and ancillary to the control of business of a market committee are not inconsistent with the provisions of article 19(1)(f) of our Constitution.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1357 B.S., Rs. 20,469/ for that year and Rs. 21,822/ for each year, which were declared as dividend for each of the three years in question, the Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax under section 16(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of long term leases after the 31st March 1948 was a receipt of income in the hands of the assessee and taxable as the income of the company from other sources. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain or not. [732 B] (2) The question of law raised in this group of cases is more extensive and it has to be decided on the basis of the form of the questions, namely, whether any sum of salaiis realized by the Ukra Estates Zamindaridaries (P) Ltd., for grant of short term leases was taxable. [632 C] (3) The expression "other sources" in section 2(6A) capital gains arising after 31st day of March 1948, and before the 1st day Of April 1956, were not part of accumulated profits. [ 739 D E] (4) The word "income" is used in a sense in which it is used to mean income from other source. It is a well settled principle that when an assessee receives money for his own benefit, he must be deemed to have received it as income and the question of fact would arise only if it is shown that the receipt was not earned by him or that it was not made in the course of business. [ 732 E F] (5) The words "other source" in the section are wide enough to include income from all sources. [ 738 D] (6) The term "income " has been defined in section 3(12) of Act, and it includes income derived from other assets. It does not mean income which is earned by an assessee or a person who is liable to pay tax under the Act. [832 F G] (7) The definition of "income ' in section 4(6) of Income Tax Act, 1961, is wide enough for the purpose of taxation under section 12 as it applies only to income from business and not income from any other source or source.

The Kerala Forest Act, 1963 was enacted to provide for the control and regulation of forests in the State. Section 2(f) (1) of the Act defines 'forest produce ' as a forest produce which includes, that is to say, the 'enumerated items in clauses 1 and 11 "wood oil" is one of the enumerate items as well as roots of sandalwood and rosewood. The expression 'timber ' defined in section 2(k) of that Act includes wood oil. Section 3 provides for the establishment of a new State with a view to regulating the production, storage, transport, processing or marketing of any forest produce. Section 4 provides for establishment of new State of Kerala and the provisions of the Kerala Forest (Vesting and Regulation of Production, Storage and Marketing) Act, 1974 were made applicable to the areas in which the Kerala State was established. The Kerala Forest Corporation was constituted under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1961. The Corporation was established by the Government of India under the Act. Section 5 provides for constitution of a committee consisting of persons who are members of the Committee and the Chairman of the committee. Section 6 provides for appointment of a Committee to advise the State Government on matters relating to the administration of the Corporation. Section 7 provides for composition of the committees. Section 8 provides for powers of the Board of Directors, the Chief Executive Officer, the Secretary and other officers of the State Board. The Board of Director of Agriculture was constituted by the State Legislature under the provisions contained in the Kerala Agricultural Produce (Vidaran) Act. The Committee submitted its report on 29th December, 1992 to the Government. The Government of Kerala issued a notification dated 30th December 1992 directing that the Committee shall consist of five members including the President and two other members who were elected by the members of that committee from among themselves. The State Government passed an order dated 31st December 1992 under section 5(1) read with section 6(2)(i) of Act No. 1 of 1974. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the expression "timber" in section 3(f)(1) must receive its colour from its context and meaning. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the word 'timbers ' used in the Act would include wood oil within the meaning of section 2 (f) of Kerala Forest Produce ( Vidaran Oil) after the word "wood Oil" and the word `timber ` in the definition of forest produce is one such thing as understood by the legislature. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The term 'timbar ' is used to denote a kind of wood oil which includes wood oils. It must be noted that the term 'imber ' has been defined in the Karnataka Forest Act 1963 and the Kerala Private Forests (Value Added Tax) Act 1974 as meaning "any other forest produce" which includes timber oil. The word 'implant ' is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary, popular and natural sense. [164F G] 2. The definition of 'building ' in section 4(f), as it stood prior to the amendment of the definition by Act No 1 of 1969, was not intended to prevent or restrict the use of wood oils for the purpose of agriculture, business or transaction known to the trade. It is a well settled principle that the words used in a statute are not meant merely to be read as meaning and understood in its ordinary sense but must be given their natural meaning. [165G H] 3. The dictionary meaning of the word is not always to be construed in its popular sense but in an exhaustive manner, it cannot be restricted in such a way so as to defeat the principle object and purpose of the legislation. [166H; 167A B] 4. The words 'timder ' and 'timmer ' are used in different senses and have different meanings.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code but was acquitted. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellant on the ground that there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal. Held, that the High Court should not set aside an order of acquittal unless it is shown to be perverse or unreasonable. The judgment of the High court does not disclose any such reason as would justify interference with the findings of the trial court. The evidence in the present case was of a very large nature and there was no compelling reason for reversal. The appellant had been given full opportunity to explain his position before he could be convicted under s 302 readwith section 34, Indian Penal code but he did not avail himself of that opportunity. The fact that the doctor who examined him gave evidence in support of the prosecution case did not disclose that he was asked to say that Bega was also present. The doctor 's evidence was accepted by the High Curt and it was held that the Doctor was not a fit person for recording his opinion. Held further, that there was nothing wrong in the High Courts taking into account the fact that there had been no compelling circumstances for reversal or acquittal of the accused. The Sessions Judge was therefore right in accepting the testimony of the doctor ' who gave evidence at various stages of the case and which have been pointed out by the Sessions Judge who said about Gyaniram and Jora, and that the judgment was not perverse. Held also, further, the HighCourt was in error in accepting his testimony as reliable.

The appellant company was an all India establishment having establishments in different parts of the country. The factory at Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. The workmen employed in that factory were paid wages at double the ordinary rate of wages as provided by the Bihar Labour Welfare Fund Rules, 1951. The appellant company had two factories, one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi. The dispute having arisen between the management and its employees, the Tribunal referred the following disputes to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication: "Whether the demands of the workmen of the appellant company are justified and if so, what relief they are entitled to ?" The Tribunal found that the union 's constitution was duly amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963, i.e., after the said purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and its workmen represented by their union the Indoxco Labour Union is incorrect and cannot be sustained". The Tribunal also held that the appellant 's establishment had been duly amended by the notification dated January 6. 1963 and therefore, the reference was not valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the constitution of the said Indox Co. was duly altered as from February 6, 1964 and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make a reference under section 10(2) of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has not committed any error in directing the appellant to grant special leave demanded by the union. [554C] (2) The award is operative in respect of the employees of the company at Jamshedpur. It is not open to the Tribunal to impose a penalty on the management of the Company for failure to comply with its directions. [555D] (3) The question whether the reference made by the Tribunal was valid or not, has to be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced before it and the award cannot be said to have been passed by the tribunal in respect thereof. [556F G] (4) The finding that the Union 's name was mentioned in the agreement and the said statement was erroneous and cannot therefore be sustained. Any award made by a Tribunal in respect to those disputes must necessarily be confined to the workmen ' of the Appellant company 's factory at Ranchi and the Tribunal 's extension of that award to workmen in the company ' s other establishments was clearly without jurisdiction. [557F G]. (5) The reference was operative only in respect the workmen in its other establishments. It did not affect the rights of the management to grant leave to any employee of the employer company 'as a matter of course. The Tribunal, on the considerations aforesaid, was not justified in obliging the appellant Company to grant Special Leave demanded by it. [558F G; 558A] (6) The conclusion that the reference is operative is correct and cannot stand.

The appellant firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939. The assessee filed a return of income for the assessment year 1943 44 and the Income tax Officer treated it as having been assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the firm had been dissolved on April 1, 1943, before the Income Tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force and the first succession to the business after April 1 , 1939 was in March 1943. The High Court held that it was not necessary for the assessee to prove that the business of the firm was carried on by him at the time of dissolution of the partnership, and that the income from the business could be deemed to have been the in come profits of the previous year. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the assessee was carrying on business when Act 7 Of 1939 was brought into operation and was on that account entitled to the benefit of section 25(4). [675 B] (ii) The assessee was not carrying on any business at the commencement of the Indian Incometax (Amendment). Act 7of 1939, which came into force on April 31, 1938, after Act 7 o 1939 had came into operation, and was therefore, on that date entitled to relief under section 25 (4). The High court was right in taking the view that the appellant was carrying out business at commencement of Indian Income Tax Act, 1918, when the Indian income tax (Amendment), Act 7 OF 1939 was enacted. [676 D] (iii) The expression "business" in section 25 of the Income 'tax Act, 1961, is not defined in the Indian Act. It is a well settled principle that the word "business " includes all activities which are carried on with the object of carrying on an activity which is incidental to or ancillary to the main purpose of the business. [650 E] (iv) The words "business as defined in section 2(15) of the Act" in the context of the definition of "business", do not mean any activity which may be carried on for profit. It does not mean a mere change of ownership or a change of user. [663 F G] (v) The word " business" is used in the sense of carrying out an activity, which is not incidental to the carrying on of that activity. The word 'business ' has been defined in Section 2(14) of Income tax (Amending Act 7/ 1939). It means any act or transaction which is done with the intention of carrying it on for the purpose of earning profits and gains of business. In the present case, the assessee had a business at its commencement and the business was taken over by the assessee. The business in timber business was carried out by the firm of Lala Hakam Mal. It was not a mere alteration of ownership but a change in the constitution of the assessee 's firm.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority Shimogarla. The permit was issued on the same day. The appellant filed an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal against the order of the State Government granting the permit. The State Transport Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that the Secretary to the Regional transport Authority, Shimagere had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Rule 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permit and further held that the appellant was entitled to have the permit renewed. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the old Rules, which was applicable to his case for the issue of a permit and that the grant was made beyond the prescribed period of Limitation under rule 118 of the new Rules after a delay of more than one year from the grant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 64(1)(a) are not attracted to the case of the applicant who seeks to obtain a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Authority granting the permits. [190G] 2. Section 64(11)(a), which is material for the purpose of this appeal, provides that any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Government or a Regional Transport authority to grant a permit may within the prescribed time and in the prescribed man ner, appeal to the State transport Appellate Tribunal constituted under sub section (2) who shall after giving such person and the original authority an opportunity of being heard, give a decision thereon which shall be final. [191A B] 3. The appeals before the High Court were not competent under section 64 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no Jurisdiction to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the order passed by the State Road Transport Appellate tribunal granting the same. [192B C] 4. Section 65(11) (a) which is relevant for this purpose, provides for an appeal against the refusal to grant the permit or by any condition attached to a permit granted to him may within 30 days from the receipt of such order, prefer an appeal to a State Transport Authority constituted under section 3. [193C] 5. Section 63 has to be read with rule 178 of the Rules which prescribes the procedure for appeal to various authorities Appeal is a creature of the statute.

The appellant was the President of Parliament. He alleged that at the meeting held on 7 February, 1967 respondent Shastri and his supporters delivered inflammatory speeches against the appellant and thereafter the said respondent Shastri filed a petition under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act 1951 for setting aside the election of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur on 7 2 1967 and there was rejection of evidence on behalf of the respondent. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that the news item in the newspaper 'Hindustan ' Exhibit 28 gave news from Hapur under the date 7 February 1967 that a meeting was conducted at Hapur and no election meeting was convened in support of respondent Shastri at the Town Hall Maidan, Hapur and therefore the appellant was denied the opportunity of meeting that case. HELD: (i) The report of the Joint Secretary of the Republican Party to the President is not an information given by the appellant to the Election Commission. [895C] (ii) The appellant 's case was that on 18 February,1967 respondent Shastri had attacked the office of the Prime Minister and his election agent with a view to preventing him from continuing the Jatav voters from going to cast their votes. The report did not mention the name of the person who was assaulted or chased and thirdly, there was no police case and no investigation, thirdly, the reports did not specify the name or names of the persons who were assaulted or apprehended. [889E F] (iii) The evidence on record shows that the appellant had been shown to have participated in the attack on the office. The witnesses on behalf o the respondent were D.W. 1 and D. W. 2 said that a Congress election meeting had been held at the town Maidyan, Hapur, and no elections were held in support thereof. The evidence of D.Ws. 3 and 4 was not established to be published with the consent of the Election Commissioner. [995G H] (iv) The alleged incident at Chhajjupur is unacceptable because, first, there is no complaint by the respondent to the Commission that the case was lodged at Hapur. Secondly, there were allegations in the petition regarding assault on Shamshad Elahi and his associate with a Congress candidate. The appellant failed to prove that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri had chased the appellant 'S ' and threatened his workers. [891A B] (v) The High court correctly came to the conclusion that no notice was given to the appellant before the election petition was dismissed.

The appellant, a judgment debtor, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property auctioned to him. The learned District Judge held that in view of Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a purchaser of property at a sale in execution of a decree would be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree was passed and all questions relating to the delivery of the possession of such property would be questions relating thereto. The appellant preferred an appeal before the District Judge who set aside the order of the District judge and remanded the case for fresh disposal on merits. The District Judge, however, held that since the sale became absolute only under the circumstances as mentioned in Rule 92 of Order XXI of the code of Civil procedure, a decree holder could not be said to have been a party in the suit. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to set aside an order passed by the District Court under Order 21 Rule 95 and not Article 134 of the Constitution of India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Order 21 Rules 90 and 91 of the Civil Procedure Code are applicable to an application for setting aside sale. [361C] 1.2 In other words, an application by auction purchaser for delivery or possession of a property at the sale in executing a decree is not maintainable and the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 134 does not apply. [362D] 1:3 The High Court has rightly held that after the amendment of section 47 of the C.P.C., an application to set up a purchaser for execution of the decree would become absolute only if the application is made within one year from the date of decree irrespective of the date on which sale is confirmed, even though the application was not one as contemplated by Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order XX of the CPC. [363E] 1 4.1 In other word, an auction purchaser will be deemed not to be in possession at all unless he has obtained a decree for possession against the property. The expression "decree holder" is defined in section 2(2) of the Act as meaning any person who has been declared by a court of competent jurisdiction to have his own or movable property valued at more than one lakh rupees and includes a person who, on account of some special circumstances, is unable to pay the amount due from him. [364F G] 1 5.1 Section 47 of C. P.C. by the auction purchaser does not make any distinction between an application made under Order XX Rule 95 or Order XXI and an application filed under Order XXII of the Court of Civil Proce dure. The provisions in Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Cr.P C. are applicable only to an applicant who has filed an appeal against the decree passed by a Civil Court. [365G H] 1 6.2 Section 47 is not attracted to an order under Order XLIII Rule 1 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966. The application for execution is made and disposed of in accordance with law. [366A B] 7.1 It is submitted that on the disposal of the application on July 21, 1979, the sale becomes absolute only after the disposal thereof, even if the applicant is not a party as contemplated under Rule 89 of Order XXII. The period of Limitation Act cannot be invoked to set off the period from the time when the application for executing the decree is filed.

The appellant was the owner of a house in which he had been residing. He had also stated that he had seen the wall poster and the wall posters, but he did not know who pasted exhibit P 1 on the said wall. The first respondent 's election agent filed an Election Petition against the appellant alleging that the appellant had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The appellant pleaded that the wall was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appellant 's returned candidate. The trial court held that the said walls were pasted on the wall at his instance and that the first respondent had not seen the act of pasting of exhibit P1 and he did so. On appeal, the High Court set aside the election of the first Respondent holding that the walls poster was pasted in a wall which was affixed to the wall and that it did so because the appellant himself was of the view that the publication was meant to create an impression and did not affect the prospectus of the defamed candidate 's Election Agent. The High Court also held that exhibit P2 was not proved by the first respond ent himself as he had not stated that the offending wall was affixed prior to the election by the workers of the appel lant with his knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the High court erred in holding that exhibit PW 1 was printed and pub lished only a day prior to his election and that he himself had not even seen the offending walls together with exhibit P3. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contents of the wall containing the wall are clear and a direct reference to the first appellant ' s statement made in the election petition. [776B] 1.2 The contents in the wall write up by the respondent clearly show that he was going to examine witnesses only in connection with the pasting. It is not necessary to prove that the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus or that it was then true of the plaintiff. [771C D] 1:3. The contents are clear, unambiguous and unambiguous. The language used by the appellant clearly shows that he has not stated in his evidence that he did anything with regard to the pastings. It does not mean that he must state what he had stated before him. He has also not stated as to how he had done so. [761D] 1 4. In a libel action it may be necessary to establish that those who were in fact present at the time of election are likely to interpret or understand the words spoken of in a defamed person 's case. The word "sole" is not defined in the Act. It has been used in the context of the Act and its object. [751D E] 1 5. In the instant case, the appellant was not able to prove his case that the respondent had taken the photographs in question on the relevant date. He did not even mention about the alleged offending wall or the wall being pasted one week prior to election. The evidence of PW 1 clearly shows the fact that he knew the contents of this wall and also that he could not know where the wall affixed was. [754F G] 6. In view of the above, the respondent ' s case both in his written statement as well as in the Court is that the house poster Ex. P1 was pasted near the wall. It may be true that the witness has stated that on the day previous to the filing of the present election petition he had gone further and stated that all the wall writings and wall posters appeared to him to be old and he had "seen them earlier".

The respondent No. 5, a public limited company, was granted permission for development of the land in question by the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for the construction of a five star hotel. The appellant No. 1, who was the owner of the said land, filed an application before the Municipal Commissioner for sanction of the plan to construct a multi star hotel on the said plot. The respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner and did not challenge the same in any appeal. The Municipal Corporation rejected the plan submitted by the respondent No 1. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the permission for construction of the multi star Hotel was granted by the State Government under section 46 of the Act and having regard to the position that in the sanctioned plan of 1966, the said property was included in the residential zone and no proposal to exclude it therefrom in the draft revised development plan had been published, the Municipal Commis sioner was not justified in rejecting the application for approval of the plans submitted by respondent No 5. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The ground for rejection of the building plan submitted on behalf the respondent no. 5 is no longer tenable, regard being had to the fact that the draft revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors. [922C] 1.2 In granting sanction to the plan, the respondent NO. 2 directed sanction of a plan out of 44,820.49 sq. yds. belonging to the respondent. The plan was sanctioned in accordance with the direction of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. The permission granted by respondent Nos 1 and 3 was not challenged by any of the parties. [ 922D] 1:3. In granting approval to the plans, the Respondent No. 2 should have considered whether it is necessary to exclude the same from consideration as one or the relevant factor. [992E] 1 4. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public was adequately considered and taken into consideration by the High Court. In this case, however, at the time the Municipal commissioner rejected the plans filed by the Respondent Nos. I and 2, the appellant No 1 had not challenged the order granting exemption to the Respondent NO. 5. The only question that arose for decision in the appeal was whether ornot sufficient quantity was kept reserved under section 48 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1948 for park or recreation ground in the original zone and whether the Municipal Council was justified in refusing to grant approval of its plan.

The appellant union, a trade union of workmen, filed two complaints against the employers in respect of lock out and had thus committed unfair labour practice. The Industrial Court, Maharashtra, Bombay, dismissed the complaints. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the employer that there was a closure of the industrial undertaking and it was not a case of lockout. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The closure has to be irrevocable, final and permanent and irrevocable. [682C] 1.2 The intention of the parties at the time when it resorts to lock out or claims to have closed down the industrial activity is normally implied from the fact that the employer has not imposed a lockout or has closed the establishment it is necessary to find out what was the intention of his employer at the date when it re employed the industrial dispute. [782C D] 1:3 The true test is whether the closure has been a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employers. If the employer does not act in accordance with law, he cannot do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device. [882F] 1 4. The intention to lockout is the refusal of the Employer to continue to employ workman. It is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closing down of the Industrial undertaking may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the appellant at the stage of closure. [820G H] 1 5. The duration of the closure may be purely temporary or permanent, but it cannot be said that the lockout has closed down. If it is claimed that the employers have imposed a ban on the employment of workmen then the Industrial Court before which the action of the respondent is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the end of the closing. [821B C] 1 6. The effect of lock off is that the employees are not being re employed and new hands are being recruited. If a closure has already been expanded, the old workmen will be re inducted in service. But there is no provision for continuing a lock out which can be continued after the expiry of the period of the notice. [822C D; 882A] 7. The question whether the employer had imposed a restriction on the right to employ workmen or that it was bonafide and not a device to terminate their services, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If there is a closure, the employer may not be able to do so. [823C D].

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The assessee company had its registered office in Calcutta and its branches at Bombay. It was registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as an Investment Company. The assessment year concerned was March 31, 1946, the relevant accounting period being July 29th, 1947 to September 30th, 1948. The Income Tax Officer treated the assessee 's income as business profits. On appeal by the assessee company the Appellate Tribunal held that in the case of the assessee not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case was a mixed question of fact and law. In reference the High Court held that the assessee was a dealer in shares, securities and properties and held that it was a business profits and therefore, was not an investor. On further appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The question as to what were the characteristics of the business of dealing in shares or that of an investor is a mixed one of fact, and the legal effect of the facts found by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal on the basis of which the High Courts have held that there was material on record to support the finding of the Appellate Authority that the appellant company was a 'dealer ' within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Income Tax Act. [655 D] (ii) The expression "business" in section 2 (g) means any activity carried on by an assessee for profit and not for profit. It is well settled that the word "business " includes all activities which are carried on with a view to make profit and it is not necessary that every activity should be carried on in a manner which would bring about a result of profit or loss. [625 D] In the present case, the question as regards the nature of the objects set out in the Memorandum was not a question of pure fact but was a pure question of law. The High Court was right in holding that the Tribunal had rightly held that even though the Memorandum did not contain any provision for the assessment of the appellant 's business, it could not be said to have been made by the Income tax Officer. [613 E] (iii) The fact that the Memorandum does not contain a provision for assessment of income or profits is a relevant factor in deciding whether the assessee is an investor or an investor and if so, what was the legal consequence of the fact found by him.

The appellant was appointed to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the post of Subordinate Judge on June 19, 1950, and on June 20, 1950 he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On April 28, 1954, he was promoted as Subordinate judge of Masilipatnam. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1955, on the ground that the charges were not proved and that the proceedings in the High Court after October 1, 1953, resulted in violation of article 311 of the constitution. The High Court held that the enquiry was without jurisdiction and that it was not open to the appellant to have his case finally decided by the Tribunal. Held, that the order passed by the High court on January 28. 1954, was a final order and could not be challenged under article 227 of the Consti tution. The order passed in the present case was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor of removal from service within article 311. Held further, that as the High Courts have no power to decide a preliminary enquiry into the conduct of a judicial officer, it is not necessary for them to go into the question finally in view of the decision of this Court in State of Madras vs K. C. P. Sarathy, ; , referred to. The fact that under the proviso to r. 4 of the Madras Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1953 a Government servant is entitled to submit his case for enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e). If he has any doubt as to whether the charge was proved or not, he may make an application to the Government for a direction that the case be referred to a Tribunal. The Government may, if it thinks fit, direct that the matter be referred by the tribunal to the Tribunal and in such a case the Government may refer the same to the tribunal.

The appellant was a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, a private limited company with its registered office in Bombay. The share capital of the company consisted of Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 1,00,000 respectively. The Income tax Officer levied tax on the dividend so deemed to be distributed under section 24B of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the dividends so deemed by the Income tax officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment but the High Court in reference held that the dividend was not taxable as income from the estate of the shareholder in the hands of his legal representative when the order was made and published in the Official Gazette. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even if after the expiry of the year of account receipts which if the person earning had not died would have been treated as his income, ceased to be liable to assessment as income of the deceased, they could still be taxed as his Income tax and that in view of section 24 B of the Act, the claim of the Income Tax Officer to make an assessment under section 23(4) must fail. HELD: (i) The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) of the I.T. Act, 1961, means a person by whom income tax is payable and not a person on whose estate income tax was payable. [601 B] (ii) The word "assessee ' in section 24A of the 1922 Act has been used in the sense of a person who is liable to pay tax under this Act if he had not received any notice of assessment or of the assessment made by him and the tax due from him. The expression 'assessee ' is defined in section 3(2)(a) of that Act as meaning a person, by whom the income tax has been paid, and includes a person whose income tax had been paid by him. [501 C D] (iii) Section 24B provides for assessment of assessable incomes and income received by a legal representative of a deceased person in the year in which such person died and no tax could be levied under section 25B on the shareholders. The word 'assessee" is defined to mean a person as a person against whom any proceeding and this includes an individual who has been assessed to tax under the Act. [500 C D]. (iv) Section 2(1)(a), which defines "assessee", in terms, means an individual or association of persons with respect to whom income is chargeable under the Indian Incometax Act, and does not include a person for whose benefit income tax or any other sum was payable by him under this section. [600 C D; 600 A] (v) The definition of "assessee " in section 4(2), as substituted by the Indian Finance Act, 1950, with effect from April 1, 1952, means any person by which income tax and any other sums were paid to a legal representatives of a Hindu undivided family or a company. [599 F G] (vi) Section 3(1) of this Act provides that where a person dies his executor, administrator or other legal representative shall be liable for the payment of tax in respect of such death if he has not died before the expiry thereof. The definition is wide enough to include a Hindu Undivided Family.

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a Ruler of that State and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The appellant contended that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute ownership of the village specified in Schedule A of the petition under article 366(22) of the constitution, and therefore, a Ruler could not be said to have any interest in the villages mentioned in Schedules B and C of his Petition under articles 227 and 227. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the appellant was an ex Ruler and as he was also a maufidar he fell within the definition of the word 'proprietor ' in article 366 (22) Of the Constitution and therefore a Ruler had no interest in him. The expression "maufidar" in section 2(m) of Act No. 1 of 1951, means a person who by or under the provisions contained in the wajib ul arz, is recognised as the successor of such Ruler. The word 'maufididar ' in section 3(m), in its ordinary sense, includes a person whose rights are conferred on him by the Act and therefore the appellant could not claim any right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages. The definition of "proprietor" in article 31(22 ) of the Indian Constitution does not make him a Ruler for purposes other than the Constitution; he is only a person having rights to recover rents or revenue, and as such he falls within the expression 'proprietor" as defined in article 363 of the Consti tution.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India. The order of transfer was challenged in a writ petition before the High Court which quashed the order of his transfer on the following reasoning: "In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the opinion that the power of transfer is not an absolute one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued by the Government. The said guidelines are applicable to the case of the respondent. Hence, the order impugned is set aside. However, it does not preclude the respondent from claiming such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. " The High Court quashed the transfer on two grounds: (i) that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer; and (ii) that there is no violation of any statutory provisions, and directed the transfer to anywhere in India. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines issued by Government ofIndia are not followed, with which finding we shall deal later.
