[440G] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; , referred to. 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by transfer. [ 430C D] Bank Of India vs Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of lndia, ; and Bank ofIndia vs Jagjit Kaur, ; ; , relied upon. The guidelines do not require the two spouses to be posted at different places. [ 431D] 2.2 In the case in hand, the respondent has been posted at one pi" as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a postings as ofright if the Departmental authorities donot consider it prudent. The only thing required is that the departmental authority should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouse to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of Jawahar. The Trial Court convicted them under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34, I P.C., and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under section 302 readwith section 109 I.p.C.. The High court also confirmed the convictions of A1to A3 under Section 325 read with Sections 109 I PC. The appellants filed appeals before this Court against their acquittal by the High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction and sentences of the accused under Section 323 read with 34, IPC are set aside. [1033C] 2.1 The intention of the appellant was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of section 325 readwith 34,I.P.,C. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of Jawahar, and the facts and circumstances of this case the accused were acquitted by the Trial Court. [1133D] 2(a) The intention to cause death and as a result of which he died on the same day was proved beyond doubt. [1233E F] 3.2 In the instant case, the offence was committed within the limits of Section 325, I PC read with Sec tion 34, and not under Section 34 I. P. C. The intention was to caused grievous hurt, as such, the accused came within the ambit of section 326 read with sections 109 IPC. Thirtone external in Juries were also found on dead body. [1333F G] 3(a). The intention is to cause simple hurt and not as such. [1434G H] 3 (b) The conviction under Section 324 read with s.109, IP. C., read with sec tion 34 I PC was set aside by the trial Court. The sentence of imprisonment already undergone by the appellants is set aside and the fine imposed on them is paid to the father/mother of deceased Jawahar. [1534H] 3.(c) The High Courts while granting special leave to appeal are directed to consider whether the accused persons could have intended to cause such injuries as would be sufficient, in the ordinary course of nature to cause murder, and if so, to what extent. [1634F G; 1635A] 4(a)(i). The appellants shall deposit Rs. 7,000 each before the Trial court within four months from today. In case of non payment of fine the appellants shall undergo rigorous Imprisonment for five year.

The appellant Bank was constituted by the Indian Parliament under which the appellant bank was constituted. The Banking Companies Act, 1949 was enacted to provide for the establishment of a special Indian law relating to banking business and for matters connected therewith. Section 4(e) of the Act provides that the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare any area to be a 'special Indian Law ' or "any other law" for the time being in force. The appellant Bank filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said provision. The High Court held that the words `Special Indian law ' were placed after the words 'an Act of Parliament of India ' and before the words "by or under" and that the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1969 was not applicable to it. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that even assuming that the expression `Special I Indian law" meant a law enacted by the British Parliament for India, the provision of section 4(a) of that Act would apply to a corporation which is the creature of a Special Indian Law and not by the law itself in order to come within the purview of section 2(f) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words `any special Indian Law" are placed after words `in pursuance of ' in section 4 (e) and by using the expression 'in pursuance Of ' in Section 4 (a) the Legislature has not meant that the corporation in question should be formed by a third party in pursuance of the law and not on the law alone in orderto come within its purview. [969C] 1.2 The words "any special or Indian law", are placed before the legislature for the purpose of Entry 54 of List I of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. It is not necessary that the word `special Indian law should be interpreted in a restricted sense so as to include a law made by Parliament of the country. [991D] Krishna Murthy vs State of Andhra Pradesh, ; , referred to. 1.3 The words 'any special IIII law ' refer and relate to a law which is made by the India Legislature and not to the Indian Law. It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by or under a special I Indian Law, for an ordinance is as much a law as an enactment of Parliament or Legislature. At this stage it may be stated that in Krishna Murthy 's case, it has been observed by the Division Bench that the language `any other Act ' refers and relates to a statute made by Indian Legislature and cannot be held to have become void as making invidious discrimination in favour of the British Corporation offending against the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution and, accordingly, void. [999F G] Krishna Rao vs State Of Andhra Pradesh & Ors., ; , relied on. Krishna Murthy & Anr. vs State o/f Orissa, ; ; Krishna Murthy and Anr. V. State of Karnataka, ; and Krishna Murthy (supra) distinguished.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of sugar in Punjab, challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that it was violative of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the impugned notifications were invalid and invalid as they contravened articles 14 and 19(2) of Part IV of the constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The impugned notification is beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and clause 5 of the Order does not authorise the Central Govern ment to fix prices at which they were in the week preceding June 27 1958 or in the last week of May. [131 E] (ii) The object of the notification was to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of general public so that the consumer may be able to sell their products at a loss. The object is to ensure fair prices for the consumer; but if fair prices are fixed for other States, the price do not exceed the cost of production. [132 F G] (iii) The notification merely fixes ex factory prices and is bad as it does not follow from this that this object can only be achieved if retail prices are determined by fixing the ex factory price. It does not mean that the Government should go on also to fix the wholesale or retail prices. The fact that the prices fixed by the Government by the impugned Notification are higher than the cost at which the factories were compelled to sell them at a profit is no reason why the Government must go on again to fix price of sugar at what they were either in the month before June 27, 1958 or even in the next week of April. [133 G H] (iv) The contention that there was discrimination between the petitioners and the respondents is not correct. The impugned notifications are therefore invalid.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948. Its factory consisted of four units, namely, Calcutta, Calcutta and Calcutta. The company had its head office at Calcutta, and its employees were employed by it as clerks and clerks. In 1951, the company made an application to the Tribunal for a reference of the dispute under section 19(6) of the , for adjudication of the workmen on the ground that the company was not a 'Tribunal ' within the meaning of section 2(7) of The . The Tribunal held that the working class cost of living index stood at Rs. 3,000 and that the appellant was entitled to 75 per cent. of the increase in the cost of food Index. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the award made by the Tribunal was bad in law and without jurisdiction; it was not open to the company to raise a dispute under s.19(6). The Tribunal had no power to make an award on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal, for ascertaining the working classes cost of the living index. The Tribunal wrongly relied upon the information furnished by the appellant and held that it was binding between the parties and therefore the reference was bad. The question whether the working Class cost of live index stood on the date of "the agreement" or not was a question of fact which could be decided in an application under section 7(6), and therefore, the Tribunal rightly relied upon it. The award made in the present case was binding on the parties as the Tribunal had already determined the working standard for living index in 1957.

The appellant was the Matadhipati of Sri Gavi Mutt. He was appointed under the scheme made no difference to the actual administration of the Mutt and its properties. The management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under a scheme made in 1952, could not be challenged on the ground that some of its provisions contravened the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens of this country under article 19(1)(f). Held, that the scheme was valid and the appellant was entitled to seek the protection of article 19. The scheme was framed as early as 1939 under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act which was valid when it was enacted. The Scheme was not a new one. The appellant 's writ petition should be entertained because he had a definite adequate alternative remedy under the latter Act, but this Court would not ordinarily interfere with the order passed by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under article 226. The result is that the appeal must fail. The provisions of section 103(d) of the Madras Act which were enacted in 1952 and which were inconsistent with the relevant sections of the latter act, under which they were purported to have been issued, could be challenged as invalid on the grounds that it contravened the Mathadhipathi 's fundamental rights under article 14. The impugned order did not come within the purview of section 104(d). The scheme had been framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early in 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the actual management of the properties, it was open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme on the basis that it contravenes his fundamental right under article 31 (1) and as such, invalid.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He continued to serve the school with repeated breaks of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12, 1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [904C] 1.2 The High Courts erred in not granting relief to the appellants on the basis of the validation Act. [9905D] 1:3. The State Government is entitled to grant regularisation as a Hindi Teacher with effect form July 12 1982. [999F] 1.:4. The Government has been given an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to the continuance of the appellant as Hindi Teachers in the school under orders of the managing committee. The management of the school is still utilising his services though there is no approval by the educational authorities for the period subsequent to 1986. [995F] 2.1 In view of the fact that the teachers had been appointed regularly, they would have been entitled to the benefits of summer vacation along with the salary and allowances payable in respect of that period and to all other privileges such as casual leave, medical leave etc. available to all the Government servants. The policy of `ad hocism ' followed by the state government for a long period has led to the breach of Article 14 of the constitution. [996F] 3.2 In view thereof, the High Court erred in allowing the prayer for regularisation and directing the respondents to treat the appellant in a substantive vacancy because of the validating Act. The order of the High court is set aside.

The appellant was a member of a Panchayat Samiti and the Chairman, Panchayat Samiti, was elected to the office of Chairman. The respondent was defeated by respondent No. 1 who was defeated on the ground that he had not paid any travelling allowance for journeys performed for any official work outside the district. The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of respondent No 1 as a member and also challenged the election on the grounds (1) that the payment of mileage allowance to a Chairman, Vice Chairman or Member was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, non official members (Payment of Travelling Allowance) Rules 1965, which were applicable to the appellant; (2) that there was no evidence from which an inference may be drawn that the amount received by the Chairman for travelling allowance or daily allowance is in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding (1 ) that the allowances paid under rules 3 to7 were not convert the office as a consolidated amount in lieu of the travelling allowance, and (2 ) that no evidence was advanced to show that out of the said amount received as daily allowance the Chairman would have made a saying, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office an office of profit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1)(a) The High court was right in holding that the allowance paid under Rules 3 and 7 did not convert it into an office or profit.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the partition wall in the hall did not constitute material alteration and that the tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin sheds were constructed by him with the permission of the landlord. The trial Court decreed the suit for ejectment against the appel lant holding that the construction was material alteration, and on that finding the trial court decreed the eviction. In second appeal the High Court held that the disputed constructions which the High court had found to be 'material alteration ' were temporary in nature and they could not be removed without causing any damage to the accommodation. The appellant filed a revision petition before the High Curt which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether the constructions have been made with the consented of the land lord and if so, whether those constructions are of such nature and character as to materially alter the accommodation or not. [975C] 1.2 The High Court was in error in interfering with the findings recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material alteration. The essential element which needs consideration is as to whether the construction has been made without any permission of landlord. [ 976D E] 1:3. The High court committed error in not interfering with findings of fact recorded by both the Courts below on the questions whether the structures have been constructed with the approval of the District Magistrate but if so whether those structures are of a substantial nature which make material alterations in the accommodation, and if not, whether these constructions are temporary or temporary. [999E F] 1 4. The question as to what material alteration means is as much as that of the construction as that which makes material alterations. If the tenant, without the landlords permission made or permitted to make construction which in the opinion of the court has materially altered the accommodation and is likely substantially to diminish its value, the landlord is free to file suit for tenant 's eviction without obtaining permission of his landlord. It is the unauthorised constructions which require a ground for eviction. [991G H] 1 5. The nature of constructions whether they are permanent or temporary in character does not affect the question as regards whether the structure materially alteres the accommodation nor does it affect the construction of the building. The mere fact that a construc tion is permanent or Temporary in nature does not effect the question of material alteration or even if the construction is temporary, but the constructions complained of are temporary in form and condition of the tenanted premises. [993A B] 1 6. The requirement of the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is that the tenant must have made a written statement of his intention to make such statement as he may wish to make or permit him to make it. If he does so, he must give notice to the landlord before making the statement. [964C D] 7. The word 'materially altered ' in section 106(1) is not used in any sense of a term which has been defined in the Act. It means something more than mere alteration or addition. It includes all material alterations, additions and alterations made by the tenant in the building but does not include any alteration or additions made by him during the period of his tenancy. [965C D; 976A B]. 8. The expression 'material alterations ' is used in section 114(1)(b) of the Act to mean all such alterations which are necessary for the purpose of effecting a material alteration in the premises.

The appellant company had filed a suit for setting aside an ex parte decree on 29 7 1975 against the respondent firm. The respondent firm was served with a notice of motion in the suit and was directed to appear at Indore on 25 3 1975. The appellant company did not appear before the Court on 25 4 1975 when the ex parte order was passed. The Trial Court held that summons in the case was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 30 7 1975 only when the respondent filed a petition under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code for setting it aside. The High Court allowed the revision petition holding that since the summons in question was not properly served on it, the summons could not be set aside. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the summons was duly served and the respondent had knowledge of the decree. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [1032C] 1.2 In order to attract the provisions of Order 9, Rule 13 C.P.C., the word 'Principal Officer ' must have been used by the respondent in his own name or in the name of his wife or son or daughter or other legal representative. The word 'principal officer ' has got to be understood in the background of the provisions contained in the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons. [1132D] 1:3.1 In order that a summons may be served by post, unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on the Company itself. The meaning of clause (b) has got no application in this case. [1233E F] 2.2 The word "Principal officer" in Clause (a), has got reference to an office assistant working in the company. It is not the case of the respondent that the company had any knowledge of its ex parte judgment, even otherwise before 29 7 1976. [1332F G] 3.3 In order for attracting the provisions under Order IX Rule 13, C. P.C. it has been provided that where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer after using all due and reasonable diligence cannot find the defendant and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix a copy of the summon on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain. [1432G H] 4.1 It is well settled that the words "principal officer" have got to he understood in their context as to what is meant by service of summon on a person who is described as an office Assistant, on 17 3 1975 at about 12.40 P.M. and not in his name or his name. [1532G] 4(a) The word `Principal Officer has got significance as the Trial Court has pointed out that the Company had no knowledge of it. [1633A B] 4.(b) The words 'Principal officer ' in clause 2(a), have got reference only to an Office Assistant, and not to any other office.

The respondent No. 1, a tenant of the appellant, filed a suit against the respondents for eviction on the ground that he had committed breach of the peace and that the Magistrate passed an order under section 145(5) Cr. P.C., directing the appellant to file his written statement and thereafter after hearing the parties, passed an final order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant as in possession of the land in dispute. The respondents filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed by the High court holding that the final order of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of peace existed at the time the order was passed. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the final orders were vitiated in view of the fact that there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final report that there had been an apprehension of breach of a peace, and (2) the High Courts erred in holding that a breach of such peace existed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of a Magistrate is limited to the extent to which he has jurisdiction to take proceedings under section145 Cr. It is not necessary that at the stage of passing the final Order the apprehension of the breach of an peace should continue or exist. [941C] 2. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach and once he records his satisfaction in the preliminary order, the High Page No. 96 of 1973 Court has no jurisdiction to go into sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the magistrate is based. [952C] 3.

The appellant was a nonresidents of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The income tax authorities treated them as "income from business" and assessed them to income tax under section 4(1) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was not liable to pay tax on the profits of its business but only those profits which were apportioned between the nonresident and non resident persons. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The finding of the Tribunal was final and a finding thereon was open to review under section 66(1). [710 B] (ii)The question whether the assessee had sold its goods to the ultimate purchasers or received the prices, there can be no question that it was not a case of pure (1) (2)710 C.R. 1171. (3)I.L.R., , referred to. (iii)The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal is final and conclusive. [711 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. ; , followed. (iv)The Tribunal was right in holding that the question was governed by section 14(2)(c), and that the profits had accrued to it both in the business and in the legal sense and that liability to tax had arisen. [611 D E] Commissioner, Bombay City vs Ahmed Bhai Umarbhai & Co., ; , referred. (v)The High Court was right on the question whether section 14 of the Income tax statutes could be said to apply only to non residents and not to non residents. The decision in Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay, vs Ahmed Haji Umarbhai, and Commissioner of income tax, Excess Profits Pax vs section Sen(2), relied on.

The assessee was a company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. The assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to him by the General Manager Shri JP Vaish in excess of tiffs amount. The Income Tax Officer determined a sum of Rs, 70,465 paid as commission to the General manager. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish and therefore the commission paid by him was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that Rs. 70465 paid to the general manager was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the business and therefore it could not be said that the amount was laid out wholly and exclusively for carrying on a business. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Tribunal was right in taking the view that the rate of commission paid was reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assessee.[557B] (2) The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid up or expended partly or exclusively or for the use of a particular business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(X.v) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 is not really related to the partners of the firm and the commission on profits clause was inserted to create the interest of the General Manger. [557C D] (3) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the appellant the entire amount of Rs 75465 paid by the general Manager Shri P. Vaish, was an allowance for half of his income.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. He was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000 as salary for the period January, 1943 to March 31, 1957. The company filed an application before the Patna High Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order dated February 26, 1957, and for a direction that the appellant should be heard before the disposal of the case. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for a writ or order under article 227 of the constitution. Held, that the High Court was right in dismissing the application on the ground that it was not competent to the Tribunal to entertain an application for the issue of a writ of certiorari and quash the Tribunal's order. The appellant was not entitled to any relief as he had not been heard by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was therefore justified in refusing to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 's case and to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter. The appeal must be dismissed. The question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken up by the Union of which the workman is a member, as a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the Industrial Disputes Act, is not a matter for the Tribunal, to decide. The scheme of the Industrial Dispute Act does appear to contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act when the same had not already been taken up.

The appellants were tenants in a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the respondents. The trial court decreed their suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the surviving appellants could not be ejected from the premises on the ground common to all of them. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the deceased appellants were competent to continue the appeal in view of O.XLI, r. 33 and not of r. 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held: (i) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellant when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated as the court could have passed a decree in favour of all or any of the respondents or parties. (ii) The provisions of OXLI r. 2 of the code, which provide for the abatement of suits and appeals, were not intended to apply to an appeal which was not a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent of the High Courts. The appeal could not therefore be taken to be an appeal filed by some of the plaintiffs against the whole decree in pursuance of O XLI r, 33. (iii) The appeal by Kedar Nath was not competent in view Of OXL r. 32 and not OXIS r. 34. [556 G H] (iv) The suit for eviction was decreed against all the appellants on the basis that Kedar Nath had a common right and interest in letting out the premises to defendant No. 2. The decree was not passed in pursuance to OXlLI, R. 33. Rule 4 of 0 XLI, r, 3 which provides for abatement of appeals, provided that where there are more plaintiffs or defendants than one in a civil suit and the decree appealed from proceeds on any ground common with all the plaintiffs or respondents, but does not exceed the amount of the decree, the decree may be set aside or varied. The rule is not applicable to an application under O. XLI, R., 3 of 0. XLI. r. 4 when the decree proceeds on a ground common in all the defendants or defendants, if all the plaintiff or defendants appeal from the decree and any of them dies and the appeal abates so far as he is concerned under OXIL, r 33 is of no greater help to the appellant because his suit was not one for the same cause of action.

The appellant landlord sought to break through these defences by alleging that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The Rent Controller held that the tenancy was determined by forfeiture and not in terms of section 111 (g). The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that the notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was not based upon any principle of justice, equity or good conscience and that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The statutory law as it now stands, however, is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111, (g) or (h), does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the lease by giving notice in that behalf. [920C D] 1.1 The statutory provision is that a written notice must be given to the lessee before the expiry of the period of lease. If the lessee does not choose to give any notice as required by section 108(g), he cannot claim that the lessor has no right to terminate the tenancy. [990D E] 1:2. The provisions of sections 106 and 111 of the TP Act are intended to regulate the matter as could be held to be consistent with the rules of equity, justice and good conscience. [991E F] 1I2. In the instant case, the High Court was directly concerned with the question whether the notice dated 30th May, 1975 had to be treated as a rule of justice. The High Court held that it did not, in terms, apply to the lease and, therefore, the principles of justice equity and good faith were not applicable. [961F G] 1l3. In view of this only such of the principles embodied in section 112(g)(h) of TP Act would regulate the matters as could have been held to have been consistent with rules of Equity, justice or good faith. [9992A B] 1i4. The Court cannot be said to have laid down any principle which is not based on any principle or rule of equity. It is a fitting finale to this part of the argument that in the High Courts arguments proceeded on the footing that the Supreme Court has ruled in Namdeo Lokman Lodhi vs Narmada Bai & Ors., ; , that the breach of a condition providing for re entry and notice in writing to the lessor of an intention to determine lease, would be tantamount to an act evidencing the intention of the lessor to avail himself of the forfeiture clause and sufficient to satisfy the justice, decree or conscience. The conclusion is irresistible that the landlord 's termination of the lease in this case was good even without a written statement. [993F G; 920A B]. 1:3. The question whether a written reply was based upon an principle of law or not could be decided by the Court on the basis of evidence adduced before it. [995B C] 1 I4. In Namdeo (supra) this Court held in Namdeesh Lokman Telna Lodhi vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , and Namdeo vs Narmadabai & Ors. ; , referred to.

The Governor of Assam, by a notification dated June 10 63, 1965, issued under section 3(2) of the Assam Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1964, directed that in the interest of security of the State it was not expedient to give any opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The Governor thereupon made a reference to the High Court under section 10 of the Act for adjudication on the question whether the Governor had the power to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of making representation against the proposed action. The High Court held that the Governor was not competent to give the appellant any opportunity to show cause against his proposed punishment and dismissed him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power conferred on the Governor under section 11(2)(a) of Act No. XIV of 1965 is a judicial power and it cannot be exercised in respect of an administrative or quasi judicial function unless it is shown that there has been failure of justice. [488 B C] (ii) The words "in the interest and for some reason" in article 311(2), do not mean that the Government should have to act judicially but must be satisfied that there was no failure of Justice. [486 E F] (iii) The word "shall" used in section 11 (2)(b) is a mandatory requirement and it has been used in the context of the provisions of the Constitution. It cannot be said that the words "may" have been used without any intention to give an opportunity of show cause. [487 E F; 488 A] (iv) The Governor 's satisfaction under section 12(2). is not a judicial function and it can only be exercised by him in accordance with the rules made under the Act. [489 C D] (v) The expression "shall", in section 10(2A)(b), has to be read as mandatory. It does not mean merely that the word 'may ' has been construed in a sense of the term. If the words are clear and unambiguous, it is difficult to say that they have been so construed as to give them an opportunity to explain their meaning.

The petitioners, who were the members of a Shia community, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification dated 26th February 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board. The High Court held that the notification was not valid and quashed the notification. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Notification dated 26 th February 1944 was not a law validly enacted and therefore, the notification could not be challenged in view of the provisions of article 31(2) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notification dated 7th January 1954 issued under Section 5(i) of 1936 Act is of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of the Shias to perform their religious ceremonies and functions over the plots and structures thereon which had been listed as Shia Wakfs under the Notification No. 5411 (vii) of 1966 dated 15th January, 1954. [1137C D] 2. The Notification dated 7 th January 1954 was issued by the Shia Community in exercise of its statutory powers under section 144 Cr. P.C. and published in the U.P. Gazette on 15th February, 1954, which is now common ground that the mosque on Plot No. 1 to 5 had been registered as Shias wakfs for performing their religious rites and functions. The petitioners and through them the Shiam community of Mohalla Doshipura Varanasi have established their existing customary rights to perform the religious ceremonies, practices and functions including observances, ceremonies and function thereon. [1237C E] 3. The impugned notification dated July 26, 1954 issued by respondent No. 2 in exercise thereof is of a no avail. It is not shown that the petitioners had any right to perform such religious ceremonies or functions on the plots or structures in question. The only thing required for this purpose is to satisfy the requirements of section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1337E F] 4. The object of the impugned notification is to ensure that the religious rites, practices, observances and functions are performed by persons who have no right to do so. It does not affect the rights of any person or members of the family of a Muslim community to perform religious ceremonies in accordance with law. [1437F] 5. The fact remains that there was no adjudication or decision on the petitioners ' rights on merits as a result of the final order passed by this Court in the appeal. [1538G] 6. The question whether the petitioners were entitled to customary rights in respect of their customary rights, to perform any religious ceremonies etc., is a matter which can be determined only after hearing the parties and after giving them an opportunity of being heard. [1637H; 1637A B] 7. The State Government has not given any reason for issuing the notification under section 4(1). It is one of the contentions of the respondents 5 and 6 that before the Allahabad High Court in a writ Petition, the then petitioners had misled the Court into believing that the Notifications issued by them were the Notification under section 6 (1) and published therein. The petition was therefore dismissed. [1737B C] 8.

The assessee, a registered firm carrying on business in manufacturing and selling cotton yarn, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1965 66. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim of set off on the ground that the loss had not been determined as required under section 24(3) of the 1922 Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss and that the claim for set off could not be allowed in accordance with the provisions of Section 24(2B). In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee had filed its return showing the loss and the Income Tax officer did not correctly assess the loss. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The benefit conferred under section24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1) of clause (a) or sub clause (ii) of that sub section, the portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following assessment year and so on. However that no loss shall be carry forward for more than eight years. [1166D] 2. The assessee had a claim for setting off the loss on the basis of loss which had not actually been determined by the Income tax Officer under section 23(3). The High Court was in error in holding that the benefit conferred by section 24 of 1922 was admissible to continue to be available to the assessee. [1066E] 3. The provisions of section 24 (2B) are applicable only where a loss has not been computed in pursuance of a return filed under Section 139. [1267F] 4. The High court was in view of the fact that the appellant had filed his return showing loss and income tax officer did so on the assumption that it was a notional loss. [1366G] 5. The claim for sets off is admissible in respect of short term capital assets, it shall be dealt with in the assessment years commencing on the 1st day of April. [1467H; 1368A] 6. The amount of setoff which has been allowed to be set off under section 72 or sub section(2) of Section 73 or sub sections (1), (2) and (3) shall be set at the end of the assessment period commencing on 1st April. The proviso to this sub section provides that where in respect o the assessment Year 1957 58, the net result of the compa ny under the head "capital gains" is a loss such loss shall not be carried for ward and set off in accordance therewith. [1567G H; 1369A] 7. Section 80 of 1922 is applicable only to cases where the loss has been computed on the first day of March, or any subsequent assessment year which is a part of the accounting year for which the loss was first computed under the Act. [1668B] 8. The provision in section 74(1)(b) and section 80 together. are applicable to cases falling under that category. [1767C] 9. Section 84 provides for computation of loss on a total income of an assessee. It is not necessary that the amount of loss should be computed as required by section 72.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), which is a separate unit under it, namely, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. The respondent was posted on October 13, 1966, in the Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Research & Development, dated October 12.86, and he was posted according tO the exigencies of the Service, in some of the three units, viz., the Defence Scientific and Technical personnel (Gazetted) under it. He joined the Directorate on October 14, 1966. The recruitment was always a separate service. The service conditions of the employees belonging to the different units were the same and their services were inter changeable between the three unit and the employees. The Service Rules governing the three Units had a common Rule which was Rule 12 in DAQAS and DQAS, and Rule 13 in DRDS which reads as follows: "Other conditions of service: (1) The conditions of Service of the members of the Services in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these rules shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect thereof. (2) The condition of service of the member of the services in respect ol the matters not specifically provided for under these Rules shall mutatis mutate between the two units. " The respondent, who was recruited to the defence Science Service, was posted at the Directorate, of Technical development and Production, on October 16, 1966 and sent to different units.

The appellant was the President of a Municipality. He filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Judge on the ground that he had been personally responsible for the distribution of the first pamphlet and as such found him guilty of corrupt practice. The High Court dismissed the petition in limine. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that having rejected the application, it could not be said that there was no fair trial of the petition to the prejudice of the petitioner. HELD: (i) The High court was right in refusing to quash the order. [975 B] (ii) The allegations of corrupt practices were of a serious nature and if the High Court found that the appellant had been guilty of a corrupt practice, it would certainly have gone into the matter and found out why there were two Gazette Publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period of limitation prescribed by section 21(1) of the Act. [ 975 C] (iii) The allegation that the first publication had been made on the 8th June, 1967 and the petition was beyond time and should not have been entertained, is not a serious irregularity which the High court could have expected to take into account while considering the question whether there were sufficient material for the Court to come to the conclusion that the order ought to be quashed on the grounds that there had been no evidence. [977 C] The allegations in the election petition were of serious nature, if not impossible, for the Judge to have come to his own conclusion as to the period or disqualification. [978 E] (iv) The appellant was guilty of trying to arouse religious sentiments of the voters of the particular ward a majority of whom were Muslims. There was also a charge in that pamphlet that he was trading in illicit liquor for which was alleged to have been convicted. In view of the evidence about the distribution and as the election petitioner had turned down the application of the electionpetitioner on the 21st August for issue of summons to them, the High Curt was not right in declining to quash it on the plea that there were no fair trials of the case to the contrary. [980 G H] (v) The evidence about distribution of pamphlet was meagre and not beyond reproach it was not for the High Courts to take a different view in exercising jurisdiction under articles 226 and 227 of the constitution and for ourselves, the Court could not take a more serious view in exercise of jurisdiction under article 227. [981 C D] (vi) The election petition was therefore liable to be dismissed on the sole ground that there is no evidence on which the Judge could have come into the conclusion he did and found that there are two Gazette publications and one of them is a newspaper publication to which the election petitioners were parties.

The petitioner company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, its registered office being at Kanpur in the State of Uttar Pradesh and it is carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State Government imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no power in the legislature to issue the impugned notification under section 3 A on March 31 1956, as that section was itself to come into force only on April 1, 1956. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Validation Act is ultra vires and void; (ii) the words "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of this Act" in section 3 must be held to have been intra vires; (iii) the validation Act is not ultra vires, as it was passed by the legislature after March 31. 1956, and that therefore the Validation act was valid. HELD: (i)(a) The Validation Act was not ultra legislative. [934 B] (b) The words "on the occasion of the sale" have reference to the character of the transaction and not to the point of time at which the duty becomes leviable. The Validation Acts are intra vires, and the validation is not a matter of policy and does not affect the competence of the legislature under entry 54, for the reason that it operates retrospectively. [999 E] (c) The impugned notification was not invalid on the ground that it was ultra vires. The Act was therefore not ultravires. [992 B C] (d) The validation Act was intra vires and the Validation Acts were valid. [1003 G] (ii)(a).

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court affirmed the conviction. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sentence of imprisonment imposed upon him was excessive. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The sentence of death is not excessive. But here, the offender is in his early twenties and signs of repentance are seen. The victim and her parents have forgiven the molester who is a first cousin, says counsel. An affidavit from the father in law of the woman has been filed and, if needed, counsel is ready to produce the victim 's statement that she has forgiven ted the criminal. [702E F] 1.2 The sentence imposed upon the appellant is not unreasonable. The sentence is excessive. It is a matter of discretion. The Court must restore the man. This Court has held in Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed, punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative. [802F G] 1:3. In the instant case, the appellant was in his last twenty and signs and he is a "habitual" victim of a woman an outrage by all men. The offence of murder is not illegal but is punishable with imprisonment for seven years. It may be marginally extenuatory to mention that modern Indian conditions are drifting into societal sentiment on the carnal front promoting proneness to pornos in life, what wit libidinous 'brahmacharis, womanising public men, lascivious dating and mating by unwed students, sex explosion in celluloid and book stalls and corrupt morals reaching a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a new GOSWAMI. [902H; 903A B] Sunil Batra vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to.

The respondent, a limited company dealing in land, owned by the appellant, filed an application before the Arbitrator for payment of compensation under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act. The Arbitrator awarded a sum of Rs.7,37,190 as compensation payable to the assessee. The High Court held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was therefore a trading receipt of the business carried on by the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the amount of compensation received was not a receipt of revenue nature. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High court was right in holding that the sum of compensation paid by the State Government related to acquisition of the land which is the stockin trade of that assessee and therefore, a receipt could be said to have accrued to it as income during the previous year ended March 31, 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1956 57. [397B] The High Courts were right in the view taken by the High Court. [398C D] Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Deputy Land Acquisition Officer & Anr., ; , referred to. (2) The legal position was explained in further detail by the Gujarat High Court in Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, and Topanji Kundanmal v Commissioner of income tax, Ahmedabad, [1962] 1 SCR 676 that where land was taken over by the Government the right of the owner to compensation was an inchoate right until the compensation had been actually determined and had become payable. The legal principle is that there is no liability in praesenti in respect of the additional amount of money claimed by the owner of the property. [399C D, 399B] (3) The HighCourt was right on the facts and circumstances of the case. [400E F] (4) The law is clear that there can be a claim for compensation only when the Court accepted the claim and not when the land was actually taken over. [404F G] (5) There is no legal obligation in praing the amount to pay an additional amount which has accrued or deemed to accrue whether in fact paid or not. The liability to pay the additional amounts cannot be said of merely quantifying the amount as received, and cases where the right to receive payment is admitted and the quantification only of the amount payable is left to be determined in accordance with settled or accepted principles. [445C D; 404A] (6) There was no legal liability in Praesenti to pay additional amounts till it was judicially determined by the final court since the entire question, namely, whether the offer made by the Land acquisition Officer was inadequate and the claimant is entitled to an additional compensation and if yes, at what rate is in flux till the question is set at rest finally. [405D] (7) The liability of the State to pay interest on the amount due under the Land Acquisi tion Act accrued or arose to the appellant when he sought a reference under section18 of the Act or when the award was made by Civil Judge though an appeal was pending against that award. The right to compensation in the nature of compensation would arise or accrue and till then there was no liability, in praed, in respect thereof.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement. The respondent contested the suit and pleaded that he was entitled to possession on one or more of the statutory grounds mentioned in the compromise. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the compromise was legal and valid. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that under the terms of the compromise the defendant had withdrawn all his defence to the application filed by him and submitted to a decree for eviction unconditionally. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree under the law. [882C] 2.1 In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act, the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a ground for passing such a decree in accordance therewith is lawful, as in any other suit so in an eviction suit the court is bound to record the compromise and pass a decree accordingly". [883C D] 2:2.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. The shares were purchased by it in Elphinstone Mills Ltd., Bombay, for a sum of Rs. 12,00,000/ . The shares had been sold to the appellant company for Rs. 11,88,000. The Income tax Officer, however, invoked the provisions of section 23A(1) and levied additional super tax @ Rs. 1/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs, 12,000 under section 23 A(2). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but held that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. On appeal to the Tribunal it was contended that the dividend received by the appellant was a revenue loss and not a capital receipt. The High Court dismissed the reference. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether in a particular year dividend should be declared or not is a matter primarily for the Directors of a company. If the Directors are justified in not declaring dividends in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he may therefore cancel the orders of assessment under section 22A(2), it is not open to the Income Tax Officer to constitute himself as a super director. [864C D] (ii) The word 'income ' has been used in the context of the Companies Act, 1956, which is a well settled rule of interpretation. It is possible to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness by considering the two matters mentioned isolated from other relevant factors. [876E F] (iii) The statute does not say having regard only to losses previously incurred by a company and to the smallness of the profits made in the previous year, that is to say on the total income as reduced by the amounts, if any, referred to in clause (a), clause (b) or clause (c).

The appellant, a displaced person, filed an application under section 12(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 (U.P. Act V of 1954) for setting aside the order of the Civil Judge on the ground that he was not justified in modifying the award by the Civil judge. The Civil Judge held that the Civil Court was not competent to modify the award and set aside the award. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Section 37 of the Act applies only to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act. In the instant case, the Civil Judges were not justified under section 15 of the , in modifying their award merely because he disagreed with the finding. The effect of section 46 and section 47 of the is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations as they are vitally different from those applicable to villages not under consolidation. (ii) Section 18 of the U.P Act V Of 1954 provides for a statutory arbitration and section 37 of that Act provides for appeals. The object of the section is to provide for appeals in respect of certain matters which are dealt with by the Code of Civil Procedure. The provisions of sections 46 and 47 apply to such appeals as they apply to proceedings before the arbitrator in the matter of procedure only. Section 18 does not apply to awards under the U P. Consolidation of holdings Act, 1954. (iii) Section 12(6) of U. P. Act VI of 1954 provides that the decision of the arbitrator under sub section(4), shall be final.

The petitioner was a diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. The respondent corporation issued a resolution on January 21, 1988 to fill up the posts of Assistant Engineers in the Engineering Department. The petitioner challenged the said resolution by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the respondent corporation was not competent to frame rules or regulation in that behalf. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to a exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [702C] 2.1 The rule provides that graduate engineers shall be entitled for such promotions as may be prescribed on the strength of their qualification. It is true that the petitioner wanted such a classification to be made, but it was not a case where the classification was already made which was challenged before the Court. It was not an existing rule or regulation framed under Section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. [750D] 2:2 The promotion which was given to the diploma holder Junior Engineers was in accordance with merit and on seniority is well known and permissible. The Junior Engineers do the same kind of work and bear the same responsibility whatever their qualification, whether they are Degree holders or Diploma holders. Hence, the observation that in the absence of rule or regulations the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions cannot be sustained except by carving out two classes in the same category of junior engineers o the basis merely of their qualifications which is not permissible in law. [751E F] 3:3 The contention that if at all such a discrimination was permissible, it could be done only by carve out two class in the category of Junior Engineers and give them equal quota like Diploma holder Junior Engineer`s out of the 50% quota for promotion a Assistant Engineers is not sustainable.

The petitioner in the writ petition was appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court of India on November 1, 1966. He was confirmed by the Chief Justice of India from time to time. On December 31, 1966 he was transferred to the National Judicial Commission for trial and disposal. The petitioner filed an application before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying that the transfer be quashed. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that it was not maintainable because there had been a change in the personnel of the Chief justice or the Chief Minister, of the State concerned. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Chief Justice is the final authority to decide whether the matter requires to be looked into again a reference should be made to the Chief Justices of India and there can be a fresh look at the matter only if the Chief Judge of India permits such a review of the case. [445C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Chief Judicial Commissioner was not competent to make a fresh reference. The Chief justice of the High Courts is the Chief Secretary of the States concerned. [427D] 1:3. The question whether the ChiefJustice of India should be transferred or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is well settled that the power of transfer of an individual Judge is a very limited one. It cannot be said that the Chief Judges are not experts in the matter of appointment to the Supreme Judicial Service. [545E] 1.:4. The decision of the majority in S.P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of con stitution, the primacy of the position the Chief President of India, and the view that the fixation of Judge strength is not justiciable should be re considered by a larger bench. [506F] 1 :5. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered in the light of the fact that by the Amendment the Chief Sevi sion of India would become the Chairman of the Commission. [504H; 505A] 1 Whether the Chief Election Commissioner should be appointed or not is a question of policy and process it becomes imperative that the role of the institution of the judicial system in the country requires reconsideration. The function of the Court is to see whether there has been any violation of the constitutional mandate. If the recommendation is to emanate di rectly from a source other than that of the chief Justices of the high courts, the Supreme court would be difficult for an appropri ate selection to be made.

The respondent was appointed as a Bank official on 20th December, 1978. He did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Shri U.B. Menon. The respondent filed an application before the Chief Executive Officer for his reinstatement in service with full back wages and continuity of service. The Chief Executive officer rejected the claim of the respondent holding that he had no locus standi to challenge the order of dismissal on the ground that he was estopped from raising such a contention for the first time in a writ petition filed by him more so because he had submitted to the jurisdiction of Shri UB Menon as an official of the bank. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was estopped by his conduct from raising any objection to the continuance or otherwise of the proceedings by the appellant and therefore, null and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order of punishment passed against the respondent is quashed. [199B] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent succeeded in getting the order dated 20th November, 1978 quashed on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the High Court for the second time and, therefore, the High court was in error in directing payment of 50% of the consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned order was bad in law. [200C] 1:3 The respondent succeeded to getting the orders of punishment quashed on the mere technical plea of incompetence.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi, was the owner of a building in which a building was constructed. The respondents applied for sanction to the plan submitted by them under section 336 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957 (Act LXI of 1957) and the same was sanctioned on May 10, 1967. The appellant 's application was rejected by the Municipal Corporation on May 11, 1967, on the ground that the building had been constructed without obtaining a licence from the Delhi Government. The respondent filed an appeal before the Chief Justice of the High Court which dismissed it on May 12, 1967 holding that the appellant had no right to obtain the sanction of the plan and that the proposed user was not in contravention of section 14 of the Development Act. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The word 'building ' has been defined in section 2(2) of the Act as meaning any building or work which is carried on with a view to make up any part of the land or building or to carry out any of the provisions of sub section (2). [167 E] (2) The expression "building" in section 14 means any structure or work constructed for the purpose of making any part or portion of a land or any building. It is not necessary that the word 'construction ' should be given a restricted meaning so as to include construction of a wall, etc. The word "construction" has been used in the context of the Building Act and it cannot be said that the expression "construction of a house" in the Development Acts must mean any structure which is constructed for residential purposes or for carrying out any other purpose. [167 G H] (3) The words "in accordance with the provisions contained in section 3(2)(a) of Delhi Development Authority Act, 1958" are wide enough to include any building which has been constructed for a public purpose. It cannot be contended that there is no violation of either the Master Plan or any provisions of the development Act or of any other law. [168 G H; 169 A] (4) The construction of buildings on the land in question was not made by any part thereof, and the building operation proposed by the respondents as per the plans submitted by the appellants did not contravene any of them. [169 C D] (5) The High Court was right in holding that there would be no violation if the respondents were permitted to use the land, as asked for by them. If the respondents are permitted to user the land as asked by them, it cannot he put to a different use. If either of the plans provide for the particular use of any land or some building in that zone, it can be put to public purpose and not a different user.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary of Industries, Government of India, in charge of the business of manufacturing and selling tobacco products. The appellant No 1 was a Minister of the Industries and was responsible for the conduct of its business. On the day of the incident the appellant was found to have been carrying on the business in tobacco products and was arrested by the police. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, and issued process against the appellant. The prosecution case was that the appellant had entered into a conspiracy with the Government of Andhra Pradesh for the purpose of selling tobacco to the Government. The accused persons were charged with offences under sections 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471, 477A, 477 B, 477 A, 477 C and 477 D of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 120B I.P.C., and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the guilt of the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the evidence of the witnesses in regard to the statement made by the appellant to them and the manner in which the statements came to be made by them were inadmissible, and (2) the fact that the statement was not recorded under section 164 Cr. P.C. was inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the statements of the two witnesses were inadmissible in view of the provisions of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1898. [477 B] (ii) The statement made to the police authorities and given to them by the accused were not recorded by them under the provisions Of section 164. [ 477 C] (iii) The evidence of these two witnesses was not corroborated by any other independent witness. The statements made by these two persons were not admissible in evidence.

The respondent was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971 which led to the prosecution of the appellant along with the Head Constable, Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The trial court dismissed the plaintiff 's suit for declaration that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the judgment of the first appellate court and remanded the case to the trial court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. In the meantime, the Senior Superintendent of Police, Patiala, again dismissed the appellant 's plaintiff on 20.4.1976. The suit was decreed by the trial Court against the plaintiff and the suit was accordingly decreed. The respondent filed a regular second appeal before the High court which was allowed by merely saving the order of dismissal passed against the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question involved in this case should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Courts in the manner it has done. [825F] 1.2 In the instant case, the trial judge had allowed the plaintiff to file additional evidence in regard to the further orders passed against Kahan and his case was distinguishable. [826H; 825A] 2.1 It is well settled that a mistake committed by an authority not in this regard can be corrected by the Court only if it is shown that such error has been committed by the authority. In other words, the mistake committed must be one which is apparent on the face of the record and cannot be said to have been committed in any manner whatsoever. [828D] 2:2 It is not correct to say that the HighCourt should not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the courts below. The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. In this case, there was no law of limitation applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. [827E] 2(a) The question raised in this appeal must not have arisen because of any error committed by a subordinate court not in the exercise of its jurisdiction under section 115 C.P.C., and the High has erred in dismissing the second appeal in limine. [826B] (b) The High Courts should call upon the records to decide the suit finally at motion stage themselves as the cases are an old ones. In case of admission of fresh evidence, theHigh Court shall permit the plaintiff, to file relevant rebutting evidence. [829F G] 2.(c) The finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law or limitation is applicable to suit where an Order is impugned, as being a nullity.

The assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that there was no evidence to show that the transaction involved mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the High Court was right in holding that the sales were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the appellant 's non speculative business High Court held that even if the transactions involved mere sale of delivery orders or sales of goods so as to bring them to charge under section 24 (1) Of the Act, it was not necessary that the transfer in question should be followed up by actual delivery. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "sale" in Explanation 2 to sec. 24(I) of Income Tax Act is not relevant for the purpose of this case. [184D] 2. The words "in any year" in section 24 are wide enough to include a transaction which is otherwise speculative and therefore, the loss suffered by an assessee in those transactions could be setoff against profits made under that provision. [185E F] 3. In order to attract the applicability of Explanation 2 it must be shown that the ultimate purchaser of the P.D.Os had taken actual delivery or delivered the goods sold. The fact that the PDOs were not actually delivered by the seller but only laid down that if there was any actual delivery, the losses would be a loss in a speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set aside only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. [186F G] 4. In the instant case, the assessee had taken delivery notes or not actually deliver the goods to the transferee but only lay down that when there was transfer of the commodity or the scrips had taken place; on the other hand, a transaction where the commodity was not physically delivered by actual deliveries had taken places in a special category for income tax purposes. [187G] 5. The question whether the transactions are mere sales of delivery order or sales thereof is to be considered as speculative transactions. If any transfer of goods is not done by actual Delivery, the transaction would be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. A transaction which was otherwise speculative would not be a speculative one within the ambit of explanation 1 to section 2(1). [187A B] 6. The Explanation to section 30 of the Income Tax is not applicable in this case because the assessee did not actually delivery of goods sold but only placed orders for sale. It is erroneous to think that if any transfer was not done, actual delivery would be an independent and separate transaction. [188B C] 7. The explanation to section 32 of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1962 does not apply to a case where the transactions in question were of such a nature as to constitute a business. [189C D] 8. In view of the fact that there is no actual delivery and delivery of any commodity or scrips has taken place, it cannot be said that the sale was not effected by actual delivered by actually delivery. The assessee had also taken delivery note of the transactions which were not completed by actual delivering them to the transferor but only fixed that if the transaction was not completed, the profit would be the loss in the speculative business against the assessee 's profits and gains under any other head in that year. [190D E] 9. The High Court erred in holding the transactions as mere sales.

The appellant, who was the candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, filed an Election Petition challenging the validity of the election of the respondent. The petition was dismissed by the Election Tribunal on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to entertain it. The High Court held that the Returning Officer had not properly considered the objections raised by the appellant and dismissed the Election Petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 33(1) of the Act requires each candidate to "deliver to the Returning officer a nomination paper completed in the prescribed form and subscribed by him as assenting to the nomination and by two persons referred to in sub section (2) as proposer and seconder. The words "in accordance with the provisions of the . , are to be read together" and not "in the special way prescribed by the Act but in the ordinary way; therefore, it is clear that they have not been " subscribed". [488 B C] (ii) Section 36(1), as amended by Act No. XI of 1953, requires each elector to "at any time" to sign the nomination paper and by a candidate himself if he has not already done so. The word "subscribe" is not defined but it is equally clear that the word "insert" is used in the general clauses Act for the purposes of the , and that where the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by Rules. [488 C D] (iii) Section 35(1)(a) requires each proposer to sign his nomination paper after the candidate has been duly elected. The Returning Officer has not been authorised to refuse any nomination on the grounds of technical defect which is not of a substantial character but he cannot remedy the defect. He must leave it as it is. [489 C D, F] (iv) Section 37(1). provides that when a person who has been nominated by the candidate himself as assented to the nominations, does not accept or reject any nomination paper on the basis of any technical defect, he cannot claim any right to be elected.

The appellants were working as Chemical Workers in the Company. They had been dismissed by the Company on September 7, 1972 and their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service. The Company sent separate communications to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence will be construed to constitute a change in the conditions of service of the appellants during the period of their service.
