On September 20, 1972, the Company sent a separate communication to the Labour Commissioner complaining about the arbitrary termination of their services and asked the appellants to report to them for duty within one month from September 18. The appellants replied that they had not abandoned their service and did not resume work on or after September 20. 1972. On October 2, 1972 the Company wrote to the Works Manager stating that since "by not reporting for duty they had confirmed its presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of Company and had totally abandoned the company 's service" their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the Company and asserting that they did not intend to abandon service. They also stated that they would report for work the moment the strike was called off by their union. On November 2, 1973, the appellants wrote to them that they should report for duties on or about September 20 1972. The company sent a letter to the Company returning the cheques sent by the company and stating that it had not accepted the plea of abandonment of their Service. On December 19, 1973 the Company forwarded the cheques to the Chief Engineer, Works Manager, and the appellants informed them that their letters dated September 21, 1972 had reached them only on September 20 and that they could report for service on or within a month from October 2. The Labour Commissioner, however, did not accept the plea and directed the company to report back the cheques. On August 26, 1973 a letter was addressed by the appellants stating that their letter dated September 7. 1972 had been received by them on September 21. 1972 and that their absence from duty would constitute a new situation in the circumstances of the case. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination of his services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the service of Respondent No. 1 and did they wish to do so, and that the action of the company in removing them from service was illegal and arbitrary. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of services could only be in terms of the contract of service and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the company had no option but to dismiss them from their rolls. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of the services of Respondent Nos. 1 & 2 was illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction. [629B] 1.1 The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the order terminating the services could be said to be illegal and invalid only if it was shown that the workmen concerned had voluntarily relinquished their service or did not voluntarily abandoned their services. [530C] 1:2. The fact that the company did not refuse to accept the offer of the respondent would not make any difference in the position of the management. It is true that the Company did not deny the fact that by its letter dated October 2 the appellants were informed that they do not intend either to abandon or abandonment of the service but had also returned the cheques send to them by the respondent on account of their leave salary gratuity etc. The letter was sent to the company on September 25, 1972.

The appellant was the trustee of a public trust. He had agreed to abandon the execution proceeding and to wait for six months for receiving payment of the mortgage dues from the trustees, abandonment of the execution proceedings was in law equivalent to payment to the decree holder of the amount specified in the proclamation of sale as that for the recovery of which the sale was ordered less any amount which may be due by the trust. The appellant filed a suit against the trustees to enforce the mortgage and claimed that the sale in execution of the decree was void, and on that account a sale in favour of the appellant was not binding on him. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that the expression 'sale ' in section 36(a) includes a sale of the property of a Public trust. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the expression "sale" in section 35(a), means a transfer of property by one person to another, and (ii) that the word "transfer" in the context in which it occurs must mean a sale or transfer of immovable property. HELD: (1) The expression 'transfer ' in Section 36(b) includes an assignment of any interest in immovable property in execution. [462 E] (2) The words "sale of mortgaged property" in Section 35(c) include a sale by one of the modes specified in section 34 of the Act, and the word 'transfer' in section 37(a). [462 F] (3) The word "sale " in section 32(b), means transfer of any immovable property to another person. In the context of which it is used, the expression includes a mortgage by one party to a contract or other instrument. [463 G H] (4) The term 'transfer of property ' in s.36(a)(i) includes sale of immovable properties in execution thereof. [464 A B] (5) The definition of "sale", in section 2(g), includes a transfer by one to another of the whole or any part of the land, and includes a lease of immovable Property. [466 C D] (6) The High Court was right in holding that a judgment delivered by a Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court after due consideration of the points before it was liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the Full Bench.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He was retired from service on June 5, 1935 and he had completed 30 years of qualifying service. The Government of India issued an order dated July 11, 1955 under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950, which laid down that the power to retire a government servant at any time after he has completed 30 year of qualifying serv ice shall be exercised to the extent of public interest. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that Rule 2 (2) was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India, as it had been struck down by this Court in Union of India vs M.P. Sharma, ; and that Rule 2046 having been framed under Article 309 of the constitution and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover ned by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative. The Division Bench dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government of Uttar Pradesh had issued instruc tions dated July 1, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that retirement under Rule 22(2)(a) of Pension Rules should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest; that para 620 of the Railway Pension Manual was discriminatory and violative of Articles 14 & 16 of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The instructions being supplementary to the Rule, according to him, the order of retirement has to be in 'Public Interest ' and as such there is no vice of arbitrariness in the Rule. [899B] 2. Rule 20 46 having been issued under Article 162 of the Consti tution, it was inconsistent with it. The object of Rule 2 of Pension Rule may also be to weed out unsuitable employees after they have attained the age of 55 years. Any Government servant who has completed thirty years of service and has not attained the said age shall be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule.[899C] 3. Rule 2 is ultra vires Article 14 and Article 16 of India. [800D] 4. The Railway Pension Rules were framed under article 309 of Constitution and being an executive instruction issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) of Constitution of lndia, they have no parity with Rule 2. They are not discriminatory. [900E] 5. Rule 22 (2)(b) of pension Rules is ultra legislative and violative Articles 14, 16 and 16. The said rule has no application to the present case.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period ended on 31st March, 1942 to 31st December, 1943. The assessee claimed that the loss in respect of the period 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st May, 1941 to 31th March, 1944 should be allowed a set off in computing the excess profits for that year under section 4(3) of the Act. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that there was no profits pertaining to the said chargeable accounting years from October 1940 to 31 st March, 1943 and as such there could not be any deficiency of profits. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended on behalf of the revenue that the deficiency in profits pertaining the chargeable accounts from 30th May, 1942 onwards should be set off against the excess profit for the year under consideration. The High Court held that the shortfall in profits attributable to the chargeable accounting periods ending March 31st, 1943 to 31.3. 1944 must be set aside and the loss of profits attributable thereto should be computed on that basis. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The deficiency in profit for a year is not an assessment of tax under section 3(2) of Act. [605B] 1.2 In the instant case, the loss was made in any charge able accounting period ending 31. March, 1941 and the deficiency of profit worked out on that account in respect thereof in respect Of the chargeable business ending 31 st May, 1944 must therefore be setoff against those chargeable accounting days ending 31th December, 1942 and April 1, 1943 respectively. [505C] 2.1 In the present case, there was a loss in the year 1940 41 to 31St March, 1945 which consisted of the periods from October 1939 to 31rd March, 1946 and January 1952 to 31nd March, 1948. The excess profits were not assessed to excess profits tax under the third proviso to section 5 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [506D] 2(a) In the absence of any evidence that the assessee carried on business at Raichur in Bombay, the excess amount was not liable to be set credit for the assessment year ending 31St May, 1943, and therefore, the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency. [504E F] (b) The loss in question was made by the assessee in any of the three years ending on 31 st April, 1942, and the shortfall of profit carried forward to be computed during the chargeable assessment period ending March 1, 1944. The loss was not assessed at all for the relevant chargeable accounting year ending 30th March 1944. [500F] (c) The excess amount of profits worked out in respect o the chargeable accountancy period ending 30st March 1944 must also be set apart for computation of the excess income for the purpose of computing the total income under section 7 of the Incometax Act, 1961. [525B C] 2.(d) The shortfall in profit during the year is to be calculated on that principle and after set off carried forward from 31st August, 1943 must be computed by taking into account the loss relating to the business which was the manufacturing activity alone and there were no sales, therefore, no part of the profit realised upon the sale could be apportioned to those chargeable accounts and consequently that it could not he said that there had been any deficiency in the profits. [405C D] 2 (e) The difference between the two amounts is only one and the same thing. The difference is not a matter of fact but is a matter which has to be determined by taking all relevant facts into consideration. [406F G] 3(a).

The petitioner who was a Mechanical Engineering degree holder, was one of the Special Leave Petitioners before this Court. He challenged the judgment and order of the High Court dated 23rd November, 1979 in Writ Petition No. 149 of 1980. The High Court dismissed his writ petitions. In the special leave petition filed by him against the judgment of the Division Bench of the Kerala High Court, it was contended that the KPSC should have been directed to effect selection and prepare separate lists of selected candidates holding Civil and Mechanical Engineering degrees. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list prepared by the Public Service Commission. [775B] 2. The KP SC was not directed to prepare a common list. The Kerala Government and the K PSC accepted the directions given by the learned Single Judge and proceeded to take steps for implementation thereof. But facing difficulties, in giving effect to the directions issued by the High Courts, the State of Kerala faced difficulties in giving effects to the direction given by this Court in its order dated 23th April, 1980. [239C D] 3. The State of Tamil Nadu has been directed not to prepare separate list for Civil and mechanical Engineering degrees but only to secure the result of Civil and Electrical Engineering degree. It is necessary to clarify that the petitioner will also be entitled for a post, if he has exercised his option in terms of this Court 's order and he is high enough in the Common list for claiming the post. The above order as it appears, also refers to a common List though no common list was directed to be prepared or was prepared by KPSSC. [240C D; 241D] 4. The Division Bench was right in dismissing the writ petitions on the ground that the Kerala Government or the K.PSC was not directing preparation of separate lists.

The respondent No. 1, a partnership firm, filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership on the ground that the plaintiff had no interest in the business and that he was a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit was governed by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, and the plaintiff was entitled to get an arbitrary valuation of the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the correct value of the plaint is beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The trial Court has examined the question whether the plaintiff can give an arbitrary and arbitrary valuation in the plaint. It will be open to the trial court to take into consideration the statement in the pleading that the defendant has been ousted from the partnership business. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of a suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [505C D] 1.2 The High Courts in India have consistently confirmed this right of the plaintiff and he has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under valued the claim at the inception of the case, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. [506D E] 1:3 The High courts in India are consistently confirmed that when a plaintiff is required to place the valuation on his claim he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate". It is true that in a suit of accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of his claim at all. [504E F] 1 4. The case of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be correctly decided. The cases of some High Courts who have taken the different view should be held not to be wrongly decided. [ 506F G] 5. In a suit relating to accounts the court is entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation given by the plaintiff, and to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. It is equally open to a Court to take note of the statement made in the pleadings that the relief claimed in the suit is reasonable and arbitrary. [511H] 6. The question whether a particular valuation should be fixed at Rs.150 as has been done in the case before us, is not correct. The plaintiff cannot arbitrarily and deliberately ask for an accurate value which needonly be approximately incorrect. The Court is bound to accept that valuation. [ 511B C] 7. In the instant case, the trial Court had examined the issue it will be at liberty to take a view of the matter. [ 512C D; 513D E F] 8. The suit of some other High Courts where the correct valuation of suit would not be beyond their pecuniary jurisdiction is not maintainable. [ 510B C].

The respondent State Government exempted the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who have set up industries in any of the districts of Madhya Pradesh specified in the annexure to this notification and have commenced production after 1st April, 1981 from pay ment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in columns (2), (3) and (4). The respondent State issued a notification dated 1st May, 1981 exempting the class 'Category ' specified in Column (1), from payment of tax. The respondent challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the exemption granted to the assessee was not retrospective and that the State Government could not have issued such a notification. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that since the exemption was granted in respect of the industries mentioned by it, the exemption would be applicable only to those industries specified in item (1). Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The exemption granted under column (3), is a general exemption and not a general one. [608C] 2. The notification dated 31st May 1981 was issued in exercise of the powers conferred by section 12(1)(i) of Madhya Bharat Sales Tax Act, 1958. It was denied to them on the ground that the industries run by them were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. No. [508C D] 3. The word 'exclusive industries ' in the notification is wide enough to include those industries which are not covered by the notification. [613D] 4. The words 'traditional industry ' in section 12 of the Act and the notification thereunder are clear and unambiguous. The intention of the legislature was to give exemption from the provisions of the Central Sales Tax Acts, and the State Legislature could not be said to have intended that the notifications should be read into the notification itself or even hold it to be ambiguous. [625E] 5. The expression 'tractive industries ' is used in the context of section 12 which includes industries which do not come within the purview of the notification but are covered by rule 4(1) (i). The word "exclusive" has been used in a sense of wide import and it cannot be said that the assesses claim that they are eligible for the exemption under the notification and that they have not opted for the scheme of deferring the payment of sales tax. [708G H] 6.

The petitioners were appointed as Additional District and Sessions Judges in the Delhi Judicial Service on a temporary basis. The appointments were made by the Administrator of Delhi, who was to hold that posts in the service would be filled up by direct recruitment. The petitioners challenged the validity of the appointment orders issued by the Government of India under Rule 5(2) of the Delhi High Court (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1954 on the ground that they were not eligible for promotion as Additional Sessions Judges. The High Court held that the appointments were not made in accordance with the rules and that the petitioners were not entitled to be promoted as Additional Judges. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the appointment of direct recruits to temporary posts in Delhi Judicial service was made by selection and after completion of a minimum of ten years judicial service, the seniority rule contained in the proviso to Rule 7(a) of Rules 1954 could not be applied to such appointments. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners were recruited to temporary post of Additional District & Sessions Judge on the recommendation of the High Court under Rule 4(2). They were appointed to temporary vacancies in accordance therewith and they were confirmed by the High court from amongst the members of Delhi Judicial Services. [395C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners had been appointed regularly that all the promotees were appointed in substantive capacity as Additional district and Sessions Judge. The seniority of direct recruit was determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed. The quota rule contained therein clearly provided for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits. [397F] 2.1 In the matter of seniority, any distinction can be made between direct recruits who are appointed to substantive vacancies in the Service and those appointed to permanent posts of Additional district & Sessions Judges on the basis of selection from amongst members of the State Judicial Service. The rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the Punjab Judicial Service is appointed in a substantive capacity to a temporary post, cannot and should not rank higher than the latter in the list of seniority. [398F G] 2:2 In view of the fact that the rule of 'quota and rota ' has been made applicable to all the members, it would be difficult to hold the appointments as ad hoc appointees on the principle of "quota" or rota". [398H; 399A] 3.1 It is not possible to accept the contention that the seniority of promotees and promotees appointed under Rule 7 (a) is determined according with the dates of their appointment from which they have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the State Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed by selection from the members thereof. [399B] 3:2 The petitioners are not appointed regularly as Additional Deputy District and sessions Judges on a regular basis so much so that persons found not fit for promotion are ignored as in the case of Shri C.D. Sharma, who is directly recruited to the post of Assistant Sessions Judge, cannot be promoted to temporary appointments.

The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant company in respect of the assessment years 1960 61 to 1961 62. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income should be deleted. The High Court held that the income was assessable under section 28(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it stood at the relevant time when the Income tax officer made an order of reassessment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to direct after setting aside the assessment that Debi Parshad represented the Hindu Undivided Family of which he was a member. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The income from the business was liable to be brought to tax on that footing. The income of the assessee was assessed to tax as income of an association of persons and the income from business was assessable in respect thereof. [392C] (2) The Income Tax officer was of the view that the business being carried on by an association, it was not liable to tax in the hands of the family of Debi Parhad. It was therefore competent to set aside this order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. [393D E] Commissioner of Income tax vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , referred to. (3) The power of the appellate Assistant Commissioner to make an assessment under section 27(1) is not and could not be delegated to him by the IncomeTax Officer.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share in the suit property and claimed that he should be paid court fees on the value of Rs. 15,00,000 as the value fixed by the High Court. The trial judge held that the plaint was not properly valued and that the proper court fee to be paid was determined by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act. On appeal the High court set aside the decree passed by the trial judge and directed the appellant to pay court fees at Rs. 5,000 on the basis of the value for the purposes of jurisdiction. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) that the High Courts were in error in directing the appellant not to pay the court fees either under section 7(iv)(b) or under section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act. The question whether the court fee on his memorandum of appeal should be levied under section7(iv) (b) was a matter for determination by the Supreme Court and it could not be reopened at this stage. (ii) that in respect of suits falling under section 6(iv), a departure has been made and liberty has been given to the plaintiff to value his claim for the purpose of court fees. The proper court fees has to be fixed on the plaint as well as on the memorandum of Appeal. In the present case, the appellant sought to pay Court fees on his plaint on the Memorandum of appeal on the ground that he was not entitled to any relief on the memo of appeal. (iii)that the HighCourt was in error when directing the plaintiff 's costs to be borne by the appellant.

The respondent No. 1, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, sought to impugn the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2. Respondent No. 2, who was the owner of a plot of land in the area of the appellant 's factory. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the decision on the ground that the structural nature and basis of its calculation of the extent of these "Refuge areas" were dealt with by Bye law 16.4.8.1, which provided for exemption from the operation of the Zonal Developmental requirements in respect of certain categories of buildings. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the building plans submitted by the respondent No 1 and 2 were not in conformity with bye law 16 4.8, but were in accordance with the provisions of Bye law 17.4 8.1. It also held that the clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged by Byelaw 17.1 was an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the DPCC to satisfy itself that the buildings plans provide for adequate fire safety measures in accordance therewith or in a better measure. The respondent No 2 filed a Writ Petition before the Delhi High Court, challenging the validity of the resolution dated 18th February, Respondent No 1, contending that the construction of refuge areas in each floor was not permissible under Bye law 33.4 and that the approval given by the Chief fire Officer envisaged in Bye law 22.4 was an extra ordinary condition and that it was not a restriction on the powers of the Municipal Corporation to satisfy themselves that the Building plans provided for adequate Fire safety measures were not available with them. The Writ Petition was dismissed, but the High court held that there was no justification for the NDMC to contend that the permission given by it was an extension of fire safety measure and that there could be no question of any violation of bye law. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the requirements of Bye laws 16.1 and 16.2 were not inflexible and that in appropriate cases where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety precautions which in judgment of the Council are considered to provide for the safety in a measure better than those envisaged by the Bye law, the NDMC would not be precluded from accepting them. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The requirement of bye laws 16(4) and 16(5) is an additional conditions and not an limitation on its power of DPCC. [608B] 1.2 The Authority has to consider whether the building plan provides for adequate safety measures or not. If it does, the Authority may refuse to accept them. If the Authority refuses to accept the plans, it would be open to the Authority to reject them. In such a case, where the plan and designs are silent on the question of the sanction, the authority has no power to reject the same. [613C D] 1:3 The Authority is not precluded from admitting them into evidence that they have not complied with the requirements under Bye laws 17.2 and 16 (5) or that the plans were not prepared in accordance thereof. [625D] 1 4.1 In the instant case, the appellants did not raise any objection to the plans on the grounds that either they were not within the permissible limits of the bye law or that they had no locus standi to file their objections. The Authority did not take into consideration the objections raised by the appellants in the writ petitions. [600D] 2.1 It is well settled that the statutory authorities are bound to act fairly and reasonably, and if they do so, they have a right to reject or accept them on the basis of any of the grounds mentioned in Bye laws. The authority has to act judicially and not arbitrarily. In the present case, there was nothing wrong in the procedure adopted by the Authority.

The appellant, who was the owner of a motor business in the State of Bombay, filed a suit for partition of his family properties and for accounts. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the compromise was made after due deliberation and consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties and that the parties were not bound by it. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree and directed the accounts to be taken from March 31, 1946, up to March 31. The appellant filed a second appeal in this Court against the judgment of the High court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the cause of action in the two suits being different, the suit was barred under Order II, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the suit should be dismissed as not maintainable. Held, that the suit being one for partition is a separate and distinct and independent and the cause must be taken to have been different from the cause. The cause of actions in the first suit was the desire and intention of the family to separate from his brothers and to divide all the properties by metes and bounds and to give effect to it. The suit was therefore barred under O. II, r. 2(1) of C.P.C. and the High Courts were right in holding that there was no bar against res judicata or by Order II Rule 2(2) of Code of Criminal Procedure. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, it is not necessary to decide whether a particular suit is barred under 0. II r. 1, C. P.C., and the question whether the cause or action in both the suits is different from one another does not arise for decision in this case.

The appellant was carrying on the business of manufacturing salt. The salt works were carried on in the Salt Works and the salt works carried on by the appellant were also carried on. The appellant 's salt works at Wadala, Bombay, without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the Indian Factories Act, 1948, read with r. 2(k) of the Rules framed thereunder. The respondents were prosecuted for contravention of the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder and the appellant was convicted by the trial court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the salt work carried on under the definition of "factory" in el. (k) Of section 2 of the Factories Act was not a factory within the meaning of the expression " factory ". On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The process of converting sea water into salt is carried on with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal is carried out in the open air and not in building. [605 D] (ii) The definition of the word "factory " in el.(k) does not include any factory within its meaning. The expression " premises" in cl. (p) of section 2 is used to mean buildings which are constructed on a land or land, and it includes all buildings which have been constructed on the land or which may be open to use for purposes other than those mentioned in els. (q) and (r). [606 D] The definition does not make any distinction between premises " and " premises " within the definition. The word " premises ", is used in cl.(k), as meaning a building which is constructed on land or building, and includes all places where it is constructed. The definition makes it clear that the premises must be used for purposes of manufacturing process. [613 E] (iii) The expression 'factory ' in el., (k), means any place where the manufacture of salt is done by the process of treatment and adaptation of sea water to salt. It does not mean a factory which has been constructed or adapted for use as a part of the premises. The words "in connection with" in Cl. (y) of s. 2 are used in the sense of building, but they do not include buildings which may have been erected on land and which may not be used as a place of business. [507 E F] (iv) The word 'factory" is defined in el.. (k). It means any premises including the precincts thereof. The term "factory", in el, (k ) of section 3(1), includes a factory where the process carried on there comes within the purview of the definition and the words "factory". [608 F G] (v) The use of the words 'in connection therewith ' in cl., (y), is not restricted to buildings which do not consist of buildings, but only those which are used as part of a building. The use must be for the purpose of manufacturing processes and adaptation. The process carried out by the respondent was not an activity of manufacture within el. 2 of Cl. 3(i) of that definition. [625 G H] (vi) The words 'factory or its adjuncts ' in cls. (m), (n) and(o) are used to indicate that they refer to buildings, which are not part of any building. They do not refer to the buildings which fall within el.(p) but refer to a factory as a whole. [600 G H; 600 A] (vii) The term 'factory " is defined by cl. 2 in el.; (k); and the expression ' premises ' is used only in relation to buildings. The meaning of these words is that they are not confined to buildings or premises which do no more than constitute a factory.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor of Tailoring in the Department of Public Instructions. He was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangere, as Instructor in the Engineering College at Devanagere. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the department of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his absorption and the High court allowed the writ petition holding that the State Government had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department, of Technical education from another department and he stayed on deputation for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date on which he was initially brought on deputation. The High Court also held that the case of the respondent did not stand on the same footing as that of Narayanaswamy Chetty because the order dated February 19, 1964 was passed in 1951 and that of the State of Mysore. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in granting relief to the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to grant relief to a person who was already on deputation with the Polytechnics and all of them except the respondent, were absorbed permanently in the service of the Department. [261C] (2) In the present case, the HighCourt was fully justified in granting the relief. [262D] (3) The State Government has evolved a rule "that whenever a person is deputed to a department of technical education from one department to another and he stay on in that other department for a period of reasonable long, his absorption will be made in the order in which he initially came on deputation and he will continue on deputation till he attains the age of superannuation.

The petitioner, a foreign parent for the purpose of adoption, filed an application before the court under section 7(1) (a) of the , praying that the child study report as well as the home study report together with other relevant material in order to enable it to decide whether it will be for the welfare of the child to be allowed to be adopted by the foreign parents and if on a consideration of these reports and materials, the court comes to the conclusion that it will not be for any purpose for the purposes of the Act. The Court, however, rejected the application holding that the petitioner was not entitled to be appointed as guardian unless it is satisfied that the application of the foreigner for adopting a child has been sponsored by such social or child welfare agency and that the court had no jurisdiction to appoint a foreigner as guardian of the minor child. In appeal before this Court, on behalf of the petitioner it was contended that (i) the petitioner should be appointed guardian of a child in the courts in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat, (ii) the child education committee should have been constituted by the Government of India for the benefit of the children to be given in inter country adoption; (iii) the court should not make an order for appointment of a foreigner under section 3(1)(a) unless it was satisfied that there should be only one social or Child welfare agency in the foreign country through which an application for adoption of a minor child may be made, and (iv) the Court should not have any jurisdiction to make an interim order for appointing a foreigner. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The court has to examine the application for guardianship made by a foreigner for adoption in accordance with the provisions of the . [804F] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner had taken a child study in Delhi and it was not possible to find placement for the child in any other country through whom an application may be moved. The court should have examined the home Study report as also documents and certificates forwarded by the sponsoring social or children welfare agency to make necessary enquiries. [805F] 2.1 In the present case, an application made by the foreigner must be processed only by a recognised social or a child welfare Agency and none else, any unrecognised institution, Centre or agency which has a child under its care would have to approach a recognised Social or Child Welfare agency if it wants such child tobe given in Inter country adoption. [ 805F G] 2:2 The court is not bound by the principles and norms laid down by this Court in the judgment of this Court. [820G H; 806A] 3.1 It is not necessary that there must be one social, or child Welfare agency which can appoint a person as guardian for the adoption of the boy. If an application is made by any foreigner for appointment as guardian, he may take the child into his custody and make an application to the court so that the Court may examine the child on a further consideration of the report and documents and certificate forwarded by him to the social or the child welfare agencies and making necessary enquiries, it must make its representation to the Court so that, the Court can be able to satisfy itself whether the principles or norms as also the procedure laid down in this judgment have been observed and followed. [821C D] 3:2 In view of the fact that an application under section 8(1), (a), (b) and (c) of section 7 of the is pending before any recognised social, child welfare organization, it would be necessary to appoint the foreigner as a guardian of his child in order that the foreign parent may take care of the juvenile. [822C D; 814F G; 815A] 4.1 Section 3(2) of The Act provides for appointment and conditions of the recognised social and child welfare Agencies.

The appellant company was a registered cooperative society. The Central Government by order dated June 23, 1967 referred for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, the following dispute "Whether the quantum of bonus payable by the appellant to its workmen is 20% of the effective salaries or wages with a further direction to set on a sum of Rs. 1,46,252.00 as bonus payable to the employees of the appellant company at the relevant accounting year 1965 66" The Tribunal held that for the accounting year 1964 66 the quantum was not properly made in accordance with the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure have to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The Tribunal was right in rejecting the claim of the Company. [655B] (2) The award of the Tribunal is set aside on the ground that it has not been accepted by the Tribunal and also on ground which had not been taken notice of by the tribunal. [600C D] (3) The question of calculation of direct tax under the Act was considered for the first time by this Court in Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , and it was held that the National Tribunal was not justified in allowing deduction of certain items from the gross profits for purposes of computing the available and allocable surplus. [700C D]. (4) The appellant company is entitled to depreciation only in the sum of the Rs. 65,764.00 which implies that the method of computation of the available surplus will have to he made after making a calculation of the direct tax without deducting bonus payable for the year 196566.

The appellant was appointed as a Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes in 1954. He was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954, and later as a Joint Commercial Tax Officer in 1957. The appellant was promoted to the post of Deputy Commercial Tax officers in 1954 and thereafter as a Director of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. In 1969 when he was working as a Sales Tax officer it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner that the charges should be dropped. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner, the Government accepted the report of the Full Board and dropped the charges making the following order on 29 11 1974: "The Government is directed to frame charges straightaway as for a major penalty against Thiru D. Ramaswami, Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer in 1954 (i) The Deputy Commissioner shall be posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. " On promotion, as Deputy Commercial Taxes officer in 1957, he was promoted and posted as member of the sales Tax Appellate tribunal in 1969. He also promoted as Joint Commercial Taxes Inspector in 1973. In 1970, the appellant was reverted to the grade of Deputy Commissioner. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the order was not sustainable and quashed the order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 When there is nothing in the conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, the promotion is possible to sustain the order retiring the appellant from service. But when there is anything adverse to the appellant after his promotion, one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. but with nothing else, it is difficult to sustain such order of the Government retiring the appel lant from service.[712C D] 1.2 When there was anything adverse against the appellant, he should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. But if there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appell lant after his promotions, one may harkback to similar and like entries. [713D E] 2.1 The Government has been given an opportunity of being heard before passing orders on the representation of the appellant. It is open to the Government to consider the representation and pass orders thereon. If there was any ambiguity about the effect of the order, it was cleared by the circumstance that within a few months, on May 7, 1975 he was promotion as Joint Commissioner of Sales Tax. [813F G] 2(a) The Government is entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the Appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion. [914G H] (b) When there are anything adverse in the present conduct casting a doubt on its wisdom, the Promotion is possible only hark Back to similar/similar or like remarks in the earlier conduct casting some doubt on such wisdom. [1015H; 1016A B] 2.(c) The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules.

The appellants were the owners of a transport vehicle. The Regional Transport Authority, Andhra Pradesh issued a notification under section 68 D of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, directing that the routes in question shall be nationalised in the first instance and the remaining routes shall be deemed to have been nationalised. The appellants challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The scheme framed by the Corporation under section68 D is not a part of the scheme and the rules made thereunder are to have effect notwithstanding anything in Ch. No doubt, in a State where there is no Regional Transport Authorities at all, the Regional Transport authority may be that which would be comprehended by section 68 F(1) but where as in Andhra Pradesh there is admit tedly a Regional Transport Officer at all [368 E] (ii) The schemes are vitiated by non compliance with the requirements of section 68 C and the Rules made thereunder. [368 G] (iii) The High Courts have to be careful in dealing with the scheme under section 69 C. It is not necessary that the scheme should be approved by the Chief Minister or acted at his behest, but it must be shown that he has been actuated by political motives to hit at his opponents. [370 A B] (iv) The Scheme framed by a Corporation under s 68 D is an Act of Parliament and not of Parliament. It does not require any delegation of power to the State Transport Undertaking. [369 E F] (v) The provisions of section 69C are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. The scheme is vitiated by noncompliance with the requirement of section 63 C. The validity of Rule 5 was one of the matters that was raised for consideration by this Court in Dosa Satyanaraya namurty etc. vs The Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, ; , distinguished. (vi) The Regional transport Authority has to be satisfied that the schemes are formulated by it alone and not that there is any other authority which functions as the Regional transport authority for the purpose of the Art. Such an authority may have been that which will be comprehended in section 68F(1). But where as a result of the conference of the 19th April 1962, and in order to give effect to the wishes of the Chief Secretary or acted on, the State Government might be that who would be described as the area to which the scheme was made by them alone. [367 G H] (vii) The Act does not contain any provision for the delegation of powers to the Regional Authority under section 63(1), but only provides for the procedure laid down in section 69A and section 68D. It has no application to a case where the scheme is proposed to be modified as if the modifications proposed were a separate scheme.

The appellant was a public limited company registered under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The appellant applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order to prove that they had issued the declaration forms duly filled up and signed by the registered dealer to whom the goods were sold by it. The Commercial Tax officer made an order of assessment disallowing the assessee 's claim for exemption under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Bengal Act, but on appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant was not entitled to exemption thereunder. On further appeal the Tribunal held that under section 6(1) of that Act the furnishing of the declaration form by the purchasing dealer was a condition for claiming exemption thereunder and therefore the furnishing was a requirement for claiming the exemption thereunder, and that the assessee had failed to produce such a declaration form. The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the appellant. Held, that section 5 (2)(b) of Act 1 of 1941 did not apply to a dealer who is a public company registered as a dealer under the Act. Section 5(1)(ii), however, does not apply where the declaration Form is furnished by the selling dealer or by such responsible person as may be authorized in writing in this behalf by such dealer that the goods in question are specified in the purchasing dealers ' certificate of registration as being intended for the purposes mentioned therein. The proviso to section 5 of the Act which was similar to section 6 (1) (ii) did not make it subject to a condition that the person claiming exemption shall furnish a declaration Form in the manner prescribed by the dealer who sells the goods.

The petitioners were convicted by the Sessions Judge of Patna in respect of offences under sections 302 and 307 read with section 34 I.P.C. for having committed murder of two persons on the night intervening 26th February, 1974 and 5th March, 1979. The High Court dismissed their revision petitions against the order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the petitioners were not afforded adequate opportunity to defend themselves before the Magistrate; (2) the under trial prisoners who were directed to be released by the Magistrates in pursuance of the proviso to section 167(2), were arbitrarily remanded to judicial custody from time to time by the Magistrate, so that they could satisfy themselves that the requirement of the said proviso was complied with. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. [529C] (b) The High Courts have been vested with the power to issue writs of habeas corpus or certiorari for quashing an order of detention passed against a person who was detained in pursuance thereof on his own personal bond, but such a power is not available to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. [506D E] (c) The petitioners are entitled to have their cases considered by the courts below and they should be given adequate opportunity of being heard before any order of remand is made. [504E F] (d) The provisions of section 167 (2), Cr. P.C., do not provide for a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail and opposing remand provided that no objection is raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for anticipatory bail is made, the Magistrates should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad outlines set out by us in our judgment dated 12th February 1979. [429F G] (e) The power under section 167 Cr.P C. is not a constitutional obligation to be exercised by the High Courts to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy disposal of cases which are pending investigation for more than six months, and also explaining why it has not been possible to dispose of such of those cases as have been pending for morethan six months. [525H] (f) The right under article 21 is an essential ingredient of 'reasonable, fair and just ' procedure guaranteed by Article 21 and it is the constitutional obligation of the State to device a procedure which would ensure expeditious trial to the accused. It is the Constitutional obligation of this Court to device the said procedure as will ensure speedy justice to the victims.

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951. The respondent filed an application under section 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar rejected the application on the ground that the notice was not given within the period of one year as required by sub section (2 A). The appellant then filed a revision petition before the High Court which allowed the same holding that the amendment did not affect notices already given and therefore the landlord could not terminate the tenancy. The High Court held that the amended sub section was applicable to proceedings under the Act and the notice having been given before the Amending Act came into force, the further limitation put on the right of the landlord by subs.(2 A) was on the date of notice. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the provision of section 34(2A) should have been taken into consideration by the Revenue Courts in deciding the application of the tenant under section 30(2 A), and that the revenue courts were wrong in holding that sub section did not apply to notices given before December 31. 1951, when the notice came into operation. HELD : (i) The amendment did affect notices earlier given before March 1952 and therefore it was not necessary for the landlord to carry out his intention. [573 D] (ii)The proviso to sub section(2 B) of section 29 is in two parts: first part provides that where a notice under section 34 (1) is merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the landlords to terminate the lease, the crucial date is not the date on which the right to terminate matures, that is, the date when the tenancy stands terminated. The proviso does not apply in cases where notices have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending act, it is only when the period has expired and the tenancy has terminated that the landlord acquires a vested right to obtain possession of land. [574 D E] (iii)The words "if the landlord bona fide requires the land for any of the purposes specified in sub section 1(2)(A), he shall be entitled to terminate such tenancy by one year 's notice, which was given in this case before the amendment in the present case. The period of notice is the same before and after the amendment. [575 D E; 575 A] (iv)The word "may" used in sub sec.(2A), means "to obtain possession". If the landlord does not require the land, he must be given a reasonable time to do so. In the present ease, the notice under s.34(1) was merely a statement to the landlord that he had terminated the tenancy and no further proceedings could be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof it was open to the landlords not to carry on their intention. The notice having therefore been given after the Amending Ordinance came into effect, the subsequent amendment did nothing more than affect notices previously given. [577 C D] In the instant case, the amendment does not affect the notices already issued. The date of the termination of the tenancy was the date which the landlord had acquired but where there was no period of limitation prescribed by sub sec. (2A). [578 G H] (v)The notice under Sec. 34(1), is merely an declaration to that tenant of his intention to terminate his tenancy and not a mere declaration to terminate it. The effect of the proviso to section 29 (2) is that the crucial dates for the application are not the dates on which notice has actually terminated. [578 C] (vi)The period of the notice is not a date of termination but the date from which the tenancy stood terminated.

The petitioners, who were the sons of Khadim Ali and Fateh Ali, filed a suit against the Custodian of Evacuee Property for declaring their properties evacuee property. The Custodian took possession of them. They also filed an appeal to the Custodian General against the order of January 10, 1952. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. Held, that the Custodian was entitled to declare the entire house evacuee property and deprive the petitioners of their right to the properties. The order of the custodian was without jurisdiction so far as the female petitioners were concerned, and it remained so in spite of the appeal. The orders of January I, 1952, were without jurisdiction. The proceedings before the Custodian were not barred by article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The Act did not affect the petitioners ' rights. The property was evacuee property within the meaning of section 2(2) of that Act and therefore the petitioners could not have vested in the Custodian without due notice to them. The provisions of the Act did apply to the proceedings before it. The petition was therefore dismissed. The appeal was allowed and the order passed by the Custodian, set aside. The properties were evacuee property as defined in section 2 (2) Of the , and they could not be declared evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the . Held, further, that it was open to the petitioners to raise all objections which might have been raised by them before the Deputy Custodian. The words "any person" in section 12(2), of the , are wide enough to include persons who were not declared evacuee and those who were declared evacuee properties.

The assessee company was carrying on the business of manufacturing yarn from raw and waste wool and yarn. The assessee company had two departments (1) for spinning of yarn from the raw and other waste wool, (2) for weaving of yarn and (3) for Spinning of yarn. In the course of its business the assessee company used to sell yarn from imported wool tops. The sales were effected by the assessee Company in the course whereof the assessee had two Departments (1). for spinning and weaving of cotton and yarn from indigenous raw and non waste wool. The sale was effected by a letter dated October 20, 1955. The price paid to the selling agents was Rs. 1,00,000/ . The assessee 's case was that the two amounts mentioned above being in the nature of commission paid to them were not expenses incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits. The Tribunal held that the agreement dated October20, 1955 amounted to a joint venture and therefore the amount paid to it could not be claimed by the appellant company as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that there was no express provision in the agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses which were to be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agents. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the agreements dated October 21, 1955 and October 20. 1955 were not a joint contract but it was clearly established that the parties entered into a joint arrangement for distribution of profits and therefore, the amount received by the agents could not form part of the profits divisible. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The agreement dated November 20, 1956 amounted to an agreement resulting in division of net profits and thus the amount was paid to a company as spelt out from the agreement. [191B] 2.1 In the instant case, the agreement did not amount to a Joint venture but it is clearly pointed out in the judgment that there is a very thin line of distinction between a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits partial or partial. [192F] 2(2) The High Court was right in holding that the payments in question were not legally deductible under section10(2). [193G H] 2 (3)(a) The agreement did amount to an arrangement resulting in a division of assets and therefore it was really a partner ship and had been given the cloak and colour of an agency to conceal the real intent and purpose the commercial venture. [193H; 194A B] 3(b) The finding that the payment in question was not legally deducted under section 2(1)(a), is correct. [194B C] 4(c) The fact that the agents had agreed to pay the amounts in dispute does not take the case of the appellant as a result of any authority cited before the Tribunal or the High court, nor is it stated in the statement of the case that there were no such provisions in the agreements. [195C D] 4 (d) The question whether the payments made by the selling agent to the respondent company are legally deductible from the income partial or otherwise does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [196F] 5(e) The Tribunal was right, on a proper construction of the agreement, that the amounts paid to each of the respondents were not properly deductible under any authority given by the Tribunal. [197G H; 197A B].

The assessee company was carrying on business in cotton yarn. The shares of the company were sold to the shareholders at a price fixed by the Board of Directors. The company paid Rs. 18,950 as dividend and Rs. 9,500 as dividend. The Income Tax Officer treated the dividend as dividend under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the dividend was not taxable under section 3(1) (a) of that Act but only income from dividends. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that Rs. 16,955 was not included in the accumulated profits as on March 31, 1958 and therefore the dividend could be treated as dividend for the purpose of section 2 (6A). The High Court answered the first question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the two sums of Rs. 17,960 were not included within the accumulated profit of the Company and therefore, the second question referred by the Tribunal was not a part of the accumulated income as contemplated by section 2 sub clause (e) and therefore could not be treated to have been included in its accumulated profits. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2 subsection (e), means profits which had accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting years in which the assessee was entitled to specify the questions of law which should be referred. [950 B C] The expression 'accumulation ' in section 3 (1) of this Act means profits as defined in section 4(2)(a). It is not necessary that the words "accusulated profits", must mean profits which have accumulated prior before the accounting Year of which income profits or gains were to be assessed, but on a reference application by the company it is open to the non applicant, in the event of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner of Income Tax, Madras II vs G. The Revenue contends that this question should not have been referred by it to the High Court at the instance of the non assessee because no reference application was made by the appellant.

The plaintiffs claimed to be the owners of certain lands in their possession for a long time. The defendants denied that they had been in possession of the lands for over 200 years under assertion of an adverse title. The trial court held that the suit lands were not Mal lands within the zamindari of Burdwan but had been granted as Lakheraj to their predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement, and that the plaintiffs were entitled to fair rent. On appeal by the defendants the High Court agreed with the District Judge that the presumption of a lost grant could be made in favour of the defendants and that they did so to the knowledge of the plaintiff. The question for decision was whether the presumption was properly raised or not. Held, that the plea of the plaintiffs that they held under a Lakhe Raj grant was not true. The fact that the defendants claimed to have been in exclusive possession of land for over 150 years under a Jana was not proved by them as they were trespassers and that their predecessors had been In possession and enjoyment of the land for a considerable period of time without payment of rent, that they were all trespassers, and therefore, the suit properties formed part of the Mal or assessed to revenue. The plea of adverse possession could be raised only if it was established by evidence that the defendant had been possessing the lands in his possession for over 100 years under an assertion of title without challenge, and not by a mere declaration of title. Held further, that on the facts found, no presumption of lost grant can be made that the possession was referable to a grant by the owner entitled to the land, but that such grant had been lost.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for specific performance of contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas bearing Survey No. 25 situated in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State for a consideration of Rs. 42,000/ . The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy Act and therefore ineligible to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Bombay Tenancy Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Tenancy act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the competent authority under the tenancy Act would alone be barred under section 85A of the Act and that the civil court would have jurisdiction to decide the incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise in a suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were not justified in interfering with the findings of fact arrived at by the trial court, that the Civil Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit for Specific performance of the contract and that since the plaintiff being an agriculturist he was not an agriculturist and, therefore, ineligible to purchased the land, the question of jurisdiction would be barred. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The civil Court would be competent to decide or dealt With any question whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist or not. [590 F] 2.1 In a suit properly constituted and cognizable by the Civil court upon a contest an issue arises which is required to settle decided or dealwith such issues under this Act. If there is an issue which has to be determined, decided and dealt with, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arise in an incidental manner in a civil suit, will be barred and it will have to be referred to the competent authorities under the provisions of the tenancy law. [592 F] 3.2 In the instant case, the Civil Judge had no territorial jurisdiction to settle the question or deal With any other questions which are required to he settled, decide and dealt wit hin the same would be a bar to the jurisdiction under section 84 of the Maharashtra Tenancy Act, 1948. [593 A B] 3:3. The High Court was in error in holding that if an issue arose in a properly constituted civil suit cognizable by a Civil Court having jurisdiction to try the same, it will not have jurisdiction. [591 F G] 4.1 The civil court will be competent under the Bombay Rent Act to settle decide or dispose of any question arising under the Act. [595 C D] 3(a) The expression "any issues which are needed to be settle, decided, dealt with or dealt wit nish by a competent authority" in section 84 is not confined to those questions which arise in the context of the provisions contained in the Tenancy and Act. It is only when there is any dispute between the parties that the Court has jurisdiction to adjudicate or deal wit h the question as to whether the suit is an agricultural land or not, that it would have no jurisdiction. The Civil Court would therefore be competent, if there was an issue pending before a civil court having jurisdiction, to decide and deal with the same. [505 F G; 594 A] 3 (b) The Civil Courts would be incompetent to entertain any suit. If the question is not referred to them under section 86 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it would be no answer to the provisions to say that the issue is an incidental issue in a proper proceeding before a competent civil court. [597 F G].

The two undertakings of the assessee company were taken over by the Government of India under the provisions of the Income tax Act, 1922. The two undertakings were taken into consideration for the purpose of computing the income of the two undertakings. The assessee company was formed by reconstruction of the business already in existence and the business of heavy engineering was carried on before April 1, 1948. The three undertakings were amalgamated with the assessee 's new industrial undertaking. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the two undertaking were not formed by the reconstruction of a new industrial unit and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 15C(2) as rightly so held by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the two units were formed by reconstructing the business earlier in existence differing from the con trary conclusion reached by the Tribunal and (2) the assessee had not been formed by them before April I, 1948, and therefore the assessee could not be said to have been formed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the three units were forming by reconstruction. [776B] 2. The fact that an assessee by establishment of a newly formed industrial undertaking expands his existing business which he undoubtedly does would not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section15C(1) merely because it goes to expand the general business of the assesses on some directions. The facts that the assessee is carrying on the general commercial activity on the basis of which exemption of tax under section 16C may be claimed are not decisive to deny the benefit of section 15 C(2). [775E F] 3. The question whether a new undertaking is formed out of the already existing business or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the two industrial undertakings, about the existence of which there can be no controversy, are distinct and not reconstruction out of their existing business, there must be a new and separate unit which may exist on its own as a viable unit. [765F G] 4. The mere fact that the articles produced by the two Undertakings are used by the Boiler Division of the asses see 's main business does not make them distinct and cannot be said that they are new and different units. Use of the articles by the assessee, is not decisive in denying the benefit to the assessee under section 14C(I) merely on the directions given by the Appellate Tribunal. [764G H] 5. The finding that the units were not forming part of the reconstruction cannot be sustained. [773B C] 6. The decision of the High court is set aside and the question referred to it is answered in favour of the Revenue.

The inamdar was granted a permanent lease of the lands in dispute for the performance of services connected therewith. The inamdars were granted a temporary lease of land for a period of five years and the inamdar continued to be in possession of the land till the date of the grant. The appellants claimed title to the lands under a grant from the inamdars on the footing that the inam lands were personal inams burdened with services connected with the temple and were resumable under section 44 B(2)(a) (i). The trial court held that the inams were personal inam burdened with service connected therewith and that the appellants and their predecessors in title were in enjoyment of the properties under the lease. On appeal, the High Court reversed this finding and held that it was not established that the plaintiffs and their predecessor in title had been in possession adverse to the Government under which the inamholders were entitled to the kudiwaram rights in the lands. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The inamdar is a person who has acquired an interest in the inam land adversely to the inam estate or the melwaram. [557 B] (ii) Section 44 B (2)(d)(i) allows a resumption of the inam where there has been an alienation of the Inam either before or after 1934. The grant of a permanent tenancy and the inams are resumments governed by section 44B(2). But there can be no doubt that section 44 A(2) permits a resumption in respect of the melwariam rights which were granted before 1934. [546 C] (iii) Section 45 B(1)(a)(i), therefore, allows a resumed inam to be resumed under section 46 B(ii) even though the alienations were made before 1934 and the lands were resold by the alienees for over 60 years. [547 D E] (iv) The grant was not in favour of the Government as it was only an resumption of land which was not adverse to Government under whom the inamants held the inam properties. [548 G] (v) Section 46 B (1)(b) permits resumption of inam where the inam is resumed under this section, the Collector or the District Collector, as the case may be, shall by order regrant such inam or part thereof. The lands in question were resilable under the grant from 1934 and they were resoluted under section 45 B (3)(a). [548 D] (vi) Section 47 B(4)(i)(ii) allows resumption of a inam where it has been granted before the 1934, but the inam holder is not a person in enjoyment thereof. [549 E F] (vii) The appellants claim to be permanent alienees of the said lands was rightly rejected by the High court and the High Curt.

The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The appellant Corporation levied a house tax on the basis of gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or any other account whatsoever. The respondent Municipality challenged the levy on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the gross annual rent less 10%. The High Court held that the tax was not liable to be assessed as the basis for levying the house tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Municipal tax is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the same basis for the two subsequent years. [131 E] (ii) The tax levied under the old Act and the rules framed thereunder on the assumption that the gross return was prepared for the year 1952 53 and that the Municipality had been levying tax at the said rate on the annual letting values less 10%, is not saved by sec. 2(c) and therefore the levy of house tax at 7% of the gross yearly letting value is also saved and thirdly, that under sec. 79(1) of the 1954, the Corporation need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year, that it has to prepare a new assessment list only once in every 4 years, that the Corporation therefore can and in fact have adopted the said list for the three years in question and that being so, the list so adopted was in force during the years in issue and has to be accepted under section 76(6) as conclusive evidence of the annual rent payable on such buildings or lands or both. [132 E F] (iii) The liability to pay tax is not a fixed charge but a fixed sum for the purpose of assessment. It is an additional charge created by the statute which is called a tax and is not liable for payment of any tax. The tax is a special duty imposed on the Corporation under the Act, and it is not bound to deduct the 10% of such tax from the gross income. [133 G H] (iv) The word "tax" in section 79(2)(c) means a tax which is levied for a specified official year or house or both and the tax is payable by the occupier of the building. The word 'tax ' has been defined in section 2(e) to mean a tax on land, building or lands, or both, in any official year in which such land, or building or land, is situate. [134 G H; 135 A] (v) The expression "taxes" in the definition of "tax", means a charge levied for the recovery of any sum due to Government under the provisions of the Act. The words "tax on lands and buildings" are not defined in the Act but they have been used in the sense of a tax or tax on lands, buildings or land. [135 C D] (vi) The definition of 'taxes ' in section 3(c), which is an inclusive one, includes a tax levied for any purpose other than agriculture and also includes a charge for the payment of such taxes. The expression 'taxation ' has not been defined either in the Indian Income Tax Act or in the [Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1954].

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 and carried on the business of manufacturing and selling chemicals. The assessee Company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as a going concern, with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. The Deputy Commissioner of Income tax, however, relying upon the Memorandum of Association of the company which allowed the assessee company to manufacture and sell chemicals and on the Directors report held that the assessee Company had not completely ceased to exist, since the assessee was carrying on manufacturing, on behalf of the purchaser, and that the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after the company was wound up. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the respondent company. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no profit other than what had been received from the purchaser and that therefore the sum of Rs. 1,15,259.00 was not liable to tax. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf o the appellant that the transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the same business, but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business and that as the assessee had been carrying on a trading busi ness, the sale was of the entire assets, and therefore liable to be taxed. HELD : (1) The transaction was in the ordinary course of trade and not with a view to trading in chemicals and raw materials. [966 B] (2) The transactions were not in the normal way of business but were part of the realisation of the trading stock and winding up of the assessee. It was not possible to infer that the chemicals and the raw materials were sold in the regular course of business or that the appellant company was carrying out a trading activity, which alone would have attracted tax, if profit resulted. [ 966 C] (3) The question whether there could be said to be a sale in the carrying out of the main business or not is a mixed question of fact and law. It is well settled that where a slump price is paid and no portion is attributable to the stockiii trade, it may not be possible to hold that there is a profit other except what results from appreciation of capital. [948 C] Commissioner of Incometax vs Doughty & Co., ; , referred to. (4) The case was decided on the finding of the special Commissioners, for which there was sufficient material in evidence. It could not therefore be said that there could not have been a profit another than what results in the appreciation of the capital. There was no substance in the contention that the amount received by the respondent Company was only by way of realisation sale and was not part of its realisation.
